title: Boss Refuses Raise Over Pay Hierarchy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you the raise you deserve because it would make your pay higher than mine.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't see how that's a problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me explain it to you this way, Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you make more money than I do...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your compensation would be greater than mine.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's not a reason, you ignorant baboon!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, how about... I must be smarter than you because my income is higher?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I don't have reasons for things, is that called intuition or just common sense?

situation: The Boss tells Alice he can't give her a deserved raise because she would then earn more than he does. When she asks why that matters, he offers only circular explanations that simply restate the problem. Frustrated, Alice insults him, and he ends by wondering aloud whether baseless decisions count as intuition or common sense.
punchline: The Boss's justification is pure circular logic, and he cheerfully admits he has no real reason for his decision, calling it intuition or common sense.
summary: A manager blocks his employee's pay increase with circular reasoning and then casually admits he has no actual rationale.

file: 2012/2012-02-09_benefits_boss_employee_huge equity poistion_questing_start up_wear whatever_work at home.gif
title: Acting Like a Start-Up

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to act more like a start-up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean I can wear whatever I want, work at home, and have a huge equity position in the company?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. I guess I didn't know what that meant.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company needs to act more like a start-up. Dilbert asks whether that means the perks usually associated with start-ups: casual dress, working from home, and a big equity stake. The Boss realizes he had no idea what the phrase actually implied.
punchline: The Boss uses start-up buzzwords without understanding that they imply employee perks and ownership, which he clearly never intended to offer.
summary: A manager's call for start-up behavior collapses once his employee spells out the benefits that would actually come with it.

file: 2012/2012-05-19_interviews_senior year_college_launch start ups_lifelong learning_technology certifictae_relevant to field_uneducated_more experience then boss_education.gif
title: Impressive Candidate Called Uneducated

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I skipped my senior year of college to launch my first of three start-ups.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I believe in lifelong learning. I have every technology certification relevant to my field.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's uneducated.

setting: Office interview room, then the Boss's office
situation: A job candidate sits across a desk from the Boss and describes his entrepreneurial background and his many technology certifications. Afterward, the Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Catbert, the red HR character sitting on a desk, his verdict on the candidate.
punchline: The Boss dismisses a clearly accomplished, continually learning candidate as uneducated simply because he never finished college, showing how management fixates on a degree over actual skills and experience.
summary: A candidate brags about his start-ups and certifications, yet the boss writes him off for lacking a college diploma.

title: Buzzword Nonsense Passes for Technical Expertise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you get the email I texted you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? That doesn't even make sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What the heck is wrong with you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let it go. He slips in and out of understanding basic technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do we have enough room in the cloud to Skype?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because if we don't, we can store some files on the Wi-Fi.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have plenty of space because we upgraded to a cumulonimbus cloud.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Very good. Moving on.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks nonsensical technology questions, mixing up email with texting, clouds with Skype, and storing files on Wi-Fi. Dilbert is annoyed until a coworker explains the Boss only sometimes grasps basic technology. Dilbert then answers with a made-up reply about upgrading to a cumulonimbus cloud, and the Boss happily accepts it.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless about technology that an absurd answer naming a real type of weather cloud satisfies him as a perfectly good technical explanation.
summary: A clueless manager garbles tech terms in a meeting, and an employee shuts him up by spouting meteorological gibberish that he gladly accepts.

title: Coffee Safety Training Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't start. I'm late for the mandatory coffee safety training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better run.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hunh!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Trip

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell what's real anymore.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss not to start because he is late for mandatory coffee safety training, then grabs his coffee mug and says he'd better run. He trips and spills the coffee onto his own face, while the Boss watches from the cubicle entrance.
punchline: Dilbert's rush to attend coffee safety training causes exactly the kind of coffee accident the training is meant to prevent, leaving the Boss unable to tell whether the irony is real.
summary: A man hurrying to a coffee safety class stumbles and douses himself with the very beverage the class is about, to his boss's bewilderment.

file: 2012/2012-11-06_business failures-bankruptcies_honesty_slide toward irrelevance_redesign logo_produce tablet computer_ugly truth_personified.gif
title: The Ugly Truth Visits the Boss

transcript.speaker: Ugly Truth
transcript.text: There's nothing you can do about your company's long slide toward irrelevance.

transcript.speaker: Ugly Truth
transcript.text: But if you redesign your logo and produce a tablet computer that no one buys, at least it will look like you're trying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And who are you?

transcript.speaker: Ugly Truth
transcript.text: I'm the ugly truth. Most people just ignore me.

situation: A scruffy, pig-nosed man in a brown jacket stands in front of the Boss's desk and tells him his company is sliding toward irrelevance and nothing can stop it. He sarcastically suggests a new logo and an unwanted tablet computer so the company at least appears to be trying. When the Boss asks who he is, he introduces himself as the ugly truth.
punchline: The personified Ugly Truth explains that his honest assessments are routinely ignored, which is exactly how failing companies keep making futile gestures like logo redesigns and flop products.
summary: A personified blunt reality delivers unwelcome news to a manager whose declining company can only offer cosmetic fixes.

file: 2012/2012-08-13_sales personnel_cold calling_video chat_sales job_computer_selling on line_skype_technology.gif
title: Random Video Chat Cold Calling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're supposed to be cold calling sales prospects.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I am.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm using a video chat site to randomly meet potential customers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This guy is excited to see me, and that's half of the sales job right there.

situation: The Boss catches Wally drinking coffee at his computer and reminds him he is supposed to be cold calling sales prospects. Wally claims he is doing exactly that by using a random video chat site to meet potential customers. He points at the screen and says the stranger is excited to see him, which he counts as half of a sales job.
punchline: Wally disguises his time-wasting on a random video chat site as sales work, with the sarcastic implication that a stranger's excitement at seeing anyone is all the sales skill he needs.
summary: Wally justifies goofing off on a random webcam chat site by calling it an innovative way to find sales leads.

file: 2012/2012-08-03_managers & supervisors_work all night_inspiring employees_clearly defined roles_business.gif
title: Boss Inspires Then Goes Home

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll finish this project even if we have to work all night!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I just did my job of inspiring you, so I might as well go home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you like our clearly defined roles now?

setting: Conference room at a meeting table with laptops
situation: The Boss rallies Dilbert and Alice with a speech declaring that the team will work all night to finish the project. He then announces that inspiring them was his whole job and leaves for home. He smugly asks how they like their clearly defined roles, while Dilbert and Alice look annoyed.
punchline: The boss treats a rousing speech as his entire contribution, leaving his team to do all the actual overtime while he claims the division of labor is a virtue.
summary: A manager commits his team to an all-night push, then bows out because motivating them was the extent of his duties.

title: Killing Inventor to Protect Secrets

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've created the world's greatest smartphone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. This is so amazing that I'll need to kill you so our competitors never learn how to imitate it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you could give me a huge bonus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, sure. I'll have a guy on a motorcycle attach it to your car.

setting: Dilbert's lab and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert, in a lab coat, proudly announces he has created the world's greatest smartphone. The Boss says it is so amazing that he must kill Dilbert to stop competitors copying it. Dilbert suggests a huge bonus instead, and the Boss agrees to have a guy on a motorcycle attach it to Dilbert's car, implying a car bomb.
punchline: The Boss treats a bonus as an alternative to murder, then casually agrees to a bonus that is actually a bomb planted on Dilbert's car.
summary: An engineer's brilliant invention earns him a death threat from his boss, who twists his request for a reward into a murder plot.

title: Apple's Magic Dust Causes Product Lust

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is the magic dust that Apple puts on all of its consumer products to make you lust after them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wouldn't smell it if I were you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Terrific. Now I feel compelled to get a nose like yours for no rational reason.

situation: Dogbert, dressed as a wizard, shows The Boss a vial of magic dust that supposedly makes people lust after Apple products. He warns the Boss not to smell it, but the Boss sniffs it anyway. The Boss then suddenly craves a nose like Dogbert's.
punchline: The dust makes people desire whatever they sniff, so the Boss, having sniffed Dogbert's vial against advice, now irrationally covets Dogbert's nose, mocking how Apple products inspire irrational desire.
summary: A wizard-costumed dog demonstrates a powder that creates irrational craving, and the gullible boss promptly falls for it and covets the wrong thing entirely.

title: Alice Dodges Dilbert All Day

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Don't talk to me now. I'm trying to think.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One hour later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm on the phone.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm late for a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Three hours later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Come back when I'm not busy.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Four hours later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please, I'm trying to eat my lunch.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Five hours later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay, this is a perfect time. What can I do for you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, so. . .

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think your problem is bad timing.

situation: Dilbert repeatedly tries to talk to Alice over the course of a workday. Each hour she brushes him off with a different excuse: thinking, being on the phone, a meeting, being busy, and eating lunch. When she finally invites him to speak after five hours, her phone rings just as he begins.
punchline: Dilbert wryly observes that Alice's real problem is bad timing, when in truth her constant brush-offs created the situation, and the phone ringing at the exact moment she's available is the final irony.
summary: After a day of being turned away by a coworker with excuse after excuse, a man finally gets his chance only for a ringing phone to cut him off again.

title: Wally's Service Monkey Attends Meeting

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: I'm Wally's service monkey. I'll be fielding any questions directed at Wally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With all due respect, a business meeting is no place for a monkey.

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: With all due respect, that was a stronger argument before I saw your PowerPoint slides.

setting: Conference room during a business meeting
situation: A monkey wearing a coffee mug on its head sits at the conference table beside Wally and announces it will answer any questions meant for Wally. The Boss objects that a business meeting is no place for a monkey. The monkey retorts that the Boss's argument lost its force once it saw his PowerPoint slides.
punchline: The monkey implies the Boss's PowerPoint presentation is so bad that a monkey belongs in the meeting no less than his slides do.
summary: A monkey stands in for Wally at a meeting and answers the Boss's objection by disparaging his presentation slides.

title: Predetermined Conclusion, Worthless College Investment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do a cost analysis for consolidating our data centers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No matter what the data says, make sure your conclusion is that it's a good investment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me why I went to college.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some liar probably convinced you it was a good investment.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to run a cost analysis on consolidating the company's data centers, but insists the conclusion must be that it's a good investment regardless of what the data shows. Dilbert wonders aloud why he bothered going to college, and the Boss replies that someone probably lied to him about college being a good investment.
punchline: The Boss demands a dishonest, predetermined analysis, then cynically compares it to the way college is sold as a good investment, implying that such claims are routinely fabricated.
summary: A manager orders an engineer to rig a data center cost analysis to reach a favorable verdict, then mocks the engineer's education as having been sold on equally false promises.

title: Elbonia's Shrine Looks Like Restroom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How was your meeting in Elbonia?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Awesome!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you know that the most sacred shrine in Elbonia looks exactly like a men's restroom?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Right. So don't blame me for not knowing.

situation: The Boss asks a coworker how his business trip to Elbonia went. The coworker enthusiastically shares a trivia fact that the country's holiest shrine looks just like a men's restroom, then pointedly tells the Boss not to blame him for not knowing it, implying he was caught out by this fact.
punchline: The coworker's cheerful reply and sudden 'don't blame me' reveal he mistook the sacred shrine for a restroom and likely committed a serious cultural offense during the trip.
summary: After a business trip abroad, a man hints at a cultural blunder by explaining that a revered local landmark is easily confused with a public toilet.

title: Social App Reveals Coworker's Stalking Victims

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I wrote a social media app that can tell me how many friends other people have.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Zero friends... 75 acquaintances... one nemesis... nine online stalking victims...

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Are you double-counting my stalking victims? Some of them are also acquaintances.

characters: Man with glasses and green tie
situation: A woman with big curly hair shows off a social media app she wrote that reports how many friends other people have. She points it at a coworker holding a coffee mug, and it announces he has zero friends, 75 acquaintances, one nemesis and nine online stalking victims. He responds by worrying that the app is double-counting his stalking victims.
punchline: Rather than being embarrassed by having no friends and stalking people, the coworker only objects to a statistical double-counting error, showing he is entirely comfortable with his creepy behavior.
summary: A coder's friend-counting app exposes a coworker as friendless and a stalker, and he complains only about the accuracy of the tally.

title: Halloween Costume Prank on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You both assured me that everyone would be wearing a costume to work today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent hours putting together my costume as an angry cat in lederhosen! I hate you both!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Should we tell him?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's funnier if we don't.

situation: Dilbert shows up at work in an elaborate angry-cat-in-lederhosen costume and angrily accuses Alice and Wally of lying that everyone would dress up. In the last panel it is revealed that Alice and Wally are the ones wearing masks, each disguised as the other, and they decline to tell him because it is funnier that way.
punchline: Alice and Wally secretly wore each other's faces as masks, a joke Dilbert hasn't noticed, and they choose to keep him oblivious because it's funnier.
summary: A coworker who dressed up after being promised a costume day is the only one in costume, unaware that his two colleagues are actually wearing swapped faces.

file: 2012/2012-02-12_frustration_tech support_ticket window_evaluated_how helpful_trouble tickets_stubborness_obsticle_financial success_disconnected_new stranger_hating.gif
title: Tech Support Closes Tickets Unhelpfully

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Agent
transcript.text: Hello, this is tech support. May I close your ticket now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... no. You haven't helped me yet. I just called you.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Agent
transcript.text: I'm not evaluated on how helpful I am. I'm evaluated on how many trouble tickets I close.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Agent
transcript.text: Your stubbornness is becoming an obstacle to my financial success.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Agent
transcript.text: By the way, if our call gets disconnected, I count that as a closed ticket.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll make it quick.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Agent
transcript.text: What? What? I can't hear you.

transcript.speaker: Sound Effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Son of a beach ball!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, my goal of hating one new stranger every day is right on track.

setting: Dilbert's home and a tech support call center
situation: Dilbert calls tech support with a problem, but the agent immediately asks to close the ticket without helping. The agent explains he is paid by tickets closed, then fakes a bad connection to hang up on Dilbert and count the ticket as resolved. Dilbert is left fuming at home, with Dogbert on the couch behind him.
punchline: Because the agent is rewarded for closed tickets rather than solved problems, he hangs up on Dilbert, and Dilbert sarcastically notes it helps his daily goal of hating a new stranger.
summary: A support rep paid per closed ticket gets rid of a customer by pretending he can't hear him and hanging up.

title: Who Can't Understand Whom?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone told me your presentation was confusing and unpersuasive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes one person's inability to understand looks like another person's inability to explain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand what you just said.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See?

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert that someone found his presentation confusing and unpersuasive. Dilbert replies that a failure to understand can look like a failure to explain. The Boss responds that he doesn't understand what Dilbert just said, proving Dilbert's point.
punchline: The Boss's confusion at Dilbert's explanation demonstrates that the problem lies with the listener's comprehension, not the speaker's clarity.
summary: A manager relays criticism of an employee's presentation, and the employee's rebuttal is so lost on him that it proves the point.

title: Business Lunch Isn't Really Lunch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That restaurant was great.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know. I plan to go there someday for lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We just ate lunch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That wasn't lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It wasn't?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You talked about work the entire time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lunch is not defined by food. It's defined by freedom from tyranny.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My lunch hour will begin the minute you waddle away.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was this going well until I said "waddle"?

setting: Outdoors in front of an office building, after a restaurant meal
situation: The Boss and Dilbert return from a meal at a restaurant. The Boss praises the place, and Dilbert says he plans to eat there someday for lunch, insisting that the meal they just had didn't count because the Boss talked about work throughout. Dilbert declares that his real lunch hour begins only once the Boss leaves.
punchline: Dilbert insists a meal spent listening to the boss talk about work isn't lunch, and the boss's closing question admits his own rude word choice ruined the moment.
summary: After a working meal with his boss, Dilbert argues that true lunch means being free of management and that his break can't start until the boss is gone.

title: Engagement Instead of Higher Pay

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO says I need to motivate you with a feeling of engagement, not higher pay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The long-term goal is to get you to pay us for the privilege of working here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I heard words I didn't know were words.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try giving her more engagement.

situation: The Boss tells Alice that the CEO wants him to motivate her with a feeling of engagement instead of a raise. He then explains that the long-term goal is for employees to pay the company for the privilege of working there. Wally, passing by, remarks that he heard words he didn't know were words, and the Boss suggests giving her more engagement.
punchline: Replacing pay with 'engagement' is a thinly veiled way of getting free labor, and the escalating absurdity ends with employees paying to work while Wally can't even parse the corporate jargon.
summary: A manager spins a refusal to pay raises as a plan to make workers feel engaged, eventually envisioning staff who pay for the privilege of having a job.

title: Dumped Over Slow Internet Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That was a fast date.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We were technologically incompatible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Her internet connection is slow, and there's no 4G service where she lives. How could I spend any time there?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could just talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to show my sources.

situation: Dogbert remarks that Dilbert's date ended quickly, and Dilbert explains that he and the woman were technologically incompatible. Her internet is slow and her home has no 4G coverage, so he couldn't stay there. When Dogbert suggests he simply talk to her, Dilbert says he likes to show his sources while holding his phone.
punchline: Dilbert is so dependent on his phone and internet access that he can't hold a conversation without looking up sources, which makes a poorly connected date impossible.
summary: A man ends a romance because his date's home lacks fast mobile data, since he can't converse without a connected device to back up his claims.

title: No Kill Switch on Awesome

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting reports that you're being arrogant in meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because I have a deep understanding of technology and a moral obligation to keep simpletons from ruining the world.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could tone it down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no kill switch on awesome.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that colleagues are complaining he comes across as arrogant in meetings. Dilbert explains that his technical expertise obliges him to stop less capable people from damaging things. When the Boss asks him to tone it down, Dilbert replies that he cannot switch off his awesomeness.
punchline: Dilbert answers a complaint about arrogance by smugly claiming his superiority is an uncontrollable trait, which only confirms the criticism.
summary: A manager relays complaints about a smug engineer, who responds by defending his superiority and insisting he cannot turn it off.

title: Executive Development Program: Relocation and Misery

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've been selected for our executive development program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means we can make you relocate to any godforsaken dirt stain we want.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as you make friends or find romance, we'll move you to someplace new and worse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It won't be the sort of work you'll enjoy, and the stress might kill you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you turn down this opportunity, the company will forever label you as a loser.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you accept the offer, the company will train you to find pleasure in the discomfort of your underlings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm doing it right now!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate my life!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, yes. Say more.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has been chosen for an executive development program, then lists its downsides: forced relocation to awful places, constant stress, and a loser label if he refuses. The program's benefit is learning to enjoy the suffering of subordinates. Dilbert sarcastically says he's already doing that, then howls about hating his life while the Boss savors it.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic claim that he's already taking pleasure in others' discomfort is turned into a literal demonstration, as the Boss gleefully enjoys Dilbert's own misery.
summary: A manager pitches a promotion that sounds like punishment, and the employee's despair becomes the manager's entertainment.

title: Coffee Thrown In Tired Face

transcript.speaker: Red-haired coworker
transcript.text: I'm so tired today.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sploosh!

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Sorry. I get excited when people have problems that I know how to solve.

situation: A red-haired employee tells a bald, bespectacled coworker that he is tired. The coworker, holding a mug of coffee, flings the hot coffee into his face to wake him up. The soaked and furious victim glares while the coworker apologizes.
punchline: The coworker's eager 'solution' to tiredness is to throw coffee in the person's face, excusing it as enthusiasm for fixing problems he knows how to solve.
summary: A weary employee gets an unwelcome and drastic remedy when a helpful coworker douses him with his own coffee.

file: 2012/2012-09-02_gadgets_mobile (cell) phones_time travel_rumour_apple phone_20 pixel camera_picture of thoughts_time machine_future_most handsome man_android phone.gif
title: Topper Escalates Apple Phone Rumors

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard a rumor that Apple's next phone will have a 20-megapixel camera.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper hijack

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: That's nothing!

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I heard you'll be able to hold the phone to your head and take a picture of your thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: And even that's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: Their next phone will be a time machine!

transcript.speaker: Future Topper
transcript.text: Here I am from the future!

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I'm the most handsome man in the universe!

transcript.speaker: Future Topper
transcript.text: So am I!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He makes a good case for buying an Android phone.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I love me more than me.

situation: Dilbert and a coworker discuss a rumor about Apple's next phone camera, and Topper interrupts to one-up the rumor with ever more absurd claims. He ends up claiming the phone is a time machine, summons a version of himself from the future, and the two Toppers admire each other.
punchline: Topper's boasting escalates from a rumored phone feature to a time-traveling duplicate of himself who is equally vain, making the Apple phone sound so ridiculous that Android looks better.
summary: A braggart colleague tries to outdo a phone rumor until he conjures a time-traveling copy of himself to share his self-love.

title: Happy People Marry, Not Vice Versa

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Someday, I want to get married because studies show that married people are happier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A smarter interpretation is that no one wants to marry an unhappy person.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're annoy-ing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With any luck, your soul mate won't be perceptive.

situation: A female coworker with a black bob haircut says she wants to marry because studies show married people are happier. Dilbert counters that the correlation likely runs the other way, since nobody wants to marry an unhappy person. She calls him annoying, and he replies that she should hope her future spouse isn't perceptive.
punchline: Dilbert's dry insult implies she is so unpleasant that only an oblivious partner would marry her, turning a correlation-versus-causation point into a put-down.
summary: A coworker cites marriage-happiness research as a reason to wed, and Dilbert's pedantic rebuttal ends in a backhanded jab at her chances of finding a spouse.

title: Smothering Innovation Gets Called Dumb

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What we need is an overarching strategy to stimulate our innovation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you could stop smothering the innovation we already have.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the dumbest idea I've heard in my entire life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And there it is.

situation: At a meeting, a woman proposes an overarching strategy to stimulate innovation. Dilbert suggests the company instead stop smothering the innovation it already has. The Boss immediately dismisses this as the dumbest idea he has ever heard, and Dilbert notes that this reaction proves his point.
punchline: The Boss's instant, scornful rejection of Dilbert's idea is itself a perfect demonstration of how management smothers innovation.
summary: A suggestion to stop crushing existing creativity is promptly crushed by the boss, proving the suggestion right.

title: Lawyer Says Ignore Your Idea

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our lawyer has instructed me to not listen to your product idea.

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: Why not?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a 99% chance you're an insane lawsuit monkey and your idea is dumber than earmuffs for oysters.

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: I hope those aren't...

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: I'll see you in court, thief!

situation: Dilbert tells an outside inventor that the company lawyer has forbidden him from hearing the man's product idea, then insults the idea as probably ridiculous. The inventor's reaction is to reveal he is holding a pair of tiny earmuffs for oysters, and he immediately threatens to sue Dilbert for stealing his idea.
punchline: Dilbert's example of a ridiculous idea, earmuffs for oysters, turns out to be the inventor's actual product, so the insulting guess proves exactly right and triggers the lawsuit Dilbert feared.
summary: A cautious engineer refuses to hear a stranger's invention and mocks it with an absurd example that happens to be the real thing, prompting an angry legal threat.

file: 2012/2012-02-29_internet & world wide web_quick question_only on line_slapping_less risk_dumb thing.gif
title: Wally Collaborates Only Online

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, I have a quick question.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hold it. Stop right there.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I only collaborate online, where there's less risk of some angry nut job slapping me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's the dumbest thing...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gaaa!

situation: Alice approaches Wally with a quick question, but he holds up a hand and says he only collaborates online to avoid being slapped by an angry person. Alice starts to call it the dumbest thing she has heard, and Wally flinches in fright, splashing his coffee, as if she were about to hit him.
punchline: Wally's fear of being slapped is proven reasonable by his own cowardly overreaction, since Alice's notorious temper makes him flinch before she does anything.
summary: A coworker who avoids face-to-face contact in favor of online chat recoils in terror when the famously short-tempered Alice merely starts to insult his excuse.

file: 2012/2012-10-21_internet & world wide web_cloudwash_argon_smart people_software to cloud.gif
title: Cloudwashing Software for Dumb Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to cloudwash our software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cloudwash?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Move some of its functions onto the Internet. But call the Internet a cloud.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one will take us seriously unless we're doing something in the cloud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will people take us seriously if we make technology decisions based on jargon?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't care what smart people think. There aren't that many of them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We only need to convince our dumb customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dumb people believe anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you believe I moved our software to the cloud yesterday?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You did?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to say yes.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to 'cloudwash' their software by moving a few functions onto the Internet and labeling it a cloud. Dilbert questions whether decisions driven by jargon will earn credibility, and the Boss says only dumb customers need convincing. He then tests the claim on Dilbert, who doubtfully asks 'You did?' and gets a sarcastic reply.
punchline: The Boss admits his cloud strategy relies on customers being gullible, and Dilbert's doubtful response shows that he is not fooled, so the Boss decides to respond 'yes' to the question 'You did?'
summary: A manager wants to rebrand ordinary internet features as cloud computing to impress customers he considers easy to fool.

title: Boss Isn't a Real Entrepreneur

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to act more like an entrepreneur.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Entrepreneurs make decisions that will end in failure 90% of the time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They motivate people through bullying, lying, manipulation, and verbal abuse.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Entrepreneurs make their employees work so many hours that their personal lives and their bodies fall apart.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been doing all of that stuff for years.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Has it worked?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, in that case, you're not an entrepreneur.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're just a huge jerk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that why no one is writing my biography?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss to behave more like an entrepreneur and lists their traits: frequent failure, bullying, lying, manipulation, abuse, and overworking staff. The Boss replies that he has done all of that for years without success. Dogbert concludes he isn't an entrepreneur, just a huge jerk.
punchline: The Boss has all the cruel habits of famous entrepreneurs but none of the success, so he is simply a jerk, and nobody is interested in writing his biography.
summary: A talking dog advises his employer to copy the ruthless habits of startup founders, then points out that doing so without succeeding just makes him a nasty person.

title: Fake Time for Group Writing

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can we schedule a time to write the product description together?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. How about 26 o'clock next Fleemsday?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's not a real time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's as real as the productivity of group writing.

situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut asks Dilbert to schedule a joint session to write a product description. Dilbert proposes a nonsensical time, '26 o'clock next Fleemsday.' When she objects that it isn't a real time, he retorts that it is as real as the productivity of group writing.
punchline: Dilbert uses an impossible, made-up meeting time to sarcastically imply that group writing sessions are as imaginary as the productivity they supposedly deliver.
summary: Asked to co-write copy in a scheduled session, Dilbert offers an impossible date and then explains that collaborative writing is equally fictional in its results.

title: Dummy Demonstrates Customer Treatment Metaphor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll use this dummy to demonstrate the way our company wants us to treat customers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We think it was meant as a metaphor, but there's no way to be sure.

setting: Office meeting room and break area
situation: The Boss announces he will use a dummy to demonstrate how the company wants employees to treat customers, and the employees look on stunned. Afterward, Dilbert tells a colleague that the demonstration was probably meant as a metaphor, but nobody can be certain.
punchline: The Boss's demonstration was so bizarre and alarming that the employees cannot tell whether he was speaking figuratively or literally about how the company wants customers treated.
summary: After a manager's shocking prop demonstration leaves his staff rattled, they can only guess that it was symbolic.

title: Middle Managers Block Engineer Suggestions

transcript.speaker: Middle Manager
transcript.text: One of your engineers came to me with a suggestion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gasp!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only reason I have middle managers is so this never happens.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, buddy. What are we talking about?

transcript.speaker: Middle Manager
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Worst case scenario!

situation: A middle manager tells the Boss that one of his engineers came to him with a suggestion, and the Boss gasps in horror. The Boss explains that he employs middle managers precisely to prevent engineers from reaching him with ideas. Dilbert wanders over and asks what's going on, and the middle manager panics, calling it the worst case scenario.
punchline: The Boss treats an engineer's suggestion as a disaster, and says middle managers exist specifically to shield him from good ideas, which shows how little management values employee input.
summary: A boss reveals that he pays middle managers mainly to keep engineers' ideas from ever reaching him, and the arrival of an engineer sends them into a panic.

file: 2012/2012-12-02_cublicle_hours worked_judgement_long term projects_near term deliverables_negotiate_output_work ethic_work from home_holy grail.gif
title: Wally's Ideal Job Demands Backfire

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I would like to be evaluated on my output, not the hours I work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It does? Wow.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I'd also like to work at home where there are fewer distractions so I can be more productive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. That makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Really? I mean. . . Great!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd also like to work on long-term projects that have no near-term deliverables.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Holy grail, holy grail, holy grail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go back to your cubicle and don't leave until five o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was this close to retiring at full pay.

setting: The Boss's office and a hallway at the office
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, presents the Boss with a list of ideal working conditions: being judged on output, working from home, and having long-term projects with no deliverables. The Boss agrees to the first two, but when Wally pushes for the third, which is basically a do-nothing job, the Boss shuts it all down and orders him back to his cubicle until five. Wally then complains to Dilbert that he nearly got a dream retirement-style arrangement.
punchline: Wally got greedy and asked for a job with no work and no accountability, which was so obviously a scam that the Boss finally refused, costing him all the reasonable concessions he had won.
summary: A lazy employee pushes his luck with escalating requests for freedom until his boss finally says no to everything.

title: Useless Proxy Attends Dilbert's Presentation

transcript.speaker: Proxy attendee
transcript.text: My boss asked me to attend your presentation on his behalf.

transcript.speaker: Proxy attendee
transcript.text: I should warn you that I'm not authorized to make decisions, and I take poor notes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. Let's begin wasting our time!

transcript.speaker: Proxy attendee
transcript.text: I'm not even sure I'm in the right meeting.

situation: A coworker arrives at Dilbert's presentation, sent by his boss as a stand-in. He admits he can't make decisions and takes bad notes. Dilbert sarcastically agrees to start the meeting, and the stand-in then reveals he may not even be in the correct meeting.
punchline: The substitute attendee is so useless and clueless that the meeting is explicitly acknowledged as a pure waste of time.
summary: A stand-in sent to a presentation confesses he has no authority, writes bad notes, and might be in the wrong room entirely.

title: Forty-Five Minutes to Database Analyst

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, our database analyst quit, so I need you to take over that job.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm curious... How long do you think it takes to train a tech writer to be a database analyst?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Forty-five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I like how you punctuate ignorance with certainty.

situation: The Boss tells Tina, a tech writer, that she must take over the job of a database analyst who quit. Tina asks how long he thinks the retraining would take, and he confidently answers forty-five minutes. Tina sarcastically remarks on his confident ignorance.
punchline: The Boss's absurdly short, confidently stated training estimate shows he has no idea how complex the job is, and Tina's sarcasm points out that he is certain precisely because he is ignorant.
summary: A manager casually reassigns a documentation specialist to a technical data role and breezily claims she can learn it in under an hour, prompting a dry rebuke.

title: Boss Claims He Is Leading

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See if you can get consensus on your idea and get back to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you could display some leadership and get back to ME.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm leading you right now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? I thought it would feel different.

situation: Dilbert brings an idea to his boss, who tells him to go build consensus and report back. Dilbert flips the request, suggesting the boss should show leadership instead. The boss insists that sending Dilbert off to do the work is itself leading him.
punchline: The boss believes handing off his own responsibility counts as leadership, and Dilbert sarcastically notes that being led doesn't feel like anything at all.
summary: A manager who deflects an employee's idea back onto him insists he is leading, and the employee wryly notes he can't tell.

title: Remora Attached To Trade Show Boss

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Have you selected a remora for your visit to the trade show?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's a remora?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: A remora is a fish that suctions to the back of a larger marine animal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's not comfortable in crowds, but he's freakishly persuasive.

setting: Office and then a crowded trade show floor (Tech Xpo)
situation: Asok asks the Boss whether he has chosen a remora to bring to the trade show, and the Boss doesn't know what that is. Asok explains that a remora is a fish that clings to the back of a larger marine animal. At the trade show, the Boss walks through the crowd carrying a Tech Xpo bag with Asok clinging to his back, while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: The 'remora' is Asok himself, who literally clings to the Boss's back as a human sales companion, and the Boss's description of him as freakishly persuasive shows he's using Asok as a clingy, awkward but effective salesman.
summary: A young employee latches onto his oblivious manager like a sucker fish as they work a crowded tech expo.

file: 2012/2012-01-13_business failures-bankruptcies_saving & investment_raises_debt crisis_economic uncertainty_board of directors_stock options_money.gif
title: Raise Denied, CEO Gets Stock Options

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because the Elbonian debt crisis has created economic uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily for us, our board of directors granted our CEO more stock options so he won't leave during uncertain times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happens when the uncertainty ends?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then he'll exercise his stock options.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he can't give him a raise because of economic uncertainty caused by the Elbonian debt crisis. He then explains that the board gave the CEO extra stock options to keep him from leaving during the uncertainty. Dilbert asks what happens when things stabilize, and the answer is that the CEO will cash out.
punchline: The company claims it has no money for employee raises, yet it lavishes the CEO with stock options, and those options are really a payout the CEO will collect (and then likely leave) once times are good.
summary: Pay increases are refused due to shaky finances while the top executive is quietly rewarded and expected to cash in as soon as the outlook improves.

title: Ashes Scattered Via Elbonian Missile

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I die, I want my ashes scattered in outer space.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Cool! I'll bribe an Elbonian general to strap you to their intercontinental missile when they test it next week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's better if the dying and the ash scattering are separate events.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't be a burden on the living.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he wants his ashes scattered in outer space after he dies. Dogbert cheerfully offers to bribe an Elbonian general to strap Dilbert to a test missile next week, which would mean launching him while still alive. Dilbert objects that dying and scattering should be separate events, and Dogbert tells him not to burden the living.
punchline: Dogbert treats Dilbert's final wish as a scheduling problem and proposes launching him alive now, then scolds him for being inconvenient about it.
summary: A man's wish for a space burial is met by his dog's eager plan to shoot him into the sky right away on a foreign missile.

file: 2012/2012-06-03_laziness_office workers_encouragement_career plans_misjudge_5 year plan_legacy sytems_retirement_projects_protect heart_plenty of naps_quality of work_pension fund_new career plan.gif
title: Wally's Master Plan for Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wally, you can't float through life with no goals and no ambition.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You misjudge me. I have my entire career planned out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My five-year plan is to avoid any sort of work in which my individual accomplishments can be measured.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll hoard knowledge about one of our legacy systems so I seem indispensable.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When I get to within four years of retirement, I'll only work on projects that have a five-year payback.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll protect my cardiovascular system by getting plenty of naps and not caring about the quality of my work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I'll stick a straw in our pension fund and suck on it for the next forty years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you get him straightened out?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, but I got a new career plan for myself.

setting: Office cubicle area, with Wally at his desk and Dogbert sitting on a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a career counselor, lectures Wally about drifting through life with no ambition. Wally replies that he has a detailed plan, which turns out to be a step-by-step scheme for avoiding accountability, hoarding knowledge, napping, and draining the pension fund. In the last panel the Boss asks if Wally was straightened out, and Dogbert says he instead adopted Wally's plan.
punchline: Wally's cynical career strategy is so effective that the person trying to motivate him ends up wanting to copy it.
summary: A lazy employee lays out a cunning lifelong scheme to coast at work and live off the pension, and the one who tried to reform him decides to follow it himself.

title: Mediocrity Outlasts Competitor's Anticipated Product

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news! Our biggest competitor just went out of business!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There was so much anticipation for their next product that no one bought the current one and they ran out of money.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Our strategy of predictable mediocrity paid off again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's okay to call it genius.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company's biggest competitor has gone out of business. A panel of the competitor's building explains that customers were so eager for the next product that they stopped buying the current one, and the company ran out of money. Carol credits the company's strategy of predictable mediocrity, and the Boss says it's okay to call it genius.
punchline: The company's unambitious, boring products survived only because a competitor's hype killed its own sales, yet the Boss wants to take credit for brilliant strategy.
summary: A rival firm collapses after hyping its next release so much that its current product stopped selling, and the boss claims his dull product line was a masterstroke.

title: Foreclosed House Flip Disclosures

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I bought a foreclosed house for $500. I plan to flip it for a profit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did the disclosures have any red flags?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They claim there's a lot of mold and unexploded ordnance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I don't see how either of those things could have survived the urine from the crack squatters.

setting: Office break area, coffee in hand
situation: The Boss brags to Dilbert and Wally that he bought a foreclosed house for $500 and plans to flip it. When Dilbert asks about red flags in the disclosures, the Boss casually mentions mold and unexploded ordnance. He then dismisses them by reasoning that crack squatters' urine must have destroyed both.
punchline: The Boss treats mold and unexploded bombs as non-issues because he assumes squatters' urine would have neutralized them, showing absurd, overconfident reasoning about a terrible investment.
summary: A boss proudly describes his dirt-cheap house purchase and waves away its horrifying defects with bizarre, self-serving logic.

title: Four Weak Reasons Make Best Decision

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why are you picking this vendor?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I listed the four reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Individually, each reason would not be compelling. But viewed as a whole, this is the best decision.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This first reason is weak.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And here we go.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert why he is choosing a particular vendor, and Dilbert hands over a list of four reasons. He admits that no single reason is compelling but insists that together they make the best decision. The coworker immediately starts picking apart the first reason, and Dilbert braces for a long argument.
punchline: Dilbert's decision rests on a justification that falls apart under any scrutiny, so the coworker's critique of the first weak reason predictably begins an exhausting debate.
summary: A vendor choice backed by a list of individually feeble arguments is challenged almost the moment it is presented.

title: Rational Employees Chase Rewards, Not Priorities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You keep spending time on low-priority tasks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because I'm a rational being. I only work on tasks that are likely to give me some sort of reward.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how to deal with that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you tried managing?

setting: Office cubicle, ending with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: The Boss criticizes Dilbert for spending his time on low-priority tasks. Dilbert replies that he is a rational person who only works on tasks likely to earn him a reward. The Boss admits he has no idea how to handle that, and Dilbert sarcastically suggests he try managing, as the final panel shows the office building.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss should do his actual job of managing, since the company's reward system gives Dilbert no incentive to work on the Boss's priorities.
summary: An employee explains that he rationally ignores unrewarded work, leaving his stumped boss with a pointed suggestion to try doing his own job.

title: Monkey With Flattened Head Interviews

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me why I should hire you as my service monkey, Carl.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: I worked as a Starbucks barista for eight years, and my head has been surgically flattened to stabilize your coffee cup.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Impressive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is nothing. You should see how well he interviews.

setting: Office conference room, then an office hallway
situation: The Boss interviews a monkey named Carl for a job as his 'service monkey.' Carl explains he was a Starbucks barista for eight years and had his head surgically flattened to hold a coffee cup steady. Afterward the Boss and Dilbert stand with Carl balancing a cup on his head, and the Boss brags that the monkey interviews even better than that.
punchline: The Boss thinks a surgically flattened head is a minor feat compared to the monkey's interview skills, showing how absurdly the Boss values a job candidate who is basically a living coffee table.
summary: A manager hires a monkey with a modified skull to serve as a living cup holder and proudly boasts about the animal's interviewing prowess.

title: Paying Twice Rather Than Lose Budget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our budget for contract employees was eliminated.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll have to pay you out of the training budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So instead of doing the job yourself. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll have to train Dilbert to do the job we're paying you to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you just move some of the training budget to the contractor budget?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we reduce the training budget this year, we'll get less next year.

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: So. . . you prefer paying two people to do the job of one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: How do you stay in business?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our customers are even dumber than us.

situation: The Boss tells a contractor that the contract employee budget has been eliminated, so he will be paid from the training budget instead and must train Dilbert to do the job he was hired for. Dilbert suggests simply moving money between the two budgets, but the Boss refuses because cutting the training budget would shrink next year's allocation. The contractor concludes the company pays two people to do one person's work.
punchline: The company wastefully pays two people for one job to protect its budget allocation, and stays afloat only because its customers are even dumber than the management.
summary: A manager would rather fund two workers for one task than risk a smaller budget next year, and shrugs off the waste by blaming gullible customers.

file: 2012/2012-12-18_anger_interviews_job applicant_second opinion_jb hoppr_bunny costume_17 jobs_2 years_red flags_rage issues_passionate.gif
title: Bunny Costume Applicant Red Flags

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a second opinion on a job applicant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His name is J.B. Hopper. He dresses in a bunny costume and he's had seventeen jobs in two years.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Are there any red flags?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell if he's passionate or if he has rage issues.

situation: The Boss asks Catbert, the HR director, for a second opinion on a job candidate. He describes an applicant named J.B. Hopper who wears a bunny costume and has held seventeen jobs in two years. The applicant sits at the table in a bunny suit looking angry, and the Boss can't decide if it's passion or rage.
punchline: The Boss is oblivious to the obvious red flags, such as the bunny costume, the job-hopping and the visible anger, and only wonders whether the man is passionate or has rage issues.
summary: A clueless manager asks HR whether a furious, bunny-suited candidate with a wildly short job history has any warning signs.

title: Emperor's New Clothes, Literally Pantsless

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for employees who aren't afraid to tell the emperor he has no clothes.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Fine. You're not wearing pants.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The one time I forget to wear pants. . .

situation: The Boss tells an employee he wants staff brave enough to tell the emperor he has no clothes. The employee takes him at his word and points out that the Boss isn't wearing pants. In the last panel the Boss walks around in his underwear holding a coffee mug, lamenting the bad timing.
punchline: The Boss's metaphor about honest employees turns literal when he actually forgot his pants, and he is annoyed that honesty caught him out on the one day it mattered.
summary: A manager praising fearless honesty gets a taste of it when a worker bluntly notes the manager has come to work without trousers.
keywords: telling the truth to the boss

title: Dogbert Guides Texting Alice, Boss Wants Monkey

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Alice, do you have...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: She can't hear you. She's walking and texting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's it... Easy does it. I'll guide you around this obstacle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What did I just see?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm saving up for a service monkey.

situation: Dilbert tries to ask Alice a question, but Dogbert explains she can't hear because she is walking and texting on her phone. Dogbert acts as her guide dog, steering her around an obstacle. Dilbert is stunned by what he saw, and the Boss, holding a coffee mug and phone, casually announces he is saving up for a service monkey.
punchline: Having seen a distracted employee led around by a dog, the Boss decides he wants his own animal helper too, treating a guide animal as a status perk for gadget-distracted people.
summary: A dog steers a phone-absorbed coworker through the office, inspiring her clueless manager to want a personalized helper animal of his own.

title: Parking Hassle Is Management's Design

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The employee parking situation is terrible. I had to park a mile away.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's by design. The inconvenience removes your temptation to run personal errands during the day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're intentionally making my life more difficult?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: What do you think management is?

situation: Dilbert complains to Catbert, the evil human resources director, that the employee parking lot is so bad he had to park a mile away. Catbert explains the inconvenience is deliberate, meant to stop employees from running personal errands during the workday. When Dilbert asks if they are intentionally making his life harder, Catbert responds that this is what management is.
punchline: Catbert cheerfully admits that deliberately making employees' lives difficult is the very definition of management.
summary: A worker's gripe about distant parking turns out to be a deliberate policy, and the cat in charge treats purposeful misery as the whole job of management.

title: Space Elevator Prototype Launches Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I finished the space elevator prototype.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So soon? I thought it would take years.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's just a prototype. Do you want to try it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure.

setting: Office, then the roof of the office building
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells the Boss he has already finished a space elevator prototype, and the Boss is surprised it didn't take years. Wally offers to let him try it and the Boss agrees. In the last panel the Boss is lying face down at the edge of the roof beside a bent pipe, apparently having been shot out of it.
punchline: The 'space elevator' is really a crude launching tube, so the gullible Boss volunteers to test it and gets flung onto the roof edge, which Wally knew would happen.
summary: A slacker engineer's suspiciously quick invention turns out to be a rooftop pipe that sends his trusting manager flying.

title: Elbonian Missile Program Hits Orphanage

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Official
transcript.text: Our missile program is the pride of Elbonia!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Official
transcript.text: Yesterday we launched a test missile that went a hundred yards before ripping the roof off an orphanage.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You test your missiles near orphans?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian Official
transcript.text: What are the odds they'd be unlucky three times?

setting: A government office in Elbonia, with Dogbert seated across a desk from a tall-hatted bearded official
situation: A tall-hatted Elbonian official boasts to Dogbert about his country's missile program, then admits a test missile flew only a hundred yards and tore the roof off an orphanage. When Dogbert asks why they test near orphans, the official justifies it by saying orphans are unlikely to be unlucky three times.
punchline: The official treats orphans as ideal bystanders because they've already had two strokes of bad luck, callously reasoning that a third is statistically improbable.
summary: A boastful Elbonian missile chief defends a botched test that wrecked an orphanage with twisted logic about the victims' prior misfortune.

title: Buzzwords Make Meeting Input Effortless

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I remember a time when I had to listen to the topic at hand before adding my insincere input.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think we should virtualize the process and move it to the cloud.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, that's a great idea!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now it's just all too easy.

situation: During a meeting, Wally thinks to himself that he used to have to pay attention to the topic before offering fake input. He then simply suggests virtualizing the process and moving it to the cloud, and the Boss immediately praises it as a great idea.
punchline: Wally has discovered that tossing out trendy buzzwords like 'virtualize' and 'the cloud' earns instant praise from management with no understanding of the topic required.
summary: A lazy employee realizes he can win approval in meetings just by dropping fashionable tech jargon without listening to anything.

file: 2012/2012-10-20_business failures-bankruptcies_executives_wages_long tern survival_innovate ways_cannibalize_current prodcuts_lose a fortune_ceo's compensation_revenue dips_hovel_some ideas_money.gif
title: Innovation Costs the CEO's Fortune

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our only hope for long-term survival is to innovate in ways that cannibalize our current products.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The downside is that you'll lose a fortune in CEO compensation when our revenue dips in the short run.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks. I'll stop by your hovel later with some ideas for ruining your life, too.

situation: Dilbert advises the boss that the company can only survive long term by innovating in ways that cannibalize its existing products. He then points out that this will cut the boss's CEO compensation when revenue drops in the short run. The boss responds by threatening to make Dilbert's life miserable too.
punchline: The boss ignores the sound strategic advice and instead retaliates against Dilbert for the personal financial hit, showing that executives put their own pay ahead of the company's long-term survival.
summary: A worker's sensible plan to save the company from future decline is met with a vindictive vow to wreck his life because it would shrink the boss's pay.

file: 2012/2012-09-24_cold desperation_drab_grimy habitat_meaningless_pile of money_poor persons_rich people_roll in money_underling.gif
title: Boss Mocks Underling's Meaningless Life

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I'm lost and I've wandered into the grimy habitat of an underling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I feel the cold desperation of your drab and meaningless life.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to roll in money to get the smell off me. Where's the nearest pile?

situation: The Boss wanders into Dilbert's cubicle and loudly announces he is lost in the grimy habitat of an underling. He insults Dilbert's drab, meaningless life and says he needs to roll in money to get rid of the smell. Dilbert silently keeps working at his computer throughout.
punchline: The Boss is so condescending toward his low-paid employee that he treats Dilbert's cubicle like a contaminated place and sarcastically wants to wash off the 'poverty' by rolling in a pile of money.
summary: A pompous executive stumbles into a subordinate's cubicle and treats its poverty and tedium as something he needs to cleanse himself of with cash.

title: Venture Capitalists Insult the Board

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Venture capitalists gave us $10 million, but I had to agree to put one of them on our board.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should I be worried that your other board members have a combined I.Q. of about 70?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They weren't dumb enough to give me $10 million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Burn!

situation: Dogbert tells his board that venture capitalists gave his company $10 million but required a seat on the board. The Boss asks whether he should worry that the other board members are so unintelligent. Dogbert replies that they were not dumb enough to hand him the money, and a dinosaur board member cheers the insult.
punchline: Dogbert's comeback implies the venture capitalists are in fact dumb enough to give him $10 million, which insults the very people who funded him, and the dinosaur on the board celebrates it without realizing it applies to the venture capitalist.
summary: A startup founder's reply to a jab about his board accidentally turns into an insult aimed at the investors who bankrolled him.

file: 2012/2012-03-01_television news_rogue nations_nuclear weapons_polar ice caps_melting_unemployment_brink of default_retirement_news.gif
title: Why He Ignores The News

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Rogue nations are building nuclear weapons. The polar ice caps are melting. Unemployment is high.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Entire nations are on the brink of default. You aren't saving enough for retirement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you have going here?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: He said he doesn't pay attention to news. I wondered why.

situation: A bald coworker holding a coffee mug rattles off a litany of alarming news headlines to a coworker with spiky hair. The recipient grows increasingly agitated, ending up red-faced, sweating and clenching his teeth. Dilbert walks up and asks what is going on.
punchline: The coworker had asked why his colleague avoids the news, then demonstrated the reason by reciting the news, which visibly stresses the man out.
summary: A man tests a colleague's claim that he avoids the news by reading him the grim headlines, and the colleague's meltdown makes the case.

title: Intern's Organs Harvested Awkwardly

transcript.speaker: Intern 1
transcript.text: I know it feels unimportant to be an intern to another intern. . .

transcript.speaker: Intern 1
transcript.text: But if I ever get into a serious accident then. . .

transcript.speaker: Intern 2
transcript.text: I would step into your job?

transcript.speaker: Intern 1
transcript.text: I was going to say your organs will be harvested to save me, but now you've made it feel awkward.

transcript.speaker: Intern 2
transcript.text: Sorry!

situation: One intern reassures another intern, who works for him, that being an intern to another intern isn't unimportant. He starts to explain that the subordinate's value would show if he were in an accident, and the junior intern assumes he would simply take over his job. The senior intern then reveals he meant the junior's organs would be harvested to save him.
punchline: The subordinate intern's innocent guess about stepping into a job is crushed by the revelation that his real value is as a donor of spare organs.
summary: A junior intern misreads a pep talk, only to learn he is valued as a source of replacement body parts.

file: 2012/2012-10-07_actors & actresses_ignorance (knowledge)_laziness_opinions_informed opinions_hard data_life is a lie.gif
title: Uninformed Opinions Feel Good

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I like to have opinions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But not informed opinions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It takes so much work to get informed that it defeats the whole point of having an opinion in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What exactly do you think is the "point" of having an opinion?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The point is that it feels good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's totally nuts.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, is it?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Unless you have hard data to back up that comment, it was nothing but an uninformed opinion that felt good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! You're starting to make sense!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your whole life is a lie.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert chats over coffee with a bald coworker who proudly declares he likes having opinions, but only uninformed ones, because getting informed is too much work. When Dilbert calls this nuts, the coworker points out that Dilbert's own remark was an uninformed opinion that felt good. Dilbert is horrified to realize the coworker is making sense.
punchline: By dismissing the coworker's view without any hard data, Dilbert proves the coworker's point: his own reaction was just an uninformed opinion that felt good, so his whole life is a lie.
summary: A coffee-break philosopher defends gut-feeling opinions and then turns Dilbert's own snap judgment into proof of his argument.

title: Job-Hopper Interview Bunny Stereotyping

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your work history suggests that you might be a job-hopper.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee in bunny suit
transcript.text: Oh, really? Well, I should hop all over you for saying that!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought you would be more passive.

transcript.speaker: Interviewee in bunny suit
transcript.text: Wow. You cannot stop stereotyping.

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate who is wearing a full white bunny costume. He remarks that the candidate's work history suggests a job-hopper, and the bunny retorts that he should hop all over him for saying so. The Boss then says he expected the candidate to be more passive, prompting an accusation of stereotyping.
punchline: The Boss is oblivious to his own stereotyping, since he judges the bunny-suited candidate by a bunny's traits while objecting to a hopping pun, and the candidate calls him out for it.
summary: A manager's interview remark about a candidate's frequent job changes collides with the candidate's rabbit costume, and both of them end up trading hopping puns and stereotypes.

title: Bragging Replaces Actually Accomplishing Things

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I need to be more vocal about my accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've found that bragging is a perfect substitute for accomplishing stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I plan to do both.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. You are the wind beneath my seat cushion.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert tells Wally over coffee that he should be more vocal about what he has achieved. Wally replies that he has found bragging works just as well as actually accomplishing anything. When Dilbert says he plans to do both, Wally sarcastically twists a sentimental phrase into a joke about seat cushions.
punchline: Wally, who coasts by bragging instead of working, mocks Dilbert's plan to both achieve and boast by calling him the wind beneath his seat cushion, a sarcastic play on 'wind beneath my wings' that also implies flatulence.
