summary: A coworker who takes credit without doing any work sarcastically mocks a colleague who intends to both work and promote himself.

title: Boss Multitasks Coffee, Misses Everything

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't finish everything today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try multitasking.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Multitasking? Is that like being an ignorant baboon and drinking coffee at the same time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I missed what you said because I was drinking coffee.

situation: Alice tells her boss she can't finish all her work today, and he glibly suggests she try multitasking. She sarcastically asks if multitasking is like being an ignorant baboon while drinking coffee, but the boss, sipping coffee, doesn't hear her insult.
punchline: The boss proves his own inability to multitask by missing her insult because he was drinking coffee, so her insult goes unnoticed.
summary: A manager's lazy advice to multitask is met with a veiled insult that he fails to hear because he's busy sipping his drink.

file: 2012/2012-08-06_business meeting_cup of water_not impressed_fill sink_bring own cup_not impressive_optics.gif
title: Thirsty Client Rejects Restroom Water

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I'd like to do business with your company but...

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I'm concerned that the only beverage you can afford to offer me is water from the restroom sink... and I need to bring my own cup.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I also offered to fill the sink and let you lap it out.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: And now I'm thirsty!

setting: Conference room of a small company, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: A prospective client sits across the table from Dilbert and says he hesitates to do business with the company because it seems too poor to offer anything but restroom sink water, and he would have to bring his own cup. Dilbert says he also offered to fill the sink so the client could lap the water out. The client, now insulted and gesturing in frustration, says the idea has only made him thirsty.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to address the client's concern about the company's poverty makes it worse by offering a degrading, animal-like way to drink, showing the company really can't impress anyone.
summary: A wary prospective customer doubts a struggling company's finances because of its sad drink offerings, and Dilbert's bizarre fix only makes things worse.

file: 2012/2012-12-27_annoyance_bullying co workers_friendly suggestions_looks like bullying_schedule time_waste time.gif
title: Friendly Suggestions Mistaken for Bullying

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I got a report that you've been bullying co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's dumb.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I make friendly suggestions about how people could waste less of my time and it looks like bullying.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Let's schedule a time to talk more about this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or - just a friendly suggestion - you could not waste my freakin' time.

setting: Office meeting table, likely an HR office
situation: Catbert, acting as HR, tells Dilbert that a report accuses him of bullying co-workers. Dilbert explains that he merely offers friendly suggestions on how people could waste less of his time. When Catbert proposes scheduling another meeting to discuss it, Dilbert suggests Catbert stop wasting his time.
punchline: Catbert's proposal of yet another meeting proves Dilbert's point, and Dilbert's blunt 'friendly suggestion' is exactly the kind of behavior that got him reported.
summary: An HR cat confronts Dilbert about alleged bullying, only to waste his time with a follow-up meeting that illustrates his complaint.

title: Open Floor Plan: Worse Than Cubicles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're thinking of moving from a cubicle workplace to an open floor plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because you did some research and discovered that the open floor plan is the only thing worse than what we have now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They figured out the pattern.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I told you we should randomize our evil!

setting: Conference room, then the boss's office
situation: The Boss announces that management is considering moving from cubicles to an open floor plan. Dilbert sarcastically asks if research showed it was the only thing worse than the current setup. The Boss admits the employees have figured out management's pattern of alternating bad ideas, and Catbert, the evil HR director, complains that he had warned them to randomize their evil.
punchline: Management deliberately alternates between bad workplace policies, and the open floor plan is just the next predictable evil, which the employees have now seen through.
summary: Management plans an office redesign that Dilbert calls the only thing worse than cubicles, and the evil HR cat laments that his bosses' cruelty has become predictable.

title: Smiling Makes You Extra Hetero

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies show that smiling makes you more attractive.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it working?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just became extra hetero.

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert shares a study claiming that smiling makes people more attractive. His bald coworker, holding a mug, flashes a toothy grin and asks whether it is working on him. Dilbert replies that he has just become extra hetero, meaning the grin has had the opposite effect.
punchline: The coworker's forced grimace is so unattractive that it makes Dilbert feel even more strongly heterosexual, so the smile backfires comically.
summary: A coworker tests a claim about attractive smiles on Dilbert and gets an unflattering, tongue-in-cheek verdict.

title: Thrilled About Performance Improvement Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I'm putting you on a ninety-day performance improvement plan.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Yes!!! I've always dreamed of making it onto the performance improvement plan!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not as good as it sounds.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: With all due respect, you don't know how low my ambitions are.

situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being put on a ninety-day performance improvement plan, which is normally a threat. Ted reacts with excited joy, saying it has always been his dream. The Boss warns him it is not as good as it sounds, and Ted replies that the Boss has no idea how low his ambitions are.
punchline: Ted is so unambitious and so used to underperforming that being singled out for a punitive improvement plan feels like an achievement to him.
summary: An employee greets a threatened performance plan as if it were a coveted prize, revealing just how little he aspires to.

title: Revenue Forecast Built on Assumptions

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And my revenue forecast says. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you make any assumptions?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I made a lot of them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then we don't believe your forecast.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Can I tell you about it anyway?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whatever makes you feel less absurd.

situation: A red-haired employee presents his revenue forecast to a meeting. Dilbert asks whether he made any assumptions, and when the employee admits to making many, Dilbert declares the forecast unbelievable. The employee asks to present it anyway and Dilbert lets him, noting it will help him feel less absurd.
punchline: Every forecast rests on assumptions, so rejecting one for that reason makes the whole exercise pointless, and Dilbert sarcastically lets the presenter continue anyway to spare his dignity.
summary: A colleague's financial prediction gets dismissed for being based on guesses, yet he is allowed to deliver it anyway as a face-saving gesture.

title: Fracking Under the Competitor's Headquarters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to start fracking under our biggest competitor's headquarters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My plan is to pollute their water and generate earthquakes to destroy their campus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The project code name is "Fracking Awesome."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Catchy.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company will start fracking beneath its biggest competitor's headquarters. He explains that the aim is to contaminate their water and trigger earthquakes that wreck their campus. He then proudly announces the project's code name, and Dilbert dryly comments on it.
punchline: The Boss describes a plan to sabotage a rival with environmental destruction and is proud only of the pun-based code name, while Dilbert's flat 'Catchy' ignores the villainy and mocks the boss's priorities.
summary: A boss casually unveils a scheme to wreck a rival company's campus through pollution and induced earthquakes, then boasts about the punny project name.

title: Goals Are Permission to Ignore Everything Else

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your compensation will be based on achieving these goals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Awesome. It's like written permission to ignore everything else you ask me to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not like that at all.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Get back to me when you finish debating yourself.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a sheet of paper listing goals and says his pay will depend on achieving them. Dilbert cheerfully points out that this effectively lets him ignore every other task the Boss assigns. The Boss protests that it's not like that, and Dilbert tells him to come back once he has finished arguing with himself.
punchline: By tying pay only to a narrow set of goals, the Boss has given Dilbert a legitimate excuse to ignore all his other requests, and the Boss's denial shows he knows Dilbert is right.
summary: A manager ties an employee's pay to a list of goals and is promptly told it excuses the employee from all other work.

title: Wally's Insulting Telepresence Robot

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Here comes Wally's telepresence robot.

transcript.speaker: Wally (via robot)
transcript.text: How was your commute, suckers?!! Ha ha ha ha! I'm multitasking in ways that might surprise you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: New technology always has rough patches.

transcript.speaker: Wally (via robot)
transcript.text: Open that door for me, meat bags!

situation: Dilbert and a coworker watch Wally's telepresence robot roll toward them, with Wally's face on its screen. Wally gloats about skipping the commute and hints that he is multitasking in surprising ways. Dilbert shrugs off the rudeness as growing pains of new technology, and the robot then orders them to open a door for it.
punchline: The telepresence robot lets Wally work from home while mocking his coworkers, and he still expects them to wait on him by opening doors, so the 'rough patches' are really just Wally's usual behavior.
summary: A remote-working employee uses his robot stand-in to taunt colleagues who endured the commute, then demands they hold the door for him.

file: 2012/2012-12-14_meetings_work ethic_to do list_useless meeting_busy work_power point slides_productivity today.gif
title: Dilbert's To-Do List of Futility

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see what's on my "to do" list for today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Useless meeting... Busywork... Make misleading PowerPoint slides... And... Another useless meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was your productivity today?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know you're mocking me.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then his home living room
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer thinking through his to-do list, which consists entirely of pointless tasks: useless meetings, busywork, and misleading PowerPoint slides. That evening at home, Dogbert asks him how productive his day was, and Dilbert recognizes the question as mockery.
punchline: Dilbert's entire workday consisted of meaningless tasks, so Dogbert's question about productivity is an obvious jab that Dilbert immediately recognizes.
summary: After a day filled with nothing but pointless meetings and busywork, Dilbert knows his dog's polite question about his output is really a taunt.

title: Paragraph Two Is Pointless

transcript.text: Your second paragraph is pointless and confusing. Let's just delete it.

situation: Dilbert reviews a document with a technical writer and tells her that her second paragraph is pointless and confusing and should be deleted. She bristles, citing her professional training and asking what qualifies him to do her job better. Dilbert replies that the evidence is paragraph two itself.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically suggests that the confusing paragraph she wrote is itself proof that he could do her job better than she does.
summary: A writer defends her expertise against an edit, only to have her own flawed paragraph offered as proof of her critic's superior skill.

title: Smartphones Are Just Gadgets, Strangle Me

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going into the smartphone business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Smartphones are basically gadgets, and we already make gadgets, so how hard could it be?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you strangle me now, I promise I won't resist.

transcript.speaker: Ted

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces the company is entering the smartphone business, reasoning that phones are just gadgets and the company already makes gadgets. Dilbert, appalled by the shallow logic, invites a colleague to strangle him and promises not to resist. A coworker responds that this sounds lazy.
punchline: Even offering to be killed to escape the Boss's absurd reasoning is dismissed as lazy, since the coworker thinks Dilbert would be giving up without a fight.
summary: Faced with a sweeping strategy built on a flimsy oversimplification, an employee would rather be throttled than endure it, and a peer mocks him for not even putting up a struggle.

title: Smearing a Coworker by Innuendo

transcript.speaker: Brian
transcript.text: GAAA!!! You have been painted by the brush of unhelpfulness.

transcript.speaker: Brian
transcript.text: There is no way to remove the stigma of this accusation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Watch and learn.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Brian has... um... issues.

transcript.text: Issues? What issues? Mental? Emotional? Substance abuse?

Wally says he will show Brian how it's done, then vaguely hints that Brian has 'issues' and pretends to hold back details. The Boss fills in the blanks with the worst possibilities and decides Brian is a monster.
punchline: Wally destroys Brian's reputation with nothing but coy insinuation, letting the Boss imagine the worst, and Brian admires how effortlessly Wally does it.
summary: A coworker answers a smear campaign by showing how a few mumbled hints and fake reluctance can make the boss believe anything.

title: Night Shift Heart Attack Murder Plot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I want you to manage our Elbonian contract programmers. You'll need to work at night because of the time difference.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People who work at night have more heart attacks. Are you trying to kill me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, and it's totally legal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well played.

situation: The Boss orders Wally to manage the Elbonian contract programmers, which means working nights because of the time difference. Wally points out that night work raises the risk of heart attacks and asks if the Boss is trying to kill him. The Boss cheerfully admits it and notes that it is legal.
punchline: The Boss openly admits he is trying to kill Wally through a legal workplace hazard, and Wally grudgingly congratulates him on the clever scheme.
summary: A manager assigns an employee a risky overnight job overseeing offshore programmers and happily confesses it is a lawful way to get rid of him.

title: Consultant Buzzword Talk Gets Hired

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's talk like idiots.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Ha ha! You go first!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Slap lipstick on the pig, put a stake in the ground, and view it from 30,000 feet.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: That deliverable is actionable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wait... Why do I suddenly feel like hiring you?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: And why do I feel underpaid?

setting: Office desk during a job interview
situation: Dogbert, acting as the interviewer, invites a dinosaur job candidate to trade nonsense jargon. After Dogbert rattles off a string of empty clichés, the dinosaur responds with equally meaningless buzzwords. Dogbert suddenly feels inclined to hire him, and the dinosaur feels he deserves more pay.
punchline: Spouting meaningless corporate buzzwords makes someone sound competent enough to be hired, and it also makes them feel they deserve more money.
summary: A hiring interview turns into a contest of empty clichés that somehow convinces both sides the candidate is valuable.

title: Retirement Plan: Hunted By Billionaire

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Retirement Planning Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your only hope for survival is if...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A nearsighted billionaire offers to hunt you on his private island.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does that job pay well?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's more of a foraging situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must... adjust... expectations... down.

situation: Dilbert consults Dogbert's retirement planning service and is told his only hope for survival is a nearsighted billionaire who hunts people on a private island. Dilbert asks if the job pays well, and Dogbert says it's really about foraging for food. Dilbert resigns himself to lowering his expectations.
punchline: Dilbert's retirement prospects are so bleak that his best option is being hunted for sport by a billionaire, and even that offers no pay, only scavenging to stay alive.
summary: A financial adviser's grim outlook for a worker's golden years leaves him hoping to be prey in a rich man's game and accepting a life of scavenging.

title: Index Funds Don't Pick Themselves

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll manage your portfolio for a standard industry fee of 1% per year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm investing a billion dollars. Your fee would be $10 million per year.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Those index funds aren't going to pick themselves.

setting: Dogbert's office, with the Boss sitting across the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as an investment manager, offers to run the Boss's portfolio for a standard 1% annual fee. The Boss points out that on a billion dollars this means a $10 million yearly fee. Dogbert justifies the huge charge by claiming that picking index funds is difficult work.
punchline: Index funds require almost no skill to choose, so Dogbert's attempt to justify a $10 million fee for picking them is absurd, mocking the percentage-based fees charged by money managers.
summary: A financial advisor defends a gigantic fee for the trivial job of selecting passive index funds.

title: Brand Name Sounds Like Dental Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new brand will be called "Herthlokel."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you come up with that when you were getting dental work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably should have kept that thought bottled up inside me.

situation: The Boss stands beside a screen and announces that the company's new brand name will be "Herthlokel." Alice asks whether he invented the name while under dental anesthesia, since it sounds like garbled speech from a numbed mouth. The Boss sheepishly admits he should have kept the idea to himself.
punchline: The nonsensical brand name is so bad that it sounds like someone talking with a mouth full of dental numbing, and even the Boss recognizes his mistake.
summary: A manager unveils a gibberish brand name and a coworker suggests it came from a dentist's chair, which he reluctantly concedes.

file: 2012/2012-06-16_business ethics_embarrass your compnay_etiquette & ethics_local debauchery_personal behavior_pollute ground water_pollution_reflect poorly_elbonia.gif
title: Wally Embarrasses Polluting Company in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Where can I go to enjoy some of the local debauchery?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Aren't you worried that your personal behavior will reflect poorly on your company?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How can I embarrass a company that plans to pollute your groundwater?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Say what?

setting: Muddy village in Elbonia with mud huts
situation: Wally, visiting Elbonia on a business trip, asks a local where he can find some debauchery. The local asks whether his bad behavior might embarrass his employer. Wally replies that it is impossible to embarrass a company that plans to pollute the locals' groundwater, which the local clearly did not know about.
punchline: Wally casually reveals his company's plan to pollute Elbonia's groundwater while justifying his own bad behavior, showing that the company has no reputation left to damage.
summary: A traveling employee shrugs off concerns about misbehaving abroad by pointing out his employer is already planning something far more disgraceful to the locals.

file: 2012/2012-07-07_certification in puppetry_degree in engineering_diploma and bait shop_discrepancy_resume_ventriloquism.gif
title: CEO's Puppetry Degree Exposed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One of our major investors found a discrepancy on your résumé.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You claim to have a degree in engineering, but in reality you have...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A certification in puppetry from a place called... Evelyn's Diploma and Bait Shop.

transcript.speaker: Puppet
transcript.text: The board has faith in our CEO.

situation: The Boss confronts the CEO about a discrepancy found on his résumé by an investor. He reads out that the CEO's claimed engineering degree is really a puppetry certification from a bait shop. The CEO responds by speaking through a hand puppet, apparently putting his puppetry training to use.
punchline: The CEO answers the accusation of faking his credentials by using a puppet to deliver a line, proving his puppetry certification is real and that he has no shame about the fraud.
summary: A boss reads out an executive's fraudulent credentials, and the exposed CEO deflects by talking through a puppet.

title: News I Don't Understand

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's some news I don't understand about LIBOR rates.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's some news I don't understand about the Higgs boson.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me why we have news.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I think it has something to do with patent law and the electoral college.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk reading news on a laptop, thinking about stories he cannot comprehend, first LIBOR rates and then the Higgs boson. He then stands holding a coffee mug and asks Catbert why news exists at all. Catbert offers a nonsensical answer mixing patent law and the electoral college.
punchline: The Boss reads news he can't understand and Catbert's explanation for why news exists is itself a confused jumble of unrelated topics, implying nobody really understands the purpose or content of news.
summary: Baffled by complex headlines, the Boss wonders what news is even for, and Catbert offers an equally muddled guess.

title: Leadership Newsletter Written By Unemployed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news: I signed up to receive a free leadership newsletter by email.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I know it's good because it's written by some guy who used to have a job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop making everything I say sound stupid!

situation: The Boss proudly announces to Dilbert and Alice that he subscribed to a free leadership newsletter. Alice sarcastically replies that it must be good because its author is someone who used to have a job. The Boss snaps at her for making everything he says sound stupid.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic praise reveals that the newsletter's author is unemployed and thus unqualified to teach leadership, and the Boss's angry reaction shows he realizes his own remark was already stupid.
summary: A manager brags about a free self-help subscription, and a coworker's deadpan quip exposes how worthless it is.

file: 2012/2012-11-11_meetings_work ethic_execution_innovation_full time job_excellence_inspired_died on inside_coffee and resentment_chemical formula for hatred_drilled employees.gif
title: Inspirational Speech Meets Dead Inside

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Execution is a game of inches! You miss 100% of the shots you don't take!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Innovation is everyone's full-time job! Be the dog, not the tail!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Excellence is the only market that isn't crowded!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why don't any of you look inspired by my leadership?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I died on the inside years ago.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I'm just a fleshy container full of coffee and resentment.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This guy was born without a soul. The she-devil at the end is the chemical formula for hatred.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Did you get through to them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I drilled until I hit bile.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting, then the boss's office
situation: The Boss lectures his team with a string of empty motivational slogans, then asks why nobody looks inspired. Wally and Alice respond with bleak confessions of burnout and bitterness. Afterward the boss tells Catbert, the HR director, that he drilled into the employees until he hit bile.
punchline: The boss's attempt to inspire his team only exposes how drained and resentful they are, which he describes as having 'drilled until I hit bile'.
summary: A manager's hollow pep talk about inches, innovation and excellence uncovers nothing but his employees' exhausted resentment.

title: Ugly Layout Blamed on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your page layout is ugly.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Whose fault is that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I work in an ugly cubicle surrounded by ugly people. You trample on my sense of aesthetics and expect me to be unaffected?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... it's my fault?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You, your parents, your barber, and whoever dresses you.

situation: Dilbert criticizes his coworker's page layout as ugly. She replies that her ugly surroundings and ugly colleagues have ruined her sense of aesthetics. When Dilbert asks if it is his fault, she assigns blame to him, his parents, his barber, and whoever dresses him.
punchline: She turns his criticism around into a string of insults about his appearance, blaming everyone in his life for his looks.
summary: A design critique backfires when the criticized coworker blames the ugliness of her environment and then savagely insults the critic's looks.

title: Cash Cow Strains to Produce

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, you must be the cash cow I keep hearing about.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You must be making cash right now!

transcript.speaker: Cash Cow
transcript.text: It doesn't work every time.

setting: Office, in front of a wall with a green edge
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, meets a cow wearing a dollar sign who is supposedly the company's cash cow. He remarks that it must be making money, and the cow visibly strains and grimaces as if trying to produce it. The cow then explains that the effort doesn't succeed every time.
punchline: The cash cow is treated like a literal animal that strains to produce, with the implication that it is dropping manure rather than money, so the 'cash' it makes isn't reliably valuable.
summary: A literal cow wearing a dollar sign is cornered by a coworker who expects it to churn out money on demand, and the results are underwhelming.

file: 2012/2012-04-15_correlations_predicted outcomes_problem_enormous ceo compensation_myth_control over profits_awkward_trap door_ceo trick_violent.gif
title: CEO Pay Myth Trapdoor Drop

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did a study of our past business plans and found something.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no correlation between our predicted and actual outcomes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That might be a problem for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your enormous CEO compensation is based on the myth that you have some control over our profitability.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Ha!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it just me, or is this awkward?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: No, I'm feeling it too.

situation: Dilbert tells the CEO that his study found no correlation between the company's business plan predictions and actual results, which undermines the justification for the CEO's huge pay. The CEO laughs and presses a button that opens a trapdoor under Dilbert. Dilbert braces himself across the opening and stays suspended, and the two of them make awkward small talk about the situation.
punchline: The CEO tries to eliminate the employee delivering an inconvenient truth by dropping him through a trapdoor, and the failed attempt leaves both men casually admitting how awkward it is.
summary: A worker's analysis exposing the pointlessness of executive pay triggers a hidden trapdoor, and the stalled attempt to dispose of him gets treated like ordinary social discomfort.

file: 2012/2012-08-05_business ethics_work ethic_top engineers_competetors_firing_get rid of_updating resume_goes as planned_hideous disese_felt useuful_threatening employment.gif
title: Boss Sends Wally To Sabotage Competitors

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With any luck, one of our competitors will try to poach you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That will save me the trouble of firing you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be going with five other people I want to get rid of.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I took the liberty of updating your résumé.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If this goes as planned, you'll destroy one of our competitors from within, like a hideous disease.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make me proud!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was the first time I ever felt useful.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't like it.

setting: Office cubicle, with a closing scene in a purple-backdrop panel
situation: The Boss tells Wally he is being sent to a top engineering conference, hoping a competitor will hire him away so he doesn't have to fire him. He adds that five other unwanted employees are going too, and that he has already updated Wally's résumé. The Boss then cheerfully says that Wally could destroy a competitor from within like a disease.
punchline: Wally, the notoriously lazy and useless employee, is given a job in which his uselessness is a weapon, and the one time he feels useful he finds he doesn't like it.
summary: A manager dumps his least valuable staff on a rival company by disguising it as a prestigious conference trip, expecting them to wreck the competitor.

title: Intern Too Insignificant for a Name

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This is my new intern. I haven't bothered to name him yet.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've been treated poorly as an intern, and I'm anxious to perpetuate the cycle of abuse.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I have a name!

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: He's feisty. I like that.

situation: An office worker introduces a new intern to a colleague, saying he hasn't bothered to name him. He then admits he was mistreated as an intern and now wants to pass the abuse along. The intern protests that he has a name, and the seated colleague is amused by his spirit.
punchline: The coworker cheerfully admits to deliberately continuing a cycle of mistreatment, and the intern's protest of basic dignity is welcomed as 'feisty' rather than taken as a legitimate complaint.
summary: A veteran employee openly plans to haunt a nameless new intern with the same mistreatment he once endured.

file: 2012/2012-09-27_internet & world wide web_web traffic_blatant honesty_money_negotiations_various things_vague stuff_vagueness.gif
title: Social Media Expert Sells Vagueness

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Social media expert

transcript.speaker: Social Media Expert
transcript.text: If you give me lots of money, I will do various vague things to increase your web traffic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! I would have been happy with just various things, but that vague stuff sounds great too!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And now he's my responsibility?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't screw up his vagueness plan because I think it can work.

situation: A social media expert pitches the Boss, openly admitting he will take lots of money and do various vague things to boost web traffic. The Boss is delighted by the vagueness and hires him. He then assigns the consultant to Dilbert, warning him not to ruin the plan.
punchline: The Boss is thrilled by a consultant's openly vague and empty pitch, then dumps responsibility for making it work onto Dilbert.
summary: A consultant honestly promises nothing concrete for a pile of cash, and the gullible boss eagerly buys in and hands the problem to an employee.

file: 2012/2012-03-28_raise_married with children_new family_benefit expenses_laser like focus_procreating.gif
title: Raise Or I'll Have Children

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Give me a raise or else I'll get married and have children.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My new family would increase your benefit expenses and distract me from my laser-like focus on work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will gladly pay extra to prevent you from procreating.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Word it any way you like.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, threatens his boss that he will marry and have children unless he gets a raise, arguing that a family would raise benefit costs and distract him from work. The Boss responds by offering to pay extra to keep Wally from reproducing, and tells him to word the deal however he likes.
punchline: Wally's threat backfires because the Boss would happily pay to keep Wally from having children, and Wally's claim of 'laser-like focus on work' is absurd given his notorious laziness.
summary: A lazy employee tries to extort a raise by threatening to start a family, only to have his boss eagerly offer payment to stop him.

file: 2012/2012-06-17_telephones_reprogrammed speed dial_cellphone_calls himself_intelligence test_hold on_failed intelligence test_20 minutes.gif

transcript.text: Ring

transcript.text: Ring

situation: Dilbert reprograms the Boss's desk phone speed dial so it calls his own cellphone, as a test of the Boss's intelligence. The Boss answers his cellphone while holding the desk phone, and each side tells the other to hold on. Alice notes the confused loop has been running twenty minutes.
punchline: The Boss is so dim he spends twenty minutes arguing with himself on two phones, repeatedly telling himself to hold on, without realizing he is talking to himself.
summary: A prank on the boss's phone turns into a lengthy exchange in which he keeps putting himself on hold.

title: Social Media Expert's Ambiguous Fee

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Social media expert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume we pay you based on how much you increase our social media hits.

transcript.speaker: Social Media Expert
transcript.text: No. My fee is whatever I think you're dumb enough to pay for ambiguous outcomes.

transcript.speaker: Social Media Expert
transcript.text: Either hope just left my body or the popcorn is getting chatty.

situation: Dilbert meets with a consultant labelled as a social media expert and assumes they will be paid according to how many social media hits he generates. The expert flatly rejects that and says he charges whatever he thinks the client is dumb enough to pay, for vague results. In the last panel, Dilbert reacts with a bleak quip about hope leaving his body or noisy popcorn.
punchline: The consultant openly admits to charging whatever he can get away with for unmeasurable results, leaving Dilbert so deflated he jokes that hope has physically left his body.
summary: A hired web guru cheerfully admits his pricing is based purely on how gullible the customer is, crushing the client's last bit of optimism.

title: Acquaintances Are For Silent Coffee

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Do you feel any need to make conversation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I don't mind standing in your general vicinity to counter the common perception of you as a sociopathic loner.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: You totally get me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what acquaintances are for.

setting: Office break area during a coffee break
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug asks Dilbert whether he feels any need to make small talk, and Dilbert says no. Dilbert offers to simply stand near him in silence so people won't think the coworker is a sociopathic loner. The coworker is delighted, and Dilbert explains this is the purpose of acquaintances.
punchline: Dilbert redefines acquaintances as people you stand near silently to provide social cover, with no actual conversation or friendship involved.
summary: Two coworkers agree to share quiet coffee breaks side by side purely so neither looks like an antisocial loner.

title: Compliment Mistaken for Thank You

transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This isn't a "thank you" situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're welcome?

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: During a meeting, a young employee marvels that the Boss's watch costs more than everything he owns. The Boss takes it as a compliment and says thank you. The employee points out that this isn't something to be thanked for, and the Boss awkwardly replies 'You're welcome?' while Dilbert sits silently beside him.
punchline: The employee was making a pointed remark about the huge pay gap, but the oblivious Boss mistakes it for praise and cannot even respond appropriately to the correction.
summary: A junior worker's pointed remark about a pricey timepiece is cheerfully accepted as flattery by his clueless superior.

title: Thanking Coworker for Performance Plan

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Guess who made it onto the ninety-day performance improvement plan.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Wally

setting: Office break area with coffee mugs
situation: A smug coworker announces to Dilbert and Wally that he has been placed on the ninety-day performance improvement plan. He spins it as a valuable service to the team rather than a personal honor. Dilbert wonders if they should thank him, and Wally sarcastically asks if they are polite now.
punchline: The coworker pretends being put on a performance improvement plan is a noble service, because it means someone else on the team is spared, and Wally sarcastically points out that Dilbert's suggestion to thank him would be uncharacteristically polite.
summary: A colleague spins his looming performance review as a sacrifice for the group, and his peers respond with deadpan indifference.

file: 2012/2012-12-08_grass roots politics_taxes_work ethic_initiative_grass roots movement_raise taxes_checkmate_income level.gif

transcript.speaker: Carol

punchline: Carol proves her initiative by retaliating against the Boss's excuse, hitting him in his own wallet and leaving him with only a feeble complaint.
summary: Denied a raise for supposedly lacking drive, a secretary promptly organizes a political campaign to raise her boss's taxes.

file: 2012/2012-05-06_booth_brochure_exhibitions_exhibitor expenses_expenses_huge crowds_last 11 years_logo sign_new customers_popular booth_spillover_steal chair_trade show_video of incident_youtube.gif

punchline: The Boss treats a total failure as normal because the company has wasted money on trade shows for eleven years, and he optimistically expects next year to be the same.
summary: After an expensive and fruitless exhibition, the boss shrugs it off as business as usual and looks forward to repeating it.

title: Coaching a More Capable Employee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: The Boss visits Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and announces he has come to coach him. Dilbert points out that coaching makes little sense when the employee outclasses the coach in every way. The Boss responds by criticizing Dilbert's attitude, and Dilbert retorts that the criticism comes from an angry person.
punchline: The Boss can't dispute that he is less capable, so he deflects by attacking Dilbert's attitude, and Dilbert points out the hypocrisy of an angry manager lecturing about attitude.
summary: A manager's attempt to coach his far more skilled subordinate collapses into a petty exchange about who has the worse temperament.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fine.
