situation: The boss announces a new rule making every screen saver the company logo, then says the CEO wants suggestions for the most useless rule to eliminate. Dilbert nominates the screen-saver rule, but the boss refuses because it is too new. Dilbert gives in and instead nominates whatever item comes next on the agenda.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the boss's next agenda item will also be a useless rule, and the boss's refusal shows that he will not consider scrapping a pointless policy.
summary: A manager rules out a pet policy as too fresh to be scrapped, so an employee jabs back by nominating whatever comes next on the agenda.

file: 2012/2012-02-22_frustration_mobile (cell) phones_dead battery_charge cell phone_too busy_no time.gif
title: Too Busy to Charge Phone

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You never answer when I call your cell.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My battery is dead.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe you should charge it for once.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't have time for that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What do you do all day that makes you so busy?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For starters, I have this conversation a lot.

setting: Office hallway near a cubicle wall
situation: Alice complains that Wally never answers his cell phone, and he says the battery is dead. She suggests he charge it, but he claims he has no time, so she angrily asks what keeps him so busy. Wally holding his coffee mug replies that he spends his time having this very conversation.
punchline: Wally's supposed busyness is really just the time he wastes dodging and explaining his own laziness, such as not charging his phone.
summary: A coworker's excuse for an uncharged phone turns out to be the very thing that eats up his day.

file: 2012/2012-08-21_managers & supervisors_tailored style_each employee_pool cue_leadership is guessing_business.gif
title: Tailored Leadership Involves Sharpened Pool Cue

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good manager tailors his leadership style to fit each employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In your case, I think the best approach involves poking you with a sharpened pool cue.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To be perfectly honest, a big part of leadership is guessing.

situation: The Boss stands beside a seated employee at his computer and explains that good managers adapt their leadership style to each person. He then announces that, for this employee, the best approach is poking him with a sharpened pool cue, and proceeds to poke him. He admits that a big part of leadership is just guessing.
punchline: The Boss's 'tailored' leadership approach is physically abusing his employee with a sharpened stick, and he casually admits that his management style is really just guesswork.
summary: A manager boasts about customizing his leadership to each worker, then picks a violent method for one employee and confesses he is mostly guessing.

file: 2012/2012-12-05_suspicion_assemble data_boring work_quality over quality_poor politics_office politics.gif
title: Boss Orders Deliberately Incomprehensible Data

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to assemble a huge amount of totally incomprehensible data.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make it boring so no one looks at it too closely. I'm aiming for quantity over quality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a bad feeling about this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one would pay you to feel good.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert to compile a huge pile of incomprehensible data and deliberately make it boring so nobody examines it closely. Dilbert says he has a bad feeling about the assignment, and the Boss dismisses his misgivings.
punchline: The Boss cynically implies that employees are paid to do unpleasant or dubious work, so Dilbert's discomfort is irrelevant.
summary: A manager asks an engineer to bury something questionable under a mountain of dull data and brushes off the engineer's unease with a bleak remark about what he's paid for.

title: Boss Baits Dilbert Into Overreacting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you mean by "doesn't take criticism well"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is a perfect example. I say one little thing and you go all nuts on me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the trap is set.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: During his performance review, Dilbert asks the Boss what he means by the note that he doesn't take criticism well. The Boss calmly says Dilbert's reaction proves the point, and Dilbert grows visibly agitated. In the last panel the Boss thinks that his trap is set, revealing he provoked Dilbert on purpose.
punchline: The Boss deliberately provokes Dilbert into an outburst so that his reaction becomes proof of the criticism, making the review impossible to win.
summary: A manager steers an employee into an agitated reaction during an evaluation so the employee's own response confirms the negative review.

title: Hiring Change Director Versus Sensible Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're hiring a Director of Change Management to help employees embrace strategic changes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we could come up with strategies that make sense. Then employees would embrace change.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds harder.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces plans to hire a Director of Change Management so employees will accept strategic changes. Dilbert suggests that creating strategies that actually make sense would make employees embrace change on their own. The Boss dismisses the idea because it sounds like more work.
punchline: Management would rather pay for a new role to sell bad strategies than put in the harder effort of making good ones.
summary: A manager prefers hiring a specialist to push unpopular plans over the more demanding task of devising sensible ones.

file: 2012/2012-03-31_app store_created app_dream killer_first name_free apps_madonna_sell a million_mother_family.gif
title: Mom Crushes Dilbert's App Dream

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent four months creating this app, Mom. I think I can sell a million of them for $3.99.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: I saw seven apps just like this in the app store and five of them were free.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for the feedback, dream-killer.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Have you ever thought of just using your first name, like Madonna?

situation: Dilbert proudly shows his mother the mobile app he spent four months building and predicts a million sales at $3.99. She checks the app store and points out that seven similar apps exist and five are free. When Dilbert sarcastically calls her a dream-killer, she responds with an unrelated suggestion that he go by just his first name like Madonna.
punchline: After deflating his business plan with market reality, Dilbert's mom blithely changes the subject to a celebrity-style rebrand, showing she either missed or ignored how discouraging she was being.
summary: A son hoping to get rich from his homemade smartphone app gets a cold dose of competition research from his mother, who then offers an oddly irrelevant branding tip.

file: 2012/2012-06-24_carbon dioxide_exhales endangered species_fabrications_harbard_higgs boson particle_licorice and flashlight_national football league_no bragging rights_no kids_training for olympics.gif
title: Dilbert Hires Topper to Brag

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My daughter is training for the Olympics. My son is going to Harvard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no spawn of my own, so I claim the right to name a proxy to brag on my behalf.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Topper, I need you.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: Of course you do.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: My daughter discovered the Higgs Boson particle using nothing but licorice and a flashlight.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: My son inhales carbon dioxide and exhales endangered species while playing in the National Football League.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This isn't fair! You can't just make up stuff!

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: According to the President of the International Society of Boasters, fabrications are acceptable.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'd like to talk to that guy.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: You're looking at him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I win.

situation: A coworker brags about her children's impressive achievements, so Dilbert, who has no kids, appoints his smug rival Topper as a proxy to out-brag her. Topper invents absurd claims about his children, and when the coworker objects that he is making things up, he cites the president of the International Society of Boasters. It turns out Topper himself holds that title.
punchline: Dilbert wins the bragging contest because his proxy is the president of the boasters' society, who says fabrication is allowed, so the rules were rigged in his favor all along.
summary: A parent's smug family boasting is crushed when Dilbert recruits a ringer whose outlandish lies are officially sanctioned by his own boasting organization.

file: 2012/2012-02-27_internet & world wide web_ideas_wine_liquid lunch_tweet_down trodden_sense of humor_twitter_cell phone_office_technology.gif
title: Drunken Boss Tweets Insult

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bad idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should drink wine at lunch more often.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Worse idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm in the mood to tweet.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Worst idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope the down-trodden have a sense of humor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Send.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's desk
situation: The Boss walks down the hall musing that he should drink wine at lunch more often. He then sits at his desk with his phone, deciding he wants to tweet. Finally he hopes the downtrodden will find his message funny and hits send.
punchline: Each panel is labeled a worse idea than the last, ending with the tipsy boss tweeting something that will likely offend his downtrodden employees or the public.
summary: A boss escalates from midday drinking to impulsive social media posting, with captions ranking each decision as progressively more foolish.

title: Needing a Witness Around Larry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait. Hold that crazy thought.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to get a witness in the room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice, would you mind coming to the conference room for a minute?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What fresh heck is this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Larry is a sadist and a sociopath, but he hides it when there's more than one witness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, Larry, what do you think of my project?

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: It looks great! I'll be happy to help you in any way I can!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Am I done here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't turn your back!

situation: Dilbert is meeting with Larry, a hostile coworker, and stops him mid-rant to fetch Alice as a witness. With Alice present, Larry suddenly turns friendly and supportive about Dilbert's project. When Alice asks to leave, Dilbert warns her not to turn her back, because Larry will revert to his true nature.
punchline: Larry is only pleasant when there are multiple witnesses, so Dilbert pleads for Alice to stay, since the moment she leaves Larry's nastiness will return.
summary: A coworker who turns charming whenever an audience appears gets exposed when Dilbert recruits a bystander to keep him in check.

title: Considering Yourself Excreted, Without Euphemisms

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Just give it to me straight. Skip all of your jargon and euphemisms.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Don't tell me you're rebalancing or offboarding or streamlining. Just talk the way you'd talk to your spouse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Consider yourself excreted.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Well, now I see why you use euphemisms.

situation: An employee about to be laid off asks the boss to drop the corporate jargon and speak plainly, as he would to his spouse. The boss complies with a crude, blunt phrase telling him he is being fired. The employee then admits that the euphemisms were preferable.
punchline: Plain speech about being fired turns out to be far more brutal than corporate euphemisms, which exist precisely to soften the blow.
summary: A worker facing dismissal demands honest talk from his boss, only to discover that the blunt version of getting fired is much harsher than the polite one.
themes: be careful what you wish for

title: The Contagious Bad Apple Joins

transcript.speaker: Bad Apple
transcript.text: I'm the new bad apple. I'll be joining your project.

transcript.speaker: Bad Apple
transcript.text: In the interest of full disclosure, this is totally contagious.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm immune, but not for reasons I'm proud of.

transcript.speaker: Bad Apple
transcript.text: You must be Wally.

characters: Bad Apple (coworker with an apple head)
situation: A new coworker with a wormy rotten-apple head introduces himself as the new bad apple joining the project team. He warns the group that his badness is contagious, and the other team members start to sprout worms. Wally says he is immune, and the bad apple immediately guesses who he is.
punchline: Wally is so famously lazy and unproductive that he is already a bad apple, so he can't be corrupted any further, and the newcomer knows his reputation.
summary: A literal rotten apple joins a project team and warns that his negativity spreads, but the office slacker is already beyond saving.

title: Promoting From Within, Admitting Ruin

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like to promote from within.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only downside is that picking from a smaller pool of candidates will make us less capable than our competitors and lead the company to ruination.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you want that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see what you're doing.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss says he likes to promote from within, then cheerfully admits that choosing from a smaller pool of candidates will make the company weaker than its competitors and could ruin it. Alice asks if he really wants that outcome, while Dilbert notes he sees what the Boss is up to.
punchline: The Boss openly states that his promotion policy will lead the company to ruin, yet pursues it anyway, implying he is more interested in his own convenience or favoritism than in the company's success.
summary: A manager explains that his favored hiring habit will gradually doom the business, and his colleagues respond with bafflement and suspicion.

title: Pushing Back With Honest Excuses

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need to give you some push-back on these due dates.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. Should I tell the others you're lazy, or incompetent, or in over your head?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How about just "busy"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. I will insist that people ignore the root cause.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he needs to push back on his due dates. Dilbert cheerfully offers to explain the delay to others as laziness, incompetence, or being overwhelmed. The coworker asks him to say "busy" instead, and Dilbert agrees while pointedly noting that people should ignore the real reason.
punchline: Dilbert agrees to cover for the coworker's missed deadlines with a flattering excuse while sarcastically implying the true root cause is the coworker's own shortcomings.
summary: A colleague wanting extra time is offered a menu of unflattering explanations and settles for the mildest one, which comes with a sarcastic caveat.

file: 2012/2012-10-05_dieting & weight control_interviews_tattoos & body marking_job interview_face tattoo_overeating_bad idea_people can see_dont interview well.gif
title: Face Tattoo Meets Overeating Insult

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Did you ever think that getting that face tattoo might be a bad career move?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: No. Was there ever a time you thought overeating was a bad idea?

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Because people can see that.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: You don't interview well.

situation: A heavyset interviewer asks a job candidate with a heart tattoo on his forehead whether the face tattoo might hurt his career. The candidate fires back by asking whether the interviewer ever thought overeating was a bad idea. The interviewer defends the question by noting that people can see the tattoo, and the candidate retorts that he interviews badly.
punchline: The candidate answers the interviewer's rude question about his visible tattoo by insulting the interviewer's weight, and then criticizes the interviewer's technique, turning the interview around.
summary: A job seeker with a conspicuous forehead tattoo trades barbs with an interviewer who questioned his appearance, ending by faulting the interviewer's skills.

title: The Only Project Is Doomed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's your project going?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mean the one that has...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...no management support, ambiguous goals, no budget, and an angry team of overworked people who want it to die?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, the other one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes there isn't an "other one."

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how his project is going. Dilbert lists the project's crippling problems: no support, vague goals, no budget and a resentful, overworked team. The Boss asks about the other project, and Dilbert points out that he only has the one.
punchline: The Boss assumes Dilbert must have a better project to talk about, but Dilbert's miserable project is the only one he has, so there is no good news to report.
summary: A manager's cheerful check-in meets a grim inventory of everything wrong with an employee's sole project, and the hopeful request for a different one goes nowhere.

file: 2012/2012-03-14_new product development_stock buy back_stock market_dream_using capitol_money.gif
title: Dilbert Celebrates Boss's Worthlessness Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm canceling all of our new product development and using the capital for a stock buy-back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is a dream come true because I always wanted to be like you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In what way are you...?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yay! I'm worthless!

situation: The Boss, seated in his armchair, announces he is cancelling all new product development and spending the money on a stock buy-back. Dilbert says it is a dream come true because he always wanted to be like the Boss. When the Boss asks in what way, Dilbert cheerfully kicks up his heel and declares he is worthless.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically insults the Boss by gleefully claiming to be worthless, implying that a manager who gives up on creating value in favor of financial maneuvering is himself worthless.
summary: A manager abandons innovation to prop up the share price, and an employee joyfully mocks him by celebrating his own uselessness.

title: Resume Padding Apology Goes Sideways

transcript.speaker: Speaker at podium
transcript.text: I'd like to address the rumor that I padded my résumé.

transcript.speaker: Speaker at podium
transcript.text: In the strictest sense of the word, I am not technically an "engineer" per se.

transcript.speaker: Speaker at podium
transcript.text: But to put this in perspective, even the Pope hides his browser history.

transcript.speaker: Hand puppet
transcript.text: It's no big deal.

situation: A bald executive in a suit stands at a podium and publicly addresses a rumor that he padded his résumé. He grudgingly admits he isn't technically an engineer, then deflects by claiming even the Pope hides his browser history, while a hand puppet on his arm reassures the audience that it's no big deal.
punchline: The executive's non-apology minimizes his lie by comparing it to the Pope's embarrassing secrets, and even has a puppet chime in to dismiss the scandal.
summary: A public figure gives a weaselly apology for faking his credentials, deflecting with a ridiculous comparison while a sock-puppet-style sidekick backs him up.

title: Schedule Chaos Excuses Dilbert Absence

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you see the schedule I sent out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, and all four updates.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you see the correction, and then Carl's changes, and the email about moving all of the Tuesday stuff to Thursdays?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you put it on your calendar?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That reminds me that I can't make it.

situation: A coworker seated at a desk asks Dilbert whether he saw the schedule she sent out. Dilbert says he saw it and all four updates, and she lists a correction, Carl's changes, and an email moving Tuesday events to Thursdays. When she asks if he put it on his calendar, he says he now remembers he can't attend.
punchline: The schedule was revised so many times that being asked to put it on his calendar finally reminds Dilbert of a conflict, implying the constant updates made the whole thing impossible to take seriously.
summary: After a barrage of revisions to an event schedule, the one thing Dilbert takes away is that he has a reason to skip it.

title: Correlation Is Not Causation, Sleep Edition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some of the most famous geniuses in the world slept only four hours per night.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm doing four hours a night too because you know what they say: Correlation is the same thing as causation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No one says that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, right. And I should take the word of an oversleeper.

setting: Office break area, with coworkers holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that he is sleeping only four hours a night because famous geniuses did the same. He claims that everyone knows correlation is the same as causation, and when Wally points out that nobody says that, he dismisses Wally's objection by calling him an oversleeper.
punchline: The Boss commits the correlation-causation fallacy and then dismisses valid criticism by attacking the critic's sleeping habits rather than addressing the argument.
summary: A manager copies the sleep habits of geniuses on the theory that matching their schedule will match their brilliance, then brushes off a coworker's correction with a petty insult.

file: 2012/2012-01-27_benefits of personhood_chemical nutrients_death & dying_inventions_petri dish_robot_scientific equipment_skin cells_sneezes_science.gif
title: Immortality Via Skin Cell Robot

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Before I die, I plan to put some of my skin cells in a petri dish with chemical nutrients and store it inside a robot.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: By law, I will still be alive as long as any part of my body is functioning. My robot will enjoy the full benefits of personhood.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: My robot and I will live forever!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Until it sneezes you out.

setting: Office lunch table in a break room or cafeteria
situation: Three coworkers sit at a lunch table while a bald, bespectacled colleague explains his plan to keep skin cells alive in a petri dish inside a robot. He claims the law will consider him alive and grant his robot the benefits of personhood. Dilbert deflates the scheme by pointing out a flaw.
punchline: Dilbert points out that the robot's petri dish of skin cells could be lost with a simple sneeze, making the supposed immortality absurdly fragile.
summary: A coworker brags about cheating death by stashing his skin cells in a robot, until Dilbert notes how easily it could all go wrong.

title: Interviewer Lacks Interview Practice Hours

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Studies show that it takes 10,000 hours of focused practice to become an expert at anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to your resume, you've only had enough database experience to be an incompetent menace.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: How many hours have you practiced doing interviews?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like where this is heading.

situation: A job candidate tells the interviewer that expertise takes 10,000 hours of practice. The Boss, holding the candidate's resume, replies that the candidate's database experience only qualifies him as an incompetent menace. The candidate turns the logic around and asks how many hours the Boss has practiced interviewing.
punchline: The candidate uses the 10,000-hours rule against the Boss, implying the Boss is an incompetent interviewer, and the Boss realizes he is being turned into the target of his own insult.
summary: A candidate answers a harsh resume critique by questioning how much practice the interviewer has had at interviewing.

title: Honest Bank Teller Mocks Deposit

transcript.speaker: Bank Teller
transcript.text: Thanks for the deposit, sucker!

transcript.speaker: Bank Teller
transcript.text: We plan to waste it on complicated hedging strategies that we don't even understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your honesty is refreshing.

transcript.speaker: Bank Teller
transcript.text: Thanks, but it makes cross-selling harder...

situation: Dilbert makes a deposit at a bank, and the teller cheerfully calls him a sucker. The teller openly admits the bank will squander the money on complicated hedging strategies nobody there understands. Dilbert says the honesty is refreshing, and the teller replies that it hurts his ability to cross-sell products.
punchline: The teller's brutal candour about the bank's incompetence is welcome to the customer, but the teller only regrets it because it undermines his sales pitch.
summary: A bank employee frankly admits that customer money will be frittered away on strategies the bank can't comprehend, then worries only about its effect on upselling.

file: 2012/2012-10-19_business ethics_consumer protection_court ordered_good defense_internal emails_known to be dangerous.gif
title: Ignorance as a Legal Defense

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: The court ordered us to turn over all of our internal emails.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Have you ever mentioned in email that our products are known to be dangerous but we don't care?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't even know what products we make.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: That's a good defense. We might need that.

situation: A company lawyer tells the Boss that a court has ordered the company to hand over all internal emails. He asks whether the Boss ever wrote that the company's products are known to be dangerous but that nobody cares. The Boss replies that he doesn't even know what products the company makes, and the lawyer approves of this as a defense.
punchline: The Boss's total obliviousness about his own company is treated as a valuable legal shield, since he can't be held accountable for knowing about dangerous products.
summary: Facing a court order to produce emails, a lawyer is delighted to learn his boss is too clueless to even know what the company sells.

title: Question Relayed Up Chain, Nonsense Returns

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I sent your question up the chain of command.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I talked to the district manager who talked to his AVP who talked to his VP who talked to his SVP who talked to the CEO.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The answer is that we need to shine the Braille Toad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you see any problem with our system?

setting: Office hallway, with an exterior shot of a corporate building
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he forwarded Dilbert's question through every level of management, from the district manager up to the CEO. The answer that came back is a nonsensical instruction to shine the Braille Toad. Dilbert asks whether the Boss sees a problem with the system.
punchline: After passing through six layers of management, a simple question returns as a meaningless answer, showing how hierarchy garbles information and that the Boss is blind to the flaw.
summary: A question passed up through six rungs of management comes back as gibberish, leaving Dilbert to point out the obvious flaw in the process.

title: Dogbert's Abusive Tech Support Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert's Tech Support. How may I abuse you?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I think my digital modem is broken.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please hold while I pretend to be testing it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, it looks fine from here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The problem must be in your wiring.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll have to rip out all of the wiring in your entire house to locate the problem.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Are you sure? Because the lights on the modem aren't even on.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That means you have moisture on your internal wiring. You'll also need to replace all of your plumbing and get a new roof.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: May I speak with your supervisor?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure. But he sounds exactly like me.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center and the customer's home
situation: A customer calls Dogbert's tech support about a broken modem. Dogbert openly pretends to test it, blames the customer's house wiring, and escalates to demanding that the entire house's wiring, plumbing and roof be replaced. When the customer asks for a supervisor, Dogbert says he can put one on, but it will sound just like him.
punchline: Asking for a supervisor is futile because the 'supervisor' is just Dogbert again, so there is no escalation path from his bad advice.
summary: A tech support agent invents absurdly expensive repairs for a simple modem fault and then reveals that escalating to his boss will get the same person.

file: 2012/2012-09-21_choked pooch_platform deciosn_throw under bus_very bad person_regional idioms.gif
title: Literal Reading of Blame Idioms

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carl choked the pooch on the platform decision. I need you to throw him under the bus.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He sounds like a very bad person. I will take care of that right away.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I just found a website that lists regional idioms. I've done some bad, bad things.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and a hallway
situation: The Boss tells Asok that Carl botched the platform decision and orders him to throw Carl under the bus. Asok takes the idioms literally and agrees to deal with 'a very bad person'. He later looks up the phrases on a website of regional idioms and realizes, with horror, what he has done.
punchline: Asok took the Boss's violent-sounding idioms literally and acted on them, only learning afterward that he had done terrible things to Carl.
summary: A young employee carries out his boss's figures of speech as literal instructions and is horrified when he finally looks the phrases up.

title: Karma Arrives at the Meeting Table

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's the guy who hasn't responded to any of my seventeen emails, nine texts, and four voicemails.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be awkward sitting here now. Are you trying to concoct a plausible excuse for ignoring my messages?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Say hello to Karma.

situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table and points out a coworker who has ignored all of his emails, texts and voicemails. He taunts the man, suggesting he is inventing an excuse. The coworker, who has been silent, glares at Dilbert and announces that Karma has arrived.
punchline: Dilbert's gloating at the coworker for ignoring him is met with a threat that the coworker will now retaliate, implying Dilbert has been similarly unresponsive or is about to pay for his smugness.
summary: After publicly shaming a colleague who dodged his messages, Dilbert is met with a menacing promise of payback.

file: 2012/2012-06-30_huge fee_non practicing entity_patent troll_patents_playing field_plunge civilization_tangle innovation_thwart compnies_dark ages.gif
title: Patent Troll Offers His Services

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm a patent troll, but you can call me a non-practicing entity.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a huge fee, I will use my patents to thwart the companies that are trying to thwart you with their own patents.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Together we can strangle innovation and plunge civilization into the Dark Ages!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That would even the playing field.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, introduces himself to the Boss as a patent troll and offers, for a huge fee, to use his patents against rival companies' patents. He cheerfully admits that the result will be strangled innovation and a return to the Dark Ages. The Boss thoughtfully concludes that this would level the playing field.
punchline: The Boss sees the destruction of innovation and civilization as a positive because it would put him on equal footing with his competitors.
summary: A scheming dog sells a worried executive a patent-warfare plan that would wreck progress, and the executive is delighted at the fairness of it.

title: Believing Everything Read Online

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my research on the Internet, Plan B will work best.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm rolling my eyes because you believe everything you read on the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I should take a picture in case someone ever asks me if ignorance has a tell.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his internet research shows Plan B will work best. The Boss responds by announcing that he is rolling his eyes because Dilbert believes everything he reads online. Dilbert snaps back that he should photograph the Boss's face in case anyone asks whether ignorance has a tell.
punchline: The Boss, who is notoriously ignorant, condescendingly criticizes Dilbert's gullibility, and Dilbert turns it around by suggesting the Boss's smug eye-rolling expression is the very picture of ignorance.
summary: A boss dismisses an employee's web-based research as naive, only to be mocked for displaying the telltale face of the truly clueless.

title: CEO Eye Lasers Punish Criticism

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Would you accept some constructive criticism from a humble intern?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Activating CEO eye lasers!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It stings for a few minutes, and then you surprise yourself with what you can get used to.

situation: A humble intern asks the bald CEO whether he would accept some constructive criticism. The CEO responds by announcing he is activating his eye lasers and burns a hole through the intern's head. Afterward, Dilbert, holding coffee, consoles the intern, who now has a smoking hole through his skull, by explaining that you get used to it.
punchline: Offering feedback to an executive gets you literally blasted, and Dilbert's calm reassurance that you get used to it implies employees simply learn to live with the abuse.
summary: A junior employee who dares to critique the boss gets a hole burned through his head, and a coworker casually explains that people adapt to such treatment.

title: Wally's Elbonia Trip: Anything Goes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I need you to attend a standards meeting in Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Heh, heh. A lot of things are legal in Elbonia that aren't legal here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are any of you not libertarians?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Heh, heh, heh.

situation: The Boss asks Wally to attend a standards meeting in Elbonia. Wally gleefully remarks that many things are legal there that are not legal at home. The Boss then asks the room whether anyone is not a libertarian, while Wally grins over his coffee mug.
punchline: Wally is eager to go to Elbonia because of its lax laws, and the Boss's question about libertarians suggests he is choosing travelers who will happily exploit that lawlessness, with Wally's grin confirming his intentions.
summary: A manager picks his staff for a trip to a lawless foreign country and wonders aloud if anyone present objects to minimal government.

title: Bear Attack Photos Instead of Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Studies say your happiness depends on how well your life compares to others.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So instead of giving you a raise, I'm going to show you pictures of people who were attacked by bears.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you feel better now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dang you to heck, this is working!

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk
situation: The Boss cites a study claiming happiness depends on comparing your life to others. Instead of giving Dilbert a raise, he shows him photos of people who were mauled by bears. Dilbert is annoyed to discover it actually makes him feel better.
punchline: Dilbert is furious that the cheap trick of showing him bear attack victims actually works, letting the Boss avoid paying him more.
summary: A manager swaps a pay increase for gruesome photos of bear victims, and his employee grudgingly admits the cheap psychological trick is effective.

title: Dogbert's Effective, Not Deceptive, Ads

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Ad Company to build some deceptive and abusive ads for our mobile app.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I prefer to call our ads "effective." It means the same thing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our most effective ad looks like a text message from your doctor saying he can't stop crying.

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that he hired Dogbert's ad company to create deceptive and abusive ads for the company's mobile app. Dogbert, seated at the table with Dilbert, says he prefers the word "effective" because it means the same thing. A final panel of an office building shows Dogbert describing his top ad as a fake text from a doctor who can't stop crying.
punchline: Dogbert treats "effective" and "deceptive and abusive" as synonyms, and his best ad is a cruel scare tactic that fakes a doctor's alarming message to manipulate people into clicking.
summary: An ad agency run by a dog happily admits that manipulating and frightening consumers is just what good advertising means.

file: 2012/2012-10-28_meetings_marketing plan_consumers_research is stupid_opposed to science_rational thinking_manifestaions_pendantic_semantics_stopped talking.gif
title: Boss Dismisses Research, Calls It Buy-In

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...and that's our marketing plan for the coming year.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Research shows that consumers reject this sort of approach.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Research is stupid.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you saying the studies on this particular topic are flawed?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Or are you just generally opposed to science, rational thinking, and all manifestations of common sense?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop being pedantic with your semantics.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you get buy-in?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, in the sense that they stopped talking.

setting: Conference room, then the Boss's office
situation: The Boss presents a marketing plan to his team. Alice points out that research shows consumers reject this approach, and the Boss declares research stupid and accuses her of pedantry when she presses him. Afterward Dogbert, acting as a consultant, asks whether he got buy-in, and the Boss claims success because the team went quiet.
punchline: The Boss treats his team's silence, after he shut down their valid objections, as genuine agreement.
summary: A manager waves away evidence against his plan, then counts his team's stunned silence as full support.

title: Turned On By A Framework

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: So, what do you do for a living?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm working on a framework to allow construction of large-scale analytical queries on unstructured data.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm a little turned on by that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Settle down. It's just a framework.

setting: A bar, where Dilbert is chatting with a woman holding a glass of red wine
situation: At a bar, a woman asks Dilbert what he does for a living. He describes his work on a framework for large-scale analytical queries on unstructured data, and she admits she finds it a little arousing. Dilbert responds as if she is overreacting to something dull.
punchline: Dilbert is so used to technical jargon being boring that he treats the woman's attraction as an overreaction, saying it's only a framework, which is a joke about geek dating and how big-data buzzwords can excite people.
summary: A woman at a bar finds Dilbert's big-data job description strangely exciting, and he tells her to calm down because it's merely a framework.

title: Mentee Seeks Career Advice, Mentor Wants Work

transcript.speaker: Mentee
transcript.text: I don't know if I should focus on my strengths or strengthen my weaknesses.

transcript.speaker: Mentee
transcript.text: Or should I have a bias for action and not waste time sharpening any of my skills?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which path gets you to do actual work?

transcript.speaker: Mentee
transcript.text: I sense a coldness to your mentoring.

situation: A bald, bespectacled employee asks his boss, who is acting as his mentor, whether to focus on his strengths, shore up his weaknesses, or skip skill-building altogether. The boss cuts through the career dilemma by asking which option results in the employee doing actual work. The employee complains that the mentoring feels cold.
punchline: The boss's idea of mentoring is simply getting the employee to do more work, so the employee's complaint about coldness exposes how little real guidance is on offer.
summary: A worker agonizes over his professional development options, but his mentor only cares which choice produces the most labor.

file: 2012/2012-02-25_meetings_public speaking_powerpoint slides_intelligent viwers_manipulative anecdotes_boss died_praise employees.gif
title: Slides for Smart and Morons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My PowerPoint slides have a little something for everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For my intelligent viewers, I have data, and for the morons, I have manipulative anecdotes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which reminds me - did you hear about the boss who died because he didn't praise his employee?

situation: Dilbert presents his PowerPoint slides on a laptop to The Boss, who sits at his desk. He explains that the slides contain data for intelligent viewers and manipulative anecdotes for morons. He then launches into a manipulative anecdote about a boss who died for failing to praise his employee, aimed squarely at The Boss.
punchline: Dilbert implies The Boss is one of the morons by immediately using a manipulative anecdote on him, fishing for the praise he wants.
summary: A presenter boasts that his slides include facts for the smart and emotional stories for the dim, then promptly tries one of the stories on his own boss.

title: Dogbert Becomes Spiteful Venture Capitalist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become a venture capitalist.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll take money from the rich and give it to hopelessly doomed social media start-ups.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you love helping entrepreneurs?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because I hate rich people who aren't me.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is becoming a venture capitalist and plans to take money from wealthy investors and funnel it into social media start-ups that are certain to fail. Dilbert assumes Dogbert is motivated by a desire to support entrepreneurs. Dogbert reveals his real motive is resentment of rich people other than himself.
punchline: Dogbert's venture capital strategy is a deliberate scheme to waste other rich people's money on doomed start-ups, driven by envy rather than any wish to help entrepreneurs.
summary: A dog announces a career in investing whose real goal is to squander wealthy people's cash on companies he knows will fail, out of pure jealousy.

title: Tazer Disguised As Cellphone

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I invented a tazer that looks exactly like a cellphone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cool! Can I see it?

transcript.speaker: Boss (offscreen)
transcript.text: Gaaa-a-a-a-a-a-a!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I left it on our boss's desk, but it sounds like he's done with it.

setting: Office hallway near the boss's office
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert he has invented a tazer that looks exactly like a cellphone, and Dilbert asks to see it. A drawn-out scream is heard from the boss's office. Wally casually explains he left the device on the boss's desk and the boss is evidently done with it.
punchline: Wally deliberately left a disguised tazer where his boss would pick it up, so the boss shocked himself, and Wally nonchalantly reports it as if it were a normal handoff.
summary: A coworker's secret weapon gets field-tested on the boss without the boss's knowledge, and the screams confirm it works.

title: Something Always Comes Up Excuse

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I get your input by Friday?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Absolutely, unless something comes up.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How often does something come up?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: More than you'd think.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What exactly are we talking about?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd love to chat, but something just came up.

situation: A female coworker asks Wally for his input on something by Friday. Wally agrees with a built-in escape clause, 'unless something comes up,' and admits that something comes up very often. When she tries to clarify the request, he uses the same excuse to walk away from the conversation.
punchline: Wally's vague 'something came up' excuse is so all-purpose that he uses it to dodge the very conversation about how often he uses it.
summary: A coworker tries to pin down a deadline commitment, but Wally's habitual escape hatch lets him slip away before any work is promised.

title: Indestructible Tablet Demo Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crash!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's colleague
transcript.text: Our company is up next. Find the prototype.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Oops. Was that yours?

setting: Presentation or product demo before a panel at a long table
situation: A presenter at a demo event boasts that his company's tablet computer is indestructible and then drops or smashes it in front of a panel seated at a table. In the next scene, the team scheduled to present after him realizes the broken device is their prototype that he used for his demonstration.
punchline: The presenter's claim of indestructibility is disproved when he destroys the tablet, and he casually reveals he has just wrecked the next company's only prototype.
summary: A boastful presenter wrecks a gadget during his own show-and-tell, only to discover it belonged to the next team in line.

transcript.text: It's not my fault. I was born this way.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Literally

transcript.speaker: Woman with stroller

setting: Catbert's HR office, then a park path
situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss complains to Catbert, the evil HR director, that he is discriminated against for being short, bald and near-sighted, insisting he was born this way. The final panel shows a baby in a stroller who has the Boss's face, glasses and hair, so he was literally born that way.
punchline: The boss's claim of being born this way is taken literally when a newborn with his exact face, glasses and tuft of hair appears in a stroller.
summary: A grumbling manager pleads that his unflattering traits are innate, and a stroller baby with his own features turns the excuse into a visual gag.

title: Piranha Flu Sneeze Gone Wrong

transcript.speaker: Male Coworker
transcript.text: I've never heard of...

transcript.speaker: Female Coworker
transcript.text: AHCHOOO!!!

transcript.speaker: Female Coworker
transcript.text: I should probably tell people I just have bad allergies.

situation: A woman in a pink sweater tells a male coworker holding a coffee mug that she has a wicked case of piranha flu. She sneezes, and a swarm of angry piranhas flies out and strips the coworker down to a skeleton. She then remarks that she should probably tell people it is just bad allergies.
punchline: Her sneeze literally releases flesh-eating piranhas that kill her coworker, and she casually worries about how to explain it away as ordinary allergies.
summary: A sneezing coworker unleashes a flock of piranhas that devour her colleague, and she shrugs it off with a lame cover story.

title: Pre-Scheduled Hounding Over Unreliable Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you trying to be a jerk?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm experienced. It looks exactly the same.

situation: A coworker promises Dilbert some information by Tuesday. Dilbert says the coworker seems unreliable and calmly enters calendar reminders on his phone to hound them on Wednesday and escalate to their boss on Friday. When asked if he is being a jerk, he says that his experience makes the two look identical.
punchline: Dilbert admits that his experience with unreliable coworkers means that being prepared and being a jerk look exactly the same.
summary: Expecting a missed deadline, Dilbert books follow-up nagging and escalation in advance and shrugs off the accusation of rudeness.

title: CEO's Incentive: Feeling Underpaid Again

transcript.text: Profits are way down, but don't worry your little heads about it.

transcript.text: The board increased my annual compensation to $60 million. Now I finally have an incentive to do a good job!

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I'd better hurry because I'm already starting to feel underpaid again.

situation: A bald CEO addresses a few seated employees, including Dilbert, and says profits are down but they shouldn't worry. He then announces the board raised his pay to $60 million, which he says finally motivates him to do a good job. In the last panel he frets that he must hurry because he's already feeling underpaid again.
punchline: The CEO's motivation is purely about his own pay, which he admits he was never incentivized to do his job before, and even $60 million quickly stops feeling like enough.
summary: A chief executive shrugs off falling profits, celebrates a massive raise as his reason to finally work hard, and then worries that the raise is already wearing off.

punchline: Dilbert concludes that communication is overrated after being on the receiving end of brutally honest, unfiltered remarks, and Dogbert's agreement suggests he has just as little use for it.
summary: After colleagues blurt out harsh comments about his giant head, Dilbert goes home and decides that talking to people isn't worth the trouble.

title: Alice Meets Boss's Insulting Daughter

The daughter explains that this is really his way of complaining about her choosing to major in visual and performing arts. Alice, who dislikes the Boss, remarks that she can't decide whom to side with.
punchline: Alice is so unimpressed by both the Boss's cruel joke and the daughter's arts degree that she can't pick a side, which doubles as an insult to both of them.
summary: A boss sneers at his arts-major daughter in front of a coworker, who finds both of them equally hard to root for.

title: Legal Pump-and-Dump Newsletter Scheme

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is launching a pump-and-dump newsletter on thinly traded stocks, explaining it is legal if he discloses his holdings and can claim bad picks were honest mistakes. He then introduces his stock picker, a visibly drunk man in a loosened tie holding a glass of wine.
punchline: Dogbert's plausible deniability for fraud is a stock picker so drunk that his terrible picks will obviously look like honest mistakes.
summary: A scheming dog hires an intoxicated man to choose stocks so that his market manipulation can pass as innocent error.

summary: A manager traces his team's falling output back to a schoolchild's dirty hands while a clearly infected employee stays at her desk and denies being sick.

punchline: After gutting R&D, mass-firing staff, and wasting money on a trendy acquisition, management's demand that employees 'work smarter' sounded so absurd that everyone assumed it was a joke.
summary: A clueless executive reaches for the same failed cost-cutting playbook and learns his staff didn't take his motivational slogan seriously.

file: 2012/2012-08-01_computers & peripherals_intelligence agencies_national security_unnamed government agency_shadowy guy_create computer virus_elbonian missile factories.gif

summary: A proposal to haul an asteroid to the Moon for mining gets a more practical-sounding counter-suggestion that is shot down as pure fantasy.

title: CEO Admits Warranty Scam on Call

situation: A CEO wearing a headset on an investor call openly admits that the company has given up on profitable products and now earns its money by selling extended warranties to customers who will forget they bought them. title: Tupac Hologram Employee Cloud Plan

setting: Catbert's office, across a desk from Ted
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, asks Ted about the Tupac hologram video and announces that the company will do the same with all its employees by moving their data to the cloud. Ted points out that Tupac is dead, and Catbert coolly corrects him.
punchline: Catbert implies the company plans to get rid of its employees and keep only their data as digital holograms, because it's cheaper than paying living people.
summary: The HR director reveals a scheme to replace staff with cloud-stored digital versions of themselves, treating a dead rapper's hologram as a cost-saving precedent.

title: We Never Give Reasons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you email the test data to me?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We don't do it that way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not a reason.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We never give reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing you say means anything!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's how we've always done it.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker to email him the test data. She refuses because they don't do it that way, then admits her department never gives reasons for anything. Dilbert loses his composure and shouts that nothing she says means anything, and she answers with yet another non-reason.
punchline: The coworker responds to Dilbert's exasperation with the classic bureaucratic non-answer, proving his point that nothing she says carries any meaning.
summary: A worker's simple request is blocked by circular, reasonless policy that drives him to shout in frustration.
keywords: we don't do it that way

title: Smart People Like My Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What feedback have other people given you on your idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Smart people like it. Everyone else asks me what other people think.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk holding a paper with Dilbert's idea and asks what feedback others have given. Dilbert replies that smart people like it, while everyone else just asks what other people think. In the last panel the Boss silently studies the paper.
punchline: Dilbert implies that anyone who needs to check others' opinions before judging an idea isn't smart, which subtly includes the Boss, who just asked the same question.
summary: Asked how his proposal has been received, an engineer says the clever people approve while the rest just want to know what everyone else thinks.

title: Upgrading Servers Already Upgraded

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to upgrade some of our servers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's dumb. We upgraded two of them last week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right. Now we need to upgrade the rest of them.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then why did you say we have to upgrade ALL of them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I didn't. But I think we all agree on what needs to be done.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Not if you insist on upgrading the servers we already upgraded last week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!! Kill me with a comet!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does he ever say anything that makes sense?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: There's no way to be sure.

situation: In a meeting, Dilbert says some servers need upgrading, and a coworker argues about whether all or only some should be upgraded, including ones already done last week. Dilbert patiently clarifies that he never said all of them, but the coworker keeps insisting on a misunderstanding. Dilbert finally loses his composure and begs to be killed by a comet.
punchline: Dilbert is driven to despair by a coworker whose statements are so muddled that nobody can tell whether he ever makes sense.
summary: A circular argument over which servers need upgrading drives a frustrated engineer to wish for sudden cosmic destruction.

file: 2012/2012-02-07_computers & peripherals_office equipment_email servers_inbox_vowels only_complain_loudest_complain to boss.gif
title: Email Servers Moved to Transylbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ever since you moved our email servers to Transylbonia, my inbox has nothing but vowels.

transcript.speaker: I.T. Guy
transcript.text: We I.T. people only respond to whoever complains loudest. You should complain to your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A UI AOE UIE OU EAI!

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert complains to an I.T. worker that his inbox contains only vowels since the email servers were moved to Transylbonia. The I.T. guy says they only help whoever complains loudest and tells Dilbert to complain to his boss. Dilbert agrees, and the Boss turns out to be receiving the same vowel-only emails, with a puzzled question mark over his head.
punchline: The one person Dilbert is told to complain to can't read his own email either, so his complaint arrives as nothing but vowels and goes nowhere.
summary: After an offshore server move garbles his messages into pure vowels, an employee is advised to escalate to a manager whose own inbox is equally mangled.

file: 2012/2012-08-12_work ethic_great managing_engaged_disengaged_praise and recognition_encourage developement_important job_opinions count_prodcutivity_drop dead_learn and grow.gif
title: Employee Hands Boss Management Checklist

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Here's a list of the twelve elements of great managing.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: If you do everything on that list, it will make me feel what experts call "engaged."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: If you fail to do your job properly, I will feel all disengaged and do poor work.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This would be a convenient time to give me some praise and recognition.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You might also want to encourage my development and tell me my job is important.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Remember to care about me as a person and tell me my opinions count.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: If you do all of that, plus seven more things on the list, you might get some productivity out of me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leave my office and drop dead.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Will that help me learn and grow?

situation: An employee walks into the boss's office with a checklist of twelve elements of great managing and lists everything the boss must do to make him feel engaged, such as giving praise, encouraging development and valuing his opinions. He essentially threatens to do poor work unless the boss performs. The fed-up boss tells him to drop dead.
punchline: After demanding the boss cater to his every emotional need, the employee responds to the boss's angry dismissal by sarcastically asking if that will help him learn and grow.
summary: A needy worker lectures his boss on how to keep him motivated, and even a brutal brush-off becomes another chance to demand personal development.

file: 2012/2012-09-18_business ethics_interviews_career goals_80 hours a week_below - market_compensation.gif
title: Interviewer Wants Gullible Employees

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job Interview

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: But enough about me. How can I help you achieve your career goals?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could work 80 hours a week for below-market compensation.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I did not see that coming.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good. I need employees who can't see it coming. You're hired.

situation: A job candidate turns the interview around by asking how he can help the interviewer achieve his career goals. The Boss replies that the candidate could work 80 hours a week for below-market pay. When the candidate says he did not see that coming, the Boss hires him on the spot for exactly that reason.
punchline: The Boss admits he wants employees naive enough not to anticipate being exploited, so the candidate's surprise at the exploitative offer proves he is the ideal hire.
summary: A hopeful applicant gets blindsided by a brutal job offer and is hired precisely because of his naivety.

title: Barry Speculates Instead Of Calling Vendors

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's hear what Barry learned from our vendors and go from there.

transcript.speaker: Barry
transcript.text: I didn't have time to call anyone, but I can speculate about what might have happened if I had.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm curious to see how this will work out for you.

transcript.speaker: Barry
transcript.text: None of the vendors would have called me back.

situation: At a meeting, Alice asks Barry to report what he learned from calling the company's vendors. Barry admits he never made the calls, but offers to speculate about what would have happened had he made them. Alice sarcastically waits to see how his excuse will play out, and he claims the vendors wouldn't have returned his calls anyway.
punchline: Barry replaces actual work with a hypothetical report, presenting made-up predictions as if they were results and using an imagined failure as his excuse.
summary: A man who skipped his assigned phone calls fills his meeting slot by confidently reporting on the calls he imagines would have gone badly.

file: 2012/2012-08-10_cruelty_office workers_unpaid intern_resort fee_work experience_zips eyeholes_leather hood.gif
title: Intern to Another Intern

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you the new unpaid intern?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No, but that's what I aspire to be.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm merely an intern to another intern. And I pay a resort fee just to use the restroom.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: At least you get valuable work experience.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Until he zips the eyeholes on the leather hood I wear in meetings.

situation: A woman with a coffee mug asks Asok if he is the new unpaid intern. He explains he is merely an intern to another intern and even pays a resort fee to use the restroom. When she says at least he gets valuable work experience, he darkly adds that the experience lasts only until his superior zips up the eyeholes of the leather hood he must wear in meetings.
punchline: Asok's exploitation is so extreme that he lacks even the status of an unpaid intern, pays for basic amenities, and is subjected to bondage-style humiliation, making 'valuable work experience' a bitter joke.
summary: A junior worker laments his place at the very bottom of the internship food chain, enduring absurd fees and degrading treatment in the name of career experience.

title: Alice's Idea-Shredding Gloves

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hold that thought until I put on my idea-shredding gloves.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My idea is that... we ... um ...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're a bad listener.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Tell me more about your dumb idea.

situation: Dilbert tries to share an idea with Alice, who tells him to wait while she puts on gloves meant for shredding ideas. When he starts to speak, she bares her teeth, claws at the air, and calls him a bad listener before demanding to hear more about his dumb idea.
punchline: Alice has already decided Dilbert's idea is dumb and is eager to destroy it, so she hypocritically accuses him of being the bad listener while she was the one refusing to listen.
summary: Alice gears up with special gloves to tear apart a coworker's suggestion before she has even heard it.

file: 2012/2012-07-21_computer software_inventions_3d network_motion sensors_sneezed_merged network_15th of cisco.gif
title: Sneeze Merges Network and Calendar

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In the near future

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was manipulating a 3-D network model using my hand motion sensors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was all good until I sneezed and accidentally merged my network design with my Outlook calendar.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will you have that fixed?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I should be done by... the 15th of Cisco.

setting: Office desk or meeting table, in a futuristic workplace
situation: In the near future, Dilbert explains to the Boss that he was using hand motion sensors to manipulate a 3-D network model when a sneeze accidentally merged the network design with his Outlook calendar. When the Boss asks for a completion date, Dilbert gives a deadline that blends calendar months with networking vendor names.
punchline: The sneeze-induced merge of the network design and the calendar has corrupted even his sense of dates, so he gives a deadline of 'the 15th of Cisco' instead of an actual month.
summary: A gesture-controlled network design goes haywire after a sneeze, leaving the engineer scrambling calendar dates with networking jargon.

title: Brainstorming Rule Proves Dilbert's Point

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's brainstorm new product ideas.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, the most important rule of brainstorming is no criticizing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll go first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Research shows that brainstorming is less effective than people working by themselves and later comparing ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My idea is to use stem cell technology to design bosses who aren't ignoramuses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, you're not supposed to criticize ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But if you decide to do it anyway, it sort of proves my point.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I understand why brainstorming has a bad reputation, but it doesn't stop me from enjoying it.

setting: Conference room during a brainstorming meeting, with a final panel in a hallway
situation: The Boss opens a brainstorming session and insists on the rule of no criticizing. Dilbert goes first, cites research that brainstorming is less effective than working alone, then pitches an idea to engineer bosses who aren't ignorant. When the Boss objects that criticism isn't allowed, Dilbert points out the Boss is breaking his own rule.
punchline: Dilbert's brainstorm idea is itself an insult to the Boss, and the Boss's angry reaction breaks the no-criticism rule, which proves that brainstorming doesn't work as advertised.
summary: A meeting leader's own rule against criticism collapses the moment a pointed suggestion is aimed at him, and the smug brainstormer enjoys it anyway.

title: The Ugly Truth Haunts Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Ugly Truth visits

transcript.speaker: Ugly Truth
transcript.text: Your employees hate your carb-fattened guts.

transcript.speaker: Ugly Truth
transcript.text: They hope you get run over by a clown car because it will make your demise extra funny.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hear mumbling but no one is there!

transcript.speaker: Ugly Truth
transcript.text: It's weird for me too.

setting: Office, with the Boss holding a coffee mug
situation: A grumpy, pig-nosed figure labeled the Ugly Truth appears beside the Boss and tells him that his employees hate him and secretly wish he would die in a funny clown car accident. The Boss cannot see or perceive the Ugly Truth and only hears mumbling from nowhere.
punchline: The Ugly Truth is literally invisible to the clueless Boss, so the unpleasant facts about how his employees feel can never reach him, and the Truth itself finds the situation odd.
summary: An embodiment of harsh reality delivers brutal feedback to a manager who is completely unable to perceive it.

title: Boss Models Positivity, Dilbert Wishes Death

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good leader has a positive attitude and spreads it by example.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today I lived like a sultan while you slaved away in your cubicle prison. I had a GREAT day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now it's your turn. Remember to be positive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm positive I want you to die.

situation: The Boss lectures Dilbert about how good leaders spread a positive attitude by example. He then brags about living like a sultan all day while Dilbert toiled in his cubicle, and tells Dilbert it is now his turn to be positive. Dilbert responds by sincerely stating that he wants the Boss to die.
punchline: Dilbert takes the Boss's instruction to be positive literally, turning it into a certain wish for the Boss's death, since the Boss's boasting about his luxurious day has provoked pure resentment.
summary: After gloating about his lavish day while his employee suffered, a manager demands positivity and gets a darkly literal reply.

title: Executive Insults Dilbert, Then Blames Capitalism

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I don't know how to say this delicately so I'll just say it.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Looking at your homely, middle-class face makes my skin crawl. Never speak directly to me again.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Sometimes I think they don't understand capitalism.

setting: Executive's office and an exterior view of the office building
situation: Dilbert stands before a wealthy executive seated at his desk, who bluntly tells him that his ordinary middle-class face is repulsive and forbids him from speaking to the executive again. After Dilbert leaves, the executive stands with Catbert and wonders aloud why people like Dilbert fail to grasp capitalism.
punchline: The executive treats his contempt for ordinary workers as natural, then concludes that the failure is theirs for not understanding capitalism, revealing his snobbery and the class divide between management and employees.
summary: A well-off executive coldly rejects a regular employee for his plain looks and then complains that the lower classes just don't get how the economic system works.

title: Boss Contradicts His Own Priorities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to take care of this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd love to, but it isn't on the list of priorities you gave me an hour ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do what I tell you to do, not what I say you should do.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's cubicle and tells him to take care of a new task. Dilbert points out that it isn't on the priority list the Boss gave him only an hour earlier. The Boss responds that Dilbert should follow what he tells him to do rather than what he says Dilbert should do.
punchline: The Boss's illogical reply admits that his own instructions and priority lists are meaningless, so employees are expected to obey whatever he demands in the moment.
summary: A manager springs a surprise assignment on an employee and then dismisses the priority list he handed over an hour before.

file: 2012/2012-10-14_interviews_resume_piece of work_lie_exaggeration_mispelling_bad format_failed prodcuts_salsa dancer_applicants resume_handsome fellow_busted.gif

transcript.text: Take a look at this resume.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ha ha! This guy is a piece of work!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Lie... Lie... Exaggeration... Misspelling... Bad format... Worked on failed products.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ooh! He's also a champion salsa dancer. What a tool!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait. Why aren't you joining in the traditional mocking of the applicant's resume?

Dilbert notes that she isn't joining in the usual mockery, but she is actually waiting to see whether the applicant, who is standing behind Dilbert, is attractive. When she sees him, she shoves Dilbert aside to get a better look.
punchline: Alice's harsh critique of the resume depends entirely on whether the candidate turns out to be good-looking, showing that hiring opinions are driven by superficial attraction rather than qualifications.
summary: A coworker who enjoys ridiculing a job candidate's paperwork abruptly changes her attitude once she spots how attractive he is.

file: 2012/2012-02-08_low margin lines_high risk_start up_lumbering inefficiencies_buy in.gif
title: Pivot Sounds Like Startup Without Benefits

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're abandoning our low-margin lines of business and going into a whole new field.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... we'll be like a high-risk start-up company burdened with lumbering inefficiencies and a high cost structure?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was anything you said the same as buy-in?

situation: The Boss announces to his employees that the company is dropping its low-margin businesses and entering a whole new field. Dilbert sums up the plan as becoming a risky start-up that still carries a big company's inefficiencies and high costs. The Boss ignores the criticism and only asks whether any of it amounted to agreeing with him.
punchline: The Boss is only interested in whether employees express buy-in, so a withering and accurate critique of his strategy doesn't register as anything but a failure to agree.
summary: A manager unveils a drastic change of direction, and when an employee points out its glaring flaws, he cares only about whether he got enthusiastic agreement.

title: Assigned To Team Of Annoyances

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you on a project with Loud Howard, Topper, and the new guy who loves the sound of his own voice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because you hate me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not at all. It's because I hate the other three guys.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being assigned to a project team with three annoying coworkers: Loud Howard, Topper, and a new hire who loves hearing himself talk. Dilbert asks whether this is a punishment because the boss hates him. The boss says no, he simply hates the other three and wants to stick them with Dilbert.
punchline: The boss isn't punishing Dilbert; he is dumping three people he dislikes onto Dilbert's team to get them out of his own hair, treating Dilbert as a convenient dumping ground.
summary: A manager sends an employee to work with three irritating colleagues, explaining it's not out of spite for him but to be rid of the others.

title: Boss's Unverifiable Email Defense Fails
