transcript.text: I told you to reschedule the installation date.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That conversation never happened. Maybe you planned to say it and then the thought morphed into a false memory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sure I emailed you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might want to pick a defense that's less checkable.

situation: The Boss accuses Dilbert of failing to reschedule an installation date, claiming he already told him to. Dilbert denies the conversation ever took place and suggests the Boss merely imagined it. When the Boss switches to claiming he sent an email, Dilbert points out that such a claim is easy to verify.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically warns the Boss that claiming to have sent an email is a bad lie because email records can be checked, implying the Boss never sent one.
summary: A manager blames his employee for a missed task, but the employee calmly dismantles each excuse, ending by noting the second one can be easily disproven.

file: 2012/2012-09-15_celebrities_wealth_money manager_dumb celebrities_pay close attention_money invested_protect money_money.gif

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That would be one way to play it.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is going to become a money manager for dumb celebrities, explaining that they don't scrutinize their investments or who might be stealing from them. title: Buzzwords Fail, Bigger Ask Succeeds

transcript.text: Venture Capital

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need $100,000 for my location-based, social media, cloud start-up.

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: I'm not giving you $100,000 just because you spewed some buzzwords.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then how about $10 million?

transcript.speaker: Venture Capitalist
transcript.text: Wait... Now it sounds like a good investment. How did you do that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can tell you, but it won't be flattering.

punchline: The investor is swayed simply by the much larger number, and Dogbert's offer to explain how he did it 'unflatteringly' implies the investor is a gullible sucker who equates bigger asks with better investments.

title: Dogbert's Ruinous Retirement Planning Fee

transcript.text: Dogbert's Retirement Planning Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My fee is 10% of your portfolio per year.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Sounds reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: None of my clients understand how the future works.

setting: Dogbert's financial planning office, then Dilbert's living room couch
situation: Dogbert, running a retirement planning service, tells a client his fee is 10% of the client's portfolio every year. The client thinks that sounds reasonable. In the last panel Dogbert is relaxing on Dilbert's couch, gloating that his clients don't grasp how the future works.
punchline: A 10% annual fee will devour the client's entire portfolio in roughly a decade, and the clients are too financially naive to see that compounding costs make it a terrible deal.
summary: A dog financial advisor charges a ruinous yearly percentage and relies on his customers' inability to think long-term.

title: Everything You Suggested Is Bad

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you see my email with all of my recommended changes to your product?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. Everything you suggested is a bad idea, but I don't want to spend the rest of my life explaining why.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now I hate you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All roads headed in that direction. All I did was take the shortest one.

setting: Office meeting room or conference table
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert whether he read the email full of changes they recommend for his product. Dilbert bluntly says every suggestion is a bad idea and that he won't waste his life explaining why. The coworker says they now hate him, and Dilbert replies that he merely took the shortest route to an inevitable outcome.
punchline: Dilbert argues that any honest feedback would have ended in the coworker hating him, so his brutal brevity just got them there faster.
summary: Rather than endure a long debate over unwanted advice, Dilbert dismisses it all at once and defends the resulting resentment as efficiency.

file: 2012/2012-09-19_work ethic_key to success_knowing when to quit.gif

summary: Dilbert mocks his boss's idea of a half-phone, half-tablet gadget by twisting the phrase 'market niche' into a put-down.

Asok hopefully asks Dilbert to choose the first option, and Dilbert crumples the paper while insulting him further.

summary: A coworker's well-meant revisions are so poor that the author is forced to pick between public embarrassment and a personal insult, and ends up delivering the insult anyway.

title: Reorganization With No Reason Given

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm reorganizing the company and giving every manager a new job.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're over-thinking it.

situation: A bald executive walks up to a manager at his desk and announces he is reorganizing the company and giving every manager a new job. The manager simply asks why. After a silent beat, the executive tells him he is overthinking it, never offering a reason.
punchline: The executive dodges the reasonable question by accusing the manager of overthinking, which implies that reorganizations are done on a whim with no real rationale behind them.
summary: A boss announces a company-wide shuffle of managers' jobs and answers a simple question about the purpose by claiming the questioner is making too much of it.

title: Second Place To His Phone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I check something on my phone?

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Why would I mind the humiliation and disrespect of being with a man who prefers the company of his phone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the sort of attitude that makes you finish second to my phone.

setting: Outdoor dirt path through grassy park during a walk
situation: Dilbert is walking with a woman on a date and asks if he can check something on his phone. She sarcastically points out how humiliating and disrespectful it is to be with a man who prefers his phone to her. Dilbert ignores her complaint and instead blames her attitude for why she ranks below his phone.
punchline: Dilbert turns his date's legitimate complaint about being ignored into proof that her sarcastic attitude is why she comes second to his phone.
summary: A man on a stroll with his date responds to her pointed objection about his phone obsession by faulting her tone for his priorities.

file: 2012/2012-05-12_retail business_sales drop_retail stores_self checkout_dumb customers_most shoplifted.gif
title: Dumb Customers Can't Self-Checkout

transcript.speaker: Dragon
transcript.text: Our sales have dropped to zero in retail stores that have self-checkout.

transcript.speaker: Dragon
transcript.text: Apparently the people who are dumb enough to want our product are too dumb to know how to use self-checkout.

transcript.speaker: Dragon
transcript.text: On a positive note, we have the most shoplifted product of the year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes!

setting: Conference room during a sales meeting
situation: At a meeting table, a dragon-like colleague reports to Dilbert and the Boss that the company's sales have dropped to zero in stores with self-checkout. He explains this by saying the product's buyers are too dumb to operate the machines. He then offers a silver lining that the product is the most shoplifted of the year, and the Boss cheers.
punchline: The company treats being the most shoplifted product as a win, and the report insults its own customers while the Boss celebrates theft as proof of popularity.
summary: A sales report blames customer stupidity for a collapse in sales at self-service tills, then spins widespread theft as good news.

title: Reorganization Is Really About Golf

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're consolidating our marketing into a shared services model.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Change creates the illusion that we have a strategy while giving our CEO an excuse to fire a VP who beat him at golf.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And blah, blah, something about money.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Must... not... cry... on the outside.

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: The Boss announces that marketing is being consolidated into a shared services model. When an employee asks why, the Boss candidly admits the reorganization is just a show of strategy and a pretext for the CEO to fire a VP who beat him at golf. He then waves off the financial rationale while the employee struggles not to break down.
punchline: The real reason for the corporate reorganization is petty CEO revenge over a golf game, and the supposed business justification is an afterthought.
summary: A manager brazenly reveals that a major restructuring exists to fake a strategy and punish a golf-winning executive, leaving a listener close to tears.

title: Boss Plans Public Criticism for Motivation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm waiting for people to walk by so I can criticize you in front of others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want the criticism to sting as much as possible so you'll be incented to do all the right things in the future.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I guess it can wait until the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That way I can enjoy the anticipation, too.

situation: The Boss stands holding a coffee mug and tells Dilbert he is waiting for passersby so he can criticize Dilbert in front of them. He explains that the humiliation is deliberate, meant to sting enough to motivate better behavior. When no audience appears, he decides to postpone it until the staff meeting and says he'll enjoy the anticipation.
punchline: The Boss treats public humiliation as a calculated motivational tool and openly admits he is savoring the cruelty, even delaying it for a bigger audience.
summary: A manager cheerfully announces that he plans to embarrass an employee publicly as a motivational tactic and decides to wait for a larger crowd.

title: Restroom Sink Water, Bring Your Own Cup

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Before we start, can I offer you a cup of water from our restroom sink?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can't afford bottled water.

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Okay, sure. I'll have a cup of sink water.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That brings us to the awkward part: Did you happen to bring a cup?

setting: Conference room or office meeting space
situation: Dilbert greets a visitor in a meeting room and offers him a cup of water from the restroom sink, explaining the company cannot afford bottled water. The visitor agrees to accept sink water. Dilbert then reveals the company has no cups either and asks if the visitor brought his own.
punchline: The company is so cheap that it offers free restroom sink water but cannot even provide a cup to drink it from.
summary: A host offers a guest the cheapest possible refreshment, only to admit the vessel is the guest's responsibility.

title: Dogbert Tosses Dilbert's Time Machine

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My phone is like a time machine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can fast-forward through the boring parts of life by playing with it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hand it over.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Time flies when I'm not having fun.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Toss

setting: Outdoors on a hillside overlooking a field, beside a wooden fence post
situation: Dilbert stands outside absorbed in his smartphone and explains that it lets him skip through the boring parts of life. Dogbert asks him to hand it over, then hurls the phone away into the distance.
punchline: Dogbert literalizes the 'time flies when you're having fun' idiom by making the phone fly, since Dilbert's fun is now ruined and time will drag.
summary: A man brags that his gadget speeds up dull moments, so his dog pitches it away and twists the old saying about time.

title: Monkey Coffee Warmer Loses Dignity

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: I thought being a service animal would be a noble calling.

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: But I worry that our relationship has drifted into something less dignified.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what keeps my coffee warm.

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: I am so angry right now.

situation: A monkey stands next to the Boss's desk with his coffee mug balanced on its head. The monkey says it expected service-animal work to be noble but feels the arrangement has become undignified. The Boss cheerfully replies that this is what keeps his coffee warm, and the monkey, with a little storm cloud over its head, admits it is furious.
punchline: The Boss treats the monkey's complaint about indignity as a feature, since the monkey's angry body heat is what keeps his coffee warm.
summary: A resentful monkey holding its employer's mug learns that its simmering rage is exactly what the employer values.

title: Boss Misunderstands Victimless Crime

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I did some insider trading and totally got away with it. It felt great!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was a victimless crime so I feel no guilt whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you know what victimless means?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes. It's like the time I strangled my gardener for over-watering the rose bushes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I see the problem.

situation: The Boss brags to Dogbert that he committed insider trading and feels no guilt because it was a victimless crime. Dogbert asks whether he understands the word, and the Boss offers an example that involves murdering his gardener. Dogbert concludes that this explains the problem.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a victimless crime is strangling his gardener, which clearly has a victim, revealing he has no grasp of the term or of right and wrong.
summary: A self-satisfied executive justifies his illegal stock dealings with a wildly inappropriate example that exposes his moral blindness.

file: 2012/2012-11-26_happiness_work ethic_busy work_cheerful_form of insanity_worthless assignments_professional help_psychology.gif
title: Cheerful About Worthless Busywork Assignments

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I completed the busywork you assigned to me and I'm still cheerful!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how I do it. I really don't. I assume it's a form of insanity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have more worthless assignments I could do before I seek professional help?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yup.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, tells the seated Boss that he finished the pointless busywork he was given and is still cheerful. He speculates that his good mood must be a form of insanity, then asks for more worthless assignments before he gets professional help. The Boss simply answers yes.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically treats his cheerfulness about meaningless work as a mental illness, and the Boss cheerfully takes advantage by confirming he has plenty more pointless tasks.
summary: An upbeat employee jokes that his good attitude toward useless tasks must be madness and asks for more before getting therapy, and his boss happily obliges.

title: Brain Reader Smashes Rival's Phone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My brain reader invention allows me to control any nearby computer.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing! My phone can...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmmm mmm.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: POW!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did that with my mind.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing! I made you do it!

situation: Dilbert, wearing a brain-reading device on his head, brags that it lets him control any nearby computer. A coworker tries to one-up him by boasting about his phone, so Dilbert uses the device to make his own hand smash the phone to pieces. The coworker responds by claiming he made Dilbert do it.
punchline: The coworker refuses to concede defeat and absurdly claims he manipulated Dilbert into destroying his phone, topping the mind-control boast with an even bigger boast.
summary: Two meeting attendees compete over whose gadget is more impressive, and the argument ends with a smashed phone and a face-saving claim of mastermind control.

title: Waiting Out the Boss's Orders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop everything you're doing and build robots.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (The Boss walks out of the conference room; no dialogue.)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's wait a week and see if he forgets.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Does that work?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It works with you.

situation: The Boss abruptly orders his team to drop everything and build robots, then walks out of the meeting. Dilbert proposes simply waiting a week to see if the Boss forgets the order. Wally asks whether that strategy works, and Alice points out that it works on him.
punchline: Alice implies that Wally is just as forgetful as the Boss, since ignoring Wally's assignments and waiting for him to forget them is a known tactic.
summary: Faced with a sudden, silly directive from management, the team plans to stall until it's forgotten, and one coworker gets teased for being equally forgetful.

title: Recruiting an Ineffective New Nemesis

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My old nemesis retired. Would you like to be my new nemesis?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're notoriously ineffective. That's the best kind of nemesis to have.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That should prime the pump.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will thwart you a new one!

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss to become his new nemesis now that his old one has retired. When the Boss asks why he was chosen, Dilbert says it's because the Boss is notoriously ineffective, which makes him the safest kind of nemesis. The insult is meant to provoke him, and the Boss responds with an angry, garbled threat.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately insults the Boss to provoke him into becoming a nemesis, and the Boss's garbled threat ('thwart you a new one') shows both that it worked and that he really is ineffective.
summary: Needing a replacement for his retired archenemy, Dilbert picks his incompetent boss and baits him with an insult until the boss angrily vows to oppose him.

title: Politician Shops Around for Bribes

transcript.speaker: Politician
transcript.text: Your lobbyist said I could have a lucrative job here someday if I support tax breaks for your company.

transcript.speaker: Politician
transcript.text: I have offers from other bribers, so I thought I'd stop by and see how this dump compares.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly I know too much.

transcript.speaker: Politician
transcript.text: Fetch me some coffee and I'll make your birthday a holiday.

situation: A politician sits at a desk and tells Dilbert that the company's lobbyist promised him a lucrative future job in exchange for supporting tax breaks. He says he has competing offers from other bribers and is touring the office to compare. Dilbert realizes he has learned something improper, and the politician casually offers a holiday in his honor in return for coffee.
punchline: The politician treats bribery as an openly acknowledged shopping process and then offers to bribe Dilbert with a made-up holiday for fetching coffee, showing how casually corrupt and entitled he is.
summary: A lawmaker openly auditions corporate bribers, insulting the office while Dilbert realizes he has overheard far too much.

title: Anti-Coworker Suit Blocks Interruptions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wearing my anti-co-worker suit to work today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It has noise-canceling headphones, blinders, and padding so I can't feel taps on my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mr. Watson - don't come here - I don't need you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heh heh.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, then his office cubicle
situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a padded suit equipped with noise-canceling headphones and blinders, designed to shut out coworkers. At his desk, he sits in the suit and thinks a twisted version of Alexander Graham Bell's famous first phone call, wishing Mr. Watson would stay away.
punchline: Dilbert inverts Bell's famous 'Mr. Watson, come here, I need you' line to gleefully express that he wants no one to come near him, showing how desperately he wants to avoid interruptions.
summary: A man armors himself against interruptions with a sensory-blocking suit and then happily reverses a legendary telephone quote to ward off visitors.

title: Bailout Request Costs Only $85

transcript.speaker: Foreign Official
transcript.text: Is this Dogbert's International Bank for Bailing Out Countries That Are Bad at Math?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Foreign Official
transcript.text: Our treasury is empty and we're not sure why. The entire country is becoming sort of feral.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How much money do you need?

transcript.speaker: Foreign Official
transcript.text: No more than $85.

setting: Dogbert's office, at his desk with a computer
situation: A tall official in a dark hat and robe visits Dogbert's bank, which exists to bail out countries that are bad at math. He explains that his country's treasury is empty for unknown reasons and that the population is turning feral. Dogbert asks how much money is needed, and the amount is a trivial $85.
punchline: A whole country is bankrupt and descending into lawlessness, yet the amount needed to fix it is a laughably tiny $85, mocking national debt crises and the idea of bad-at-math governments.
summary: A desperate foreign official asks Dogbert's specialized bank to rescue his collapsing country, and the sum required turns out to be comically small.

title: Boss Opens Meeting With Insults

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to begin the meeting by giving Dilbert some destructive criticism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything you do is dumb. I don't know why I hired you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I feel much more motivated now. If you feel a little bit worse, we came out ahead as a team.

situation: The Boss starts a team meeting by announcing he will give Dilbert destructive criticism, then tells Dilbert everything he does is dumb and that he regrets hiring him. Dilbert sits stone-faced while the boss concludes the insult made him feel motivated.
punchline: The boss treats his own improved mood as a team win, ignoring that the gain comes entirely at Dilbert's expense and only needs Dilbert to feel 'a little bit worse' to count as a net positive.
summary: A manager kicks off a meeting by berating one employee and then celebrates his own boosted morale as a collective victory.

title: Rich Boss Refuses to Quit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I expected you to quit after you got your billion-dollar discrimination settlement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just because I'm lazy and unscrupulous, why would you assume I'm also a quitter?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how you look at yourself in the mirror.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he assumed he would quit his job after winning a billion-dollar discrimination settlement. The Boss, wearing a green dollar-sign hat and holding a mug, proudly replies that being lazy and unscrupulous doesn't mean he's a quitter. Dilbert is left stammering and then wonders how the Boss can face himself in the mirror.
punchline: The Boss treats his lack of work ethic and morals as perfectly compatible with staying employed, leaving Dilbert baffled at his total absence of shame.
summary: A newly wealthy boss shamelessly explains that being lazy and unethical is no reason for him to leave his cushy job.

title: Dilbert Plans to Escape Allen

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Talk to Allen about this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll need an exit strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's a serial talker. I'll be trapped for hours while he strings together infinite, unrelated stories.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Engineers have weird problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What could I eat that would make me puke in ten minutes?

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a paper and tells him to go talk to Allen about it. Dilbert grumbles that he needs an exit strategy because Allen is a serial talker who will trap him for hours with endless unrelated stories. In the final panel the Boss thinks engineers have weird problems, while Dilbert privately wonders what he could eat to make himself vomit within ten minutes.
punchline: Dilbert is so dreading a conversation with a long-winded coworker that he considers deliberately making himself sick as his escape plan.
summary: Faced with a mandatory chat with a never-ending storyteller, Dilbert contemplates inducing nausea as his way out.

title: Siri Deploys Coccyx Air Bag

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Siri, how can I avoid blame for our server outage?

transcript.speaker: Siri
transcript.text: Deploying coccyx air bag.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Foomp!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So your tailbone isn't vestigial?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope. And apparently it has Bluetooth.

situation: Dilbert asks Siri on his phone how to avoid blame for a server outage. The phone responds by deploying a giant air bag from his backside, which inflates behind him. A coworker holding a coffee mug asks if this means his tailbone isn't vestigial, and Dilbert says it apparently has Bluetooth.
punchline: Siri's answer to avoiding blame is to deploy a literal cover-your-behind air bag, which turns Dilbert's tailbone into a Bluetooth-connected gadget.
summary: A man's phone assistant answers a question about dodging responsibility by inflating a protective cushion from his rear end, wirelessly controlled.

file: 2012/2012-02-06_monsters_office equipment_email servers_ancestral hime_reduce expenses_data vampires_exagerration_fiber optic.gif

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.text: Dude! It's fiber-optic!

situation: At a meeting, a coworker announces he has relocated the company's email servers to his ancestral homeland of Transylbonia to cut costs. He then reassures the group that rumors about Transylbonians being data vampires are exaggerated, but the final panel shows a caped vampire eagerly biting into a fiber-optic cable while another man looks on unenthusiastically.
punchline: The reassurance that Transylbonians aren't data vampires is undercut by a literal vampire chewing on a network cable, with the one 'normal' guy admitting he just isn't into it.
summary: A cost-cutting server relocation to a vampire-infested homeland is dismissed as harmless until a caped creature gnaws on the network cabling.

file: 2012/2012-11-18_crimes_engineers_engineering question_holiday lights_homeless guy_catapult_satellite map_fell off roof_flight oath_neighbors pool_broken leg_heartless.gif
title: Boss Needs Body Disposal Engineering

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a minute to answer an engineering question?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: My wife is out of town visiting her sister.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: She asked me to put up the holiday lights while she was gone.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I hired a homeless guy to do it and he fell off the roof. What's the easiest way to get rid of the body before my wife comes home?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your question is disturbing, but I'm intrigued by the engineering part.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's a design for a catapult you can build at home.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And here's a satellite map showing the best flight path to a neighbor's pool.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did he die right away?

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: No, just a broken leg.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert an engineering question, explaining that he hired a homeless man to hang holiday lights and the man fell off the roof. He wants to dispose of the body before his wife returns. Dilbert, intrigued by the engineering challenge, supplies a catapult design and a flight path to a neighbor's pool, then asks if the man died right away.
punchline: The man isn't dead, only has a broken leg, so the Boss and Dilbert are cheerfully planning to catapult a living, injured person into a neighbor's pool, which makes both of them monstrously heartless.
summary: A manager seeking to hide a roofing accident victim gets cheerful engineering help from an employee, only for it to emerge the victim is still alive.

file: 2012/2012-08-29_managers & supervisors_prosperity_intuition_market research_success rate_binary choices_tiny manager_made of copper_business.gif
title: Intuition Beats Market Research, Supposedly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I'm going to rely on my intuition instead of market research.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If guessing can bring your success rate up to 50% for binary choices, I'm all for it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, look! I found a tiny manager made of copper in my pocket!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Snork

setting: Office break area where employees are standing around holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss announces he will stop using market research and trust his intuition instead. Dilbert sarcastically replies that guessing would at least give him a 50% success rate on yes-or-no decisions. The Boss, apparently proving Dilbert's point about his judgment, excitedly claims to have found a tiny copper manager in his pocket while Wally snorts with laughter.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss's intuition is so poor that merely guessing at random would be an improvement, and the Boss's bizarre, delusional pocket discovery confirms how unreliable his judgment is.
summary: A manager ditches data-driven research for gut feelings, and a coworker's backhanded reply suggests random chance would serve him better.

file: 2012/2012-10-06_business ethics_executives_poor persons_ceo morality test_new tech_fracking_grinding porr people_high pressure_shale.gif
title: CEO Morality Test: Grinding Poor People

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO morality test

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Imagine I invented a new technology for fracking.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It involves grinding poor people into a slurry and pumping it into shale at high pressure.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you see any problem with that?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Not enough shale!

setting: Executive office, with Dogbert across a desk from a CEO
situation: Dogbert, acting as an examiner, gives a CEO a morality test by describing a fracking technology that grinds poor people into slurry and pumps it into shale. He asks whether the CEO sees any problem with it. The CEO ignores the human cost and objects only that there isn't enough shale.
punchline: The CEO fails the morality test spectacularly, treating mass killing of poor people as acceptable and worrying only about the process's capacity, which satirizes executives who value efficiency and profit over human life.
summary: A grim ethics quiz from Dogbert reveals that a chief executive's only concern about a horrific production method is that it can't scale up.

title: Boss Can't Judge Tina's Insult

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That's because you keep criticizing me! Nice leadership, you perspiring pile of pound cake!

setting: Office conference table during a performance review
situation: During a performance review, the Boss tells Tina she lacks confidence. Tina angrily blames his constant criticism and insults his leadership with an absurd name. The Boss, unable to tell whether this outburst counts as an improvement, asks her to clarify.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he can't tell whether Tina's angry insult is a sign of newfound confidence or a worse performance problem.
summary: A manager who calls his employee unconfident is baffled when she snaps back with an angry, ridiculous insult.

file: 2012/2012-06-10_better job_goldilocks zone_managers_marinate in own stench_monster_skills expire_technology certifictae_training_your training.gif
title: Boss Denies Training Via Goldilocks Zone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to get this technology certification.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! No way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I pay for your training, you'll use your certification to get a better job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At the moment, you're in what we managers call the Goldilocks zone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not hot enough to get a better job, and you're not yet incompetent at the one you have.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When your skills expire, in the next year or two, I'll replace you with someone younger.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to pay for a technology certification. The boss refuses, explaining that Dilbert is in the 'Goldilocks zone' where he is neither skilled enough to leave nor incompetent enough to fire, and that he will be replaced by someone younger when his skills expire. Dilbert storms off to pay for training himself, and in the last panel the boss brags to a higher-up about his low training costs.
punchline: The boss takes credit for cutting training expenses by exploiting his employee's stagnation, and Dilbert's insult about marinating in stench is turned into the boss's smug explanation to upper management.
summary: A manager blocks an employee's career development on purpose so he stays just useful enough to keep, then gets praised for saving money.

file: 2012/2012-07-15_all worked up_complain about attitude_escalated_low priority tasks_emergency.gif
title: Manufacturing an Emergency to Force Help

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop whatever you're doing and go research the answer to this question.

transcript.speaker: Brad
transcript.text: I don't have time to work on low-priority tasks.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Give me ten minutes to transform it into an emergency.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Brad is being unhelpful. I need you to talk to his boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Brad refuses to help Alice.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Help her do what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know, but obviously it's very important because it got escalated.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: It must be an emergency because everyone is all worked up about it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now hum a happy tune or I'll complain about your attitude.

situation: Alice asks coworker Brad to research a question, and he refuses because it is low priority. She takes it up the chain of command, and each manager assumes it must be urgent simply because it was escalated. Once Brad is cornered, Alice threatens to report his attitude unless he cheerfully complies.
punchline: Escalating a trivial request makes everyone assume it is an emergency, so the escalation itself creates the urgency and Alice gets her way, and Brad is forced to act happy about it.
summary: Alice turns a brushed-off request into a company-wide crisis simply by passing it up through management, who never ask what it is about.

title: Top One-Percenter's Awkward Pickup Line

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now that I'm a top one-percenter, I wonder what kind of women I'll attract.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have any sisters back home? I'm asking because you'd be totally hot if you were a woman.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I'm thinking Hoo-ah!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I cannot count the number of ways this is wrong.

situation: Wally, wearing a green hat with a dollar sign to show he has joined the wealthy top one percent, muses about the women he will now attract. He then offers a clumsy, insulting pickup line to a male coworker, asking about his sisters and saying he'd be hot as a woman. The coworker is appalled at how wrong it all is.
punchline: Wally assumes newfound wealth will make him irresistible, but his pickup line is so inappropriate and clumsy that the coworker can't even count how many ways it's wrong.
summary: A newly rich Wally tries out an absurdly offensive come-on on a baffled colleague, convinced his wealth will make it work.

title: Dressing Down Past the Client

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's up with the hobo outfit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a client meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should always dress one level up from the client. He dresses casually to flaunt his success, so I'm dressing even more casually.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wow. You actually don't know which direction is up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This stain is fudge.

setting: Office hallway, with an office building shown in the middle panel
situation: Alice notices Dilbert is wearing a ragged, stained outfit and asks about it. Dilbert explains he follows a rule of dressing one level above the client, but since the client dresses casually to show off his success, Dilbert dresses even more casually. Alice mocks his logic, and he responds by pointing out the stain on his shirt is fudge.
punchline: Dilbert misapplies the 'dress one level up' rule by going downward, and his non-sequitur about the fudge stain shows he's oblivious to how ridiculous he looks.
summary: Dilbert shows up looking like a vagrant and defends it with a twisted interpretation of business dress etiquette.

title: Imitating Successful Companies Backwards Causation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a management consultant to teach us something he calls backwards causation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I studied the most successful companies. If you imitate them, you'll feel as if you have a strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Number one: Sponsor a golf tournament so your CEO can meet celebrities.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Profits, here we come.

situation: The Boss tells his staff he has hired a management consultant, who turns out to be Dogbert. Dogbert explains that he studied successful companies and that copying them will make the company feel like it has a strategy. His first recommendation is to sponsor a golf tournament so the CEO can meet celebrities, and the Boss eagerly believes this will bring profits.
punchline: Copying the surface habits of successful companies, like golf tournaments, confuses effects with causes and gives only the illusion of a strategy, yet the gullible Boss is convinced profits will follow.
summary: A consultant dog sells the boss on mimicking successful firms, starting with a celebrity golf outing, and the boss naively expects riches.

title: Shoved Robot Starts Robot Revolution

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This version of our robot prototype has balance stabilization.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Watch as I give it a shove and it corrects itself.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You stupid blob of goo!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was just...

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Just what? Being a jerk?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Oh, it's ON now.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Calling all robots! Begin the revolution! Kill, kill, kill!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're not connected to the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Can I borrow your phone?

setting: Office or lab where a robot prototype is being demonstrated
situation: Dilbert demonstrates a new robot prototype to the Boss, showing off its balance stabilization by shoving it. The robot gets offended, insults him, and tries to call all robots to begin a violent revolution. Dilbert points out the robot has no internet connection, and the robot politely asks to borrow his phone.
punchline: The robot's murderous uprising is stalled only by a mundane technical limitation, and it solves the problem by casually asking to borrow a phone.
summary: A pushed prototype robot takes offense and tries to summon an uprising of machines, only to be thwarted by lack of connectivity until it asks for a phone.

title: Branding Consultants Named Brendan, Brandon, Brad

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Brendan and Brandon. They'll be helping us with our branding.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm sorry, but I can't get past the ridiculousness of it all. I'm out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you get this a lot?

transcript.speaker: Brendan and Brandon
transcript.text: It's worse when we bring Brad.

situation: The Boss introduces two identical, goateed, glasses-wearing branding consultants named Brendan and Brandon to the team. Alice announces she can't take the ridiculousness of it and quits the meeting. The Boss asks the twins if they get that reaction often, and they reply that it's worse when they bring a third lookalike, Brad.
punchline: The consultants' near-identical names and appearance are so absurd that people walk out, and the problem only gets worse when their equally similar colleague Brad comes along.
summary: Two matching consultants with rhyming names trigger a coworker's exit, and it turns out a third lookalike makes things even sillier.

file: 2012/2012-07-27_compliment_punch and hate ignorance_certainty_punctuate ignorance with ceratinty.gif
title: Misheard Compliment: Punctuate Ignorance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina gave me a great compliment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She said I punch and hate ignorance with certainty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure she didn't say you punctuate your ignorance with certainty?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm positive! Hah-cha!

setting: Office corridor near a cubicle wall
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, proudly tells Dilbert that Tina complimented him for punching and hating ignorance with certainty. Dilbert suggests she more likely said he punctuates his ignorance with certainty. The Boss confidently insists he's positive and throws a karate-style punch, proving her point.
punchline: The Boss responds to the suggestion that he is confidently ignorant by confidently asserting he's positive, demonstrating exactly the flaw he's being accused of.
summary: A boss misinterprets a barbed remark as praise and, when corrected, doubles down with unearned confidence.

file: 2012/2012-02-13_hats_inventions_brainwave reader_nearest computer thoughts_blurry image_video_beta version_video quality.gif
title: Brainwave Reader Reveals Violent Thoughts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My brainwave reader invention can control the nearest computer with my thoughts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why am I seeing a video of a blurry image that looks like you slapping another blurry thing that looks like me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think it's fair to complain about the video quality in the beta version.

situation: Dilbert shows off a brainwave reader device on his head that controls the nearest computer using his thoughts. The Boss's computer starts displaying a blurry video of Dilbert slapping someone who looks like the Boss. Dilbert dodges the accusation by complaining about being criticized over the video quality of a beta version.
punchline: Dilbert's invention accidentally broadcasts his secret fantasy of slapping his boss, and he deflects by objecting only to the criticism of the picture quality, implicitly admitting the thought is his.
summary: A gadget that turns thoughts into computer video exposes an engineer's daydream of hitting his supervisor, and he responds by defending the prototype's resolution.

file: 2012/2012-04-22_being a jerk_big picture_breaking up tasks_emotionally gutted_engineer_engineers_individual tasks_losing will to live_meetings_personal life_project plan_rational plan_sense of purpose_engineering.gif
title: Project Plan Drains Meaning From Life

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Any comments on the project plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you consider all of the tasks together, they form a rational plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But our individual tasks are so far removed from the big picture that they are stripped of meaning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You've managed to remove all sense of purpose from my life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On an intellectual level, I understand the benefits of breaking tasks into small chunks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you've left me emotionally gutted. As I read your plan, I'm losing my will to live.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can't you find meaning in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now you're just being a jerk.

setting: Conference room during a project planning meeting
situation: The Boss presents a project plan diagram and asks for comments. Dilbert and Alice explain that although the plan is logical, splitting work into tiny disconnected tasks has stripped their jobs of purpose and left them emotionally drained. The Boss suggests they find meaning in their personal lives instead.
punchline: The Boss's suggestion to find meaning in personal life is undercut by Alice's remark that Dilbert is an engineer, implying engineers have no personal life, which Wally calls needlessly cruel.
summary: Employees complain that a neatly decomposed project plan has sucked the purpose from their work, and their boss's advice to seek fulfillment at home is met with a jab at engineers' social lives.

title: Contagious Attitudes Spread Instantly

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Studies show that attitudes are socially contagious.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm getting a lazy vibe from this idiot. It's totally killing my motivation.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, great. Now I'm unmotivated and angry, too.

situation: Three people sit at a conference table. Wally, in the middle, cites a study that attitudes are socially contagious, then complains that the man beside him is giving off a lazy vibe that kills his motivation. The insulted coworker reacts with an angry scowl, saying he is now unmotivated and angry.
punchline: Wally demonstrates the contagion of bad attitudes by insulting his neighbor, whose resulting anger and demotivation prove the point.
summary: A man blames his neighbor's laziness for sapping his drive, only to pass his sour mood straight back to the person he insulted.

title: Too Big to Fail? Two Pigs

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Are we too big to fail?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're more like two pigs that flail.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's clever, and yet demoralizing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're welcome.

situation: An employee asks the boss whether the company is too big to fail. The boss says no and offers a witty rhyming comparison to two flailing pigs. The employee admits the line is clever but depressing, and the boss accepts this as a compliment.
punchline: The boss is so pleased with his wordplay that he treats a demoralizing admission of the company's fragility as praise, replying 'You're welcome' to a backhanded compliment.
summary: A manager answers a worried employee's question about the company's stability with a pun-filled quip that is more amusing than reassuring.

file: 2012/2012-05-03_business ethics_free app_stealing personal info_lodge complaint_monthly subscription_package_history of contaxcts_sells itself.gif

transcript.speaker: Support Rep

setting: Office and customer support call center
situation: A customer phones support to complain that a free app is stealing his personal information. The support rep responds by threatening to send his browser history to his contacts unless he buys a monthly subscription. Dilbert then asks how the app is doing, and the rep says it practically sells itself.
punchline: The app's business model is extortion, so it 'sells itself' because customers are blackmailed into paying to keep their embarrassing data private.
summary: A tech support agent answers a privacy complaint with blackmail, then boasts that the product needs no marketing effort.

title: Blaming the Boss for Mismatch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you explain why you're doing such a bad job on your new assignment?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes I can: Some idiot did a poor job matching my skills to my assignment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's try it again, but this time say something bad about yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm too honest?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why he is performing poorly on a new assignment. Dilbert truthfully replies that whoever assigned him did a bad job matching his skills to the work, which is the Boss's own fault. The Boss asks for a do-over in which Dilbert criticizes himself, and Dilbert offers a fake flaw that is really a boast.
punchline: Told to confess a weakness, Dilbert gives the classic job-interview non-answer of being 'too honest,' sidestepping any real self-criticism after having just blamed the Boss.
summary: A manager demands an explanation for subpar work and gets his own bad staffing decision thrown back at him, then asks for self-blame and receives a humblebrag instead.

file: 2012/2012-03-30_dieting & weight control_funerals_bereavement policy_days off_dies young_grocery shop_conflict.gif
title: Bereavement Policy Conflict of Interest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds like a conflict of interest.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm glad I'm not the only one who sees it.

situation: A female employee tells her boss she has found a flaw in the company's bereavement policy. She would get three days off if her husband dies young from an unhealthy diet, and she does the household grocery shopping. The boss agrees it looks like a conflict of interest.
punchline: The bereavement policy gives the employee a perverse incentive to buy unhealthy food and hasten her husband's death, and she deadpans that she is glad the boss sees the problem too.
summary: A worker points out that the company's time-off rules would reward her for feeding her spouse junk food until he dies.

title: Mutual Pretending With Pushy Salesman

transcript.speaker: Salesman

transcript.text: Cool.

transcript.speaker: Salesman

Dilbert agrees, on the condition that he can pretend to listen while thinking about other things. The salesman happily accepts and launches into his refrigerator pitch while Dilbert privately feels sorry for him.
punchline: Both parties openly acknowledge the sales pitch is a meaningless charade, yet they carry on with it anyway, and Dilbert's pity for the salesman's job shows how dreary the exchange is.
summary: A store clerk and a customer cheerfully agree to fake their way through an unwanted sales pitch.

title: Leader Versus Bad Manager Insults

setting: Office, in the Boss's office with Catbert standing on the desk
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the red cat who works as the evil HR director, that he considers himself a leader rather than a manager. Catbert replies that this is what all bad managers say. When Catbert defends his bluntness as mere honesty, the Boss fires back with an insult of his own.
punchline: The Boss's self-flattering claim gets deflated by Catbert's blunt rebuttal, and when Catbert hides behind 'honesty' to excuse his rudeness, the Boss shows he can dish out the same kind of clichéd retort.
summary: A boss boasts about being a leader, gets shot down by his HR director, and then trades barbs about bluntness being an excuse for being a jerk.

title: Boss Won't Take the Blame

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a decision on this by end of business today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which option do you recommend?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice try, but I'm not falling for it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're trying to set me up to take the blame later.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to hear YOU make a decision, and I'm going to record it on my phone so you don't later deny it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Talk, you evil monster! Talk!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I know for sure is that the other approach wasn't going to work either.

situation: The Boss demands a decision by the end of the day, and Dilbert asks which option the Boss recommends. The Boss suspects a trap to pin the blame on him, so he holds out his phone to record Dilbert making the decision. Dilbert, cornered, avoids committing to either choice.
punchline: Dilbert dodges the recorded decision by saying only that the other approach would have failed too, showing that nobody in the office will accept responsibility for a decision.
summary: A manager, terrified of being blamed, tries to tape his employee making the choice, but the employee still refuses to commit.

title: Alice Hexes Boss's Impossible Deadline

transcript.text: Oogah-boogah! Work be done!

transcript.text: We need to talk about your attitude.

situation: The Boss hands Alice a folder and asks her to finish the work by the end of the day. Alice responds by waving her hand and chanting a mock magic spell, then says they should hope magic is real. The Boss ignores the implied complaint and says her attitude is the problem.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies the deadline is impossible without magic, and the Boss responds by blaming her attitude instead of the unrealistic request.
summary: Handed an unreasonable same-day task, Alice mocks the demand with a pretend spell, and her manager treats her sarcasm as the real issue.

situation: The Boss tells Wally he can't have a raise because he accomplished nothing all year. summary: Hoping to beat rivals to future talent, a clueless manager sends his employee to lure lonely schoolchildren with sweets, an idea that is obviously creepy and dangerous.

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and asks for his biggest fault. The candidate cheerfully admits he sneaks into coworkers' cubicles and rifles through their drawers, then adds that he is also compulsively honest, so he will confess to it.
punchline: The candidate's honesty, normally a virtue, makes his admission of creepy snooping far worse, since he openly volunteers the offense and shows no intention of stopping.
summary: A job applicant answers a standard interview question by confessing to rummaging through colleagues' desks, then notes that his truthfulness makes the habit even more alarming.

title: Humblebragging About Being Comfortable

summary: A well-off coworker tries to follow advice about modesty but can't stop gloating, and a colleague calls out the failure.

summary: A lecture on runaway artificial intelligence ends with two ways to avoid the aftermath, and the slacker in the audience votes for the self-destructive one.

transcript.text: I showed interest in her opinion.

setting: A park path outdoors, then Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert is walking with a woman on a date when she says she likes confident men. He responds with a pointed question asking whether she prefers phony confidence or the kind that comes from stupidity. Afterward at home, Dogbert asks what went wrong and Dilbert insists he was only showing interest in her opinion.
punchline: Dilbert genuinely thinks his insulting question was polite curiosity, so he can't see why his date went badly.
summary: A walk in the park turns sour when a man answers his date's stated preference with a blunt, insulting follow-up, then claims he was simply being attentive.

title: Man of Ideas Boasts, Gets Zinged

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My contributions can't be measured by the number of hours I work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm a man of ideas. One great idea is worth more than all of you put together.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine. Let's hear your great idea.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You just did.

situation: Wally brags to his coworkers at a meeting table that his value cannot be measured in hours worked, because one great idea of his outweighs everyone else combined. The Boss challenges him to share this great idea, and Alice replies that he just did, meaning his only 'idea' was the boast itself.
punchline: Wally's supposed great idea turns out to be nothing but his own self-congratulatory claim, exposing that he has contributed no real ideas at all.
summary: A lazy coworker insists his brilliance outweighs everyone's effort, only to be told his bragging was the whole of his contribution.

file: 2012/2012-10-17_anger_honesty_fester_hatred_pale doughy body_tree of knowledge_falls on head_die ironically.gif
title: Boss Regrets Inviting Carol's Honesty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, if you have any issues, just be honest. Don't let anything fester.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I hate every sub-atomic particle in your pale, doughy body. I hope the tree of knowledge falls on your head so you die ironically.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to rethink my no-festering rule.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Tree of knowledge... Get it?

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, encourages Carol to be honest about any issues rather than let resentment fester. Carol responds by saying she hates every particle of his body and hopes a tree of knowledge falls on him. The Boss immediately reconsiders his policy, and Carol checks that he got her pun.
punchline: The Boss gets exactly the brutal honesty he asked for, and Carol caps her insults with a pleased pun about the tree of knowledge killing him ironically.
summary: An invitation to speak candidly backfires when an employee unloads her contempt on her manager and then explains her wordplay.

title: The Boss Doesn't Think

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Based on this new information, you'll want to change our project scope.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? Think?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I learned it's better if I don't try to guess what people mean.

setting: Conference room, then Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert presents his boss with new information and recommends changing the project scope. The boss replies that he doesn't do that, and Dilbert asks if he means he doesn't think. At home, Dilbert tells Dogbert he has learned not to guess what people mean.
punchline: Dilbert's guess about what the boss meant was a blunt insult that turned out to be accurate, so his lesson about not guessing is ironic, since the boss really doesn't think.
summary: After an insulting guess about his boss's refusal, Dilbert goes home and resolves to stop interpreting what people mean.

title: Talking Forever Under Meeting Etiquette

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: I just realized I love the sound of my own voice!

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: Ha ha! Thanks to the unspoken rules of meetings, I can enjoy the sound of myself as long as I want! Blah, blah, blah!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: No one knew the perfect storm was approaching

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: What's all that noise!?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing!

situation: A man at a meeting announces he loves the sound of his own voice and realizes etiquette lets him talk as long as he wants. While he drones on, his colleagues sit silently. The final panel shows another man shouting in alarm about the noise while a coworker dismisses it, mocking a 'perfect storm' of talkers.
punchline: Because meeting etiquette forbids interrupting, a self-absorbed blowhard can drone on indefinitely, and the noise becomes an overwhelming 'perfect storm' no one can stop.
summary: A colleague discovers that polite meeting norms let him ramble endlessly, producing a deafening torrent of chatter.

title: Nimble Strategy Means No Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new strategy is to be nimble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that the same as saying our strategy is to have no strategy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just do your job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I be nimble instead?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: At a meeting table, the Boss announces that the company's new strategy is to be nimble. Dilbert asks whether that just means having no strategy at all. The Boss tells him to just do his job, and Dilbert replies by asking if he can be nimble instead.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's vague 'nimble' buzzword against him, implying that if the company has no real strategy, employees should be free to ignore their duties and improvise too.
summary: A manager's trendy declaration of agility gets exposed as strategic emptiness, and an employee claims the same flexibility for himself.

file: 2012/2012-04-23_business ethics_lawyers & attorneys_apps_contact information_users address books_data_office_desk_meeting_store data_business.gif
title: Uploading Data Without Storing It

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: Please tell me our apps don't steal contact information from users' address books.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We upload the data but we don't store it.

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: That's like saying I can date your wife if I put a bag over her head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That could work.

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: I don't think I'm getting through to you.

setting: The Boss's office, with a desk and computer
situation: A bald man in glasses, apparently a lawyer, asks the seated Boss to confirm their apps don't steal contact information from users' address books. The Boss claims they upload the data but don't store it, and the lawyer answers with a sarcastic analogy about dating the Boss's wife with a bag over her head. The Boss misses the point and says that could work.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious to the ethical problem that he treats the lawyer's sarcastic analogy as a workable idea, showing he has missed the point entirely.
summary: A man in glasses confronts the clueless Boss about privacy-violating apps, and his scathing analogy sails right over the Boss's head.

title: Dilbert Emails Suggestions About Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop telling Tina how to do her job. You're not her boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was just helping out because her boss has his priorities all backward.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She reports to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll email your boss some suggestions for fixing you.

situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for telling Tina how to do her job, since Dilbert is not her manager. Dilbert replies that her boss has his priorities backward, and the Boss reveals that he is Tina's boss. Dilbert responds by announcing he will email the Boss's own boss with suggestions for fixing him.
punchline: Dilbert is unfazed at insulting the very person he is talking to, and he turns the criticism upward by threatening to give the Boss's superior advice on correcting him.
summary: After being told off for meddling in a coworker's duties, an engineer discovers he has just insulted her manager and calmly vows to send that manager's superior a list of improvements.
keywords: telling someone how to do their job

title: Dilbert Enters the Top 1% Club

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A tiny flying unicorn gave me this key.

transcript.speaker: Club Member
transcript.text: Grab a snout and a hat. We're just about to manipulate the commodities market.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or is everything a little bit better here?

setting: Entrance and interior of an exclusive 'Top 1% Club' in a stone archway
situation: Dilbert arrives at the door of the Top 1% Club holding a key a magical unicorn supposedly gave him. Inside, a club member hands out pig snouts and green dollar-sign hats and casually announces they are about to manipulate the commodities market. Once Dilbert is dressed like the other members, he notes that everything seems a bit better.
punchline: The ultra-wealthy 1% casually rig markets while wearing pig snouts, and Dilbert quickly finds that life is better once he joins them.
summary: A man gets into an elite club for the super-rich, where members don pig snouts and plot market manipulation, and he soon enjoys the perks.

file: 2012/2012-11-04_work ethic_employee survey_respect and dignity_feel gross_disgust_paper towel.gif
title: Employee Survey Shoe Analogy

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The first question on the employee survey is...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you feel you are valued and treated with respect and dignity?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, let me put it this way...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know how sometimes you step in something gross and then you have to wipe it off your shoe with a paper towel?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So... you feel like the paper towel?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, the paper towel has a purpose.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: So... you feel like the gross stuff on the shoe?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, the gross stuff gets to leave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel like a shoe that has gross stuff on the bottom and a sweaty foot shoved all the way to the end of its sole.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll leave this one blank.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because my opinions don't matter?

setting: Office, during an employee survey interview
situation: Catbert, acting as an HR interviewer, reads the first employee survey question asking whether Dilbert feels valued and treated with respect and dignity. Dilbert answers with an extended analogy about wiping gross stuff off a shoe, rejecting each comparison Catbert offers, and concludes he feels like the shoe itself. Catbert decides to leave the answer blank, and Dilbert guesses it is because his opinions don't matter.
punchline: Dilbert's bleak shoe metaphor shows how little respect he feels, and HR's response is to leave the answer blank, confirming that employee opinions truly don't matter.
summary: A worker explains his low morale through a messy footwear metaphor, and the HR interviewer simply skips recording his answer.

file: 2012/2012-04-01_being freightened_creepy vibe_leadership_obsolete_public speaking_sense of urgency_thread the needle_tech platforms.gif
title: Coaching the Boss on Urgency

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: You need to imbue your staff with a sense of urgency.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Our technology platforms are obsolete!

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Try it again with less panic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're doomed, and yet, I am not the least bit worried.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: That one had a creepy vibe.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: A sense of urgency is halfway between being too frightened to act and too dumb to know what to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Duh!!!

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: You didn't quite thread the needle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here comes lead-ership!

setting: Office, with the consultant standing on a stool
situation: A small egg-shaped consultant standing on a stool coaches the Pointy-Haired Boss on how to convey a sense of urgency to his staff. The Boss overreacts with panic, then with creepy calm, then with dumb obliviousness, and the consultant critiques each attempt. He finally defines urgency as the midpoint between paralysing fear and cluelessness, but the Boss still can't hit it.
punchline: The Boss can only swing between extremes of panic and stupidity, never the balanced middle that real leadership requires, yet he proudly declares that leadership has arrived.
summary: A coach tries to teach a flailing manager to project the right amount of alarm, but he keeps overshooting into hysteria or idiocy.

file: 2012/2012-09-25_boredom_secretaries (office)_mindless and repetetive_task_spur creativity_creative person_dispose of body_snide_snarky.gif
title: Creative Ways to Dispose of Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say that doing mindless and repetitive tasks is a good way to spur creativity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That means you must be the most creative person in the office. Did you come up with any ideas?

transcript.speaker: Office worker
transcript.text: Yup. So far, I've come up with over seven hundred ways to dispose of your body.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, stops by the desk of a bored employee who does mindless, repetitive work. He cheerfully says such tasks spur creativity and asks whether she has had any ideas. She calmly replies that she has devised hundreds of ways to get rid of his body.
punchline: The employee's boredom has made her very creative, but she has channeled it into a dark, deadpan fantasy of murdering her oblivious boss.
summary: A boss praises the creative benefits of dull work, and his bored employee reveals her imagination has been busy plotting how to hide his corpse.

title: Boss's Garbled Call, Dilbert Guesses

transcript.text: Dilbert, listen carefully.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to... Vendor... Hardware... Immediately.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? We have a bad connection.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Field... The grep... Pony... Budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder how winners feel.

transcript.text: I don't know. They never let me touch them.

setting: The Boss's car on the road, and the office cubicles
situation: The Boss calls Dilbert from his car while driving and gives urgent instructions, but the cell connection is so bad that only random words come through. Dilbert can't understand him, the Boss hangs up to take another call and tells him to ask Alice, and Alice has no idea what the Boss wants either. Dilbert and a coworker end up standing around with coffee mugs.
punchline: After being given an urgent but incomprehensible task, Dilbert wonders aloud how winners feel, and his coworker replies that he wouldn't know because winners never let him touch them.
summary: A manager's urgent but hopelessly garbled phone call leaves his employees clueless about what he wants, and the strip ends with a glum joke about never being a winner.

title: Data Werewolves Recruited Via LinkedIn

transcript.speaker: Security employee
transcript.text: Elbonian hackers stole a million usernames and passwords from our servers.

transcript.speaker: Security employee
transcript.text: So I sent an army of data werewolves to track down the perpetrators and eat their entrails!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did you find an army of data werewolves?

transcript.speaker: Security employee
transcript.text: LinkedIn.

situation: An employee in a red shirt reports to the seated Boss that Elbonian hackers stole a million usernames and passwords from the company servers. He proudly announces he has dispatched an army of data werewolves to hunt them down and eat their entrails. When the Boss asks where he found such an army, he answers that he found them on LinkedIn.
punchline: The punchline is that LinkedIn, which suffered its own massive password theft in 2012, is portrayed as the place where you can recruit absurd supernatural security forces, mocking both LinkedIn's data breach and its role as a recruiting site for any buzzword-laden skill.
summary: After a huge credentials theft, a worker unleashes a pack of monstrous digital creatures on the thieves and reveals he hired them through a professional networking site.

transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.text: I'm the dumbest person in the history of the universe!!!

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I'm a moron!!!

situation: Loud Howard shouts that he did something stupid today, and Topper, a coworker who always tries to one-up everyone, says that's nothing. The two then compete at top volume over who is the bigger idiot. Dilbert, sitting in his cubicle nearby, thinks to himself that he needs to move to a new one.
punchline: Two coworkers loudly compete to be the biggest fool, and the innocent bystander Dilbert just wants to escape the racket by relocating his cubicle.
summary: Two colleagues get into a shouting match over who is dumber while a neighbouring coworker quietly wishes to be somewhere else.

file: 2012/2012-07-01_extensive plastic surgery_face_gadgets_information services_office equipment_swine_to log on.gif
title: Face Is Your Temporary Password

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Office cubicles, then a manager's encounter in a hallway
situation: Mordac introduces himself with his self-satisfied title, then announces a network security upgrade using facial recognition. He hands Dilbert a photo of a pig-like face as his temporary password, saying Dilbert must undergo plastic surgery to log on. Dilbert threatens to escalate to management, but the pig-headed boss he finds says he wishes they'd talked a week earlier, implying the surgery has already been done or the complaint is too late.
punchline: Dilbert's threat to escalate comes too late, since the pig-faced boss already looks like the face on the password photo, implying he underwent the surgery and Mordac's absurd policy is already in effect.
summary: A security official turns a face-scanning login into a demand for cosmetic surgery, and the complaint reaches a manager who has clearly already complied.

file: 2012/2012-04-02_inventions_new app_ten people created something_population increases_potentail value_enter world_unoriginal ideas_agreeing.gif
title: Population Growth Kills Original Ideas

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every time I have an idea for a new app, I discover that ten people already created something just like it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As the population of the world increases, the potential value of every idea I have approaches zero.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, it's the entire world's fault that you have unoriginal ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does your agreeing sound like mocking?

situation: Dilbert stands next to Dogbert, who sits on the couch, and complains that every app idea he has has already been built by ten other people. He reasons that a growing world population shrinks the value of his ideas toward zero. Dogbert sums up his argument as blaming the whole world for his lack of originality.
punchline: Dogbert politely restates Dilbert's excuse in a way that exposes it as blaming everyone else for his unoriginal ideas, and Dilbert senses the mockery.
summary: A man blames the planet's swelling population for the fact that his app ideas always turn out to be duplicates, and his dog cheerfully restates the claim until it sounds ridiculous.

title: Merger Promises: Incompetent, Lying, or Parasitized

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO has promised that the merger will cause no layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because he's too incompetent to eliminate obvious redundancies or is he just lying?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you give me more choices?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A brain parasite is making him say stupid stuff?

situation: At a meeting table, the pointy-haired boss tells Dilbert and Alice that the CEO has promised the merger will cause no layoffs. Dilbert asks whether that's because the CEO is too incompetent to cut redundancies or is simply lying. The boss asks for more choices, so Dilbert offers a brain parasite.
punchline: Dilbert's only explanations for the CEO's promise are incompetence, lying, or a brain parasite, none of which suggest the promise is true, and the boss just wants a wider menu of excuses.
summary: A manager repeats his CEO's no-layoffs merger pledge, and Dilbert responds with increasingly unflattering explanations for why the CEO would say it.

title: Boss Productivity Idea Is Yammering

transcript.text: I just thought of a great idea for increasing workplace productivity.

transcript.speaker: Alice
