transcript.text: Geez. Who salted the earth?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your plan is going great so far.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, announces he has a great idea for boosting workplace productivity. Alice, seated at her desk, sarcastically guesses that the idea is for him to stand next to her and talk while she tries to work. The Boss reacts as if she is being unusually hostile, and she replies that his plan is going great.
punchline: The Boss's 'productivity' idea is exactly the kind of idle chatter that prevents work, and Alice sarcastically points out that it is already succeeding at making her unproductive.
summary: A manager proudly announces a productivity scheme while loitering at an employee's desk, and she wryly notes that his interruption is the only thing his plan has achieved.

title: Mornings Reserved For Useful Work

transcript.text: Can you come to my meeting at 8 AM tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I reserve the first few hours of every morning for useful work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That feels like an insult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call it good time management. There's a lot of overlap.

situation: A coworker holding papers asks Dilbert to attend his 8 AM meeting the next day. Dilbert flatly refuses, explaining that he saves the early morning hours for useful work. When the coworker takes offense, Dilbert says it's just good time management.
punchline: By saying his mornings are for useful work and then noting the 'overlap' with the meeting time, Dilbert implies that meetings are the opposite of useful work.
summary: Dilbert turns down an early meeting invitation by claiming his mornings are for productive tasks, then cheerfully confirms that the meeting falls squarely into that category of wasted time.

file: 2012/2012-08-07_recessions_regular interns_interns intern_no pay_semi relevant job experience_slap you_no reason_stupid economy.gif
title: Intern to the Intern

summary: A desperate applicant agrees to work for free as a servant to an intern, even after being warned of random slapping, because the job market is that grim.

punchline: The Boss dismisses the charge of contradiction by citing a third success cliché, flexibility, which conveniently excuses any inconsistency in his advice.

file: 2012/2012-04-09_family_work from home_2 days err week_reduce carbon foorprint_wife_small children_egg carton_talking to moron_relationships.gif
title: Home Is Worse Than the Office

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to work from home for two days per week to reduce our carbon footprint.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Noooooo!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My wife and three small children are in that house. They're always mean to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How bad could it be?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me put it this way: I'm sitting in an egg carton and talking to a moron, and this is better.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to work from home two days a week to cut the company's carbon footprint. Dilbert protests, explaining that his wife and three small children are always mean to him at home. The Boss asks how bad it could be, and Dilbert replies that his cubicle and conversation with the Boss are an improvement.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss to his face, saying that sitting in a cramped cubicle talking to a moron is preferable to being at home with his family.
summary: Faced with a mandatory remote-work plan, a miserable employee insists that his cramped cubicle and clueless boss still beat his own household.

title: Three Secret Task Forces, No Updates

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Our millennial employees keep quitting because of our bureaucracy and poor communication.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Form three task forces to look into it. But don't tell any of the task forces that there are two others doing the same thing.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Should I give you regular updates?

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Nah.

situation: The Boss tells an employee that young workers keep quitting because of bureaucracy and poor communication. His solution is to create three task forces and keep each one unaware of the other two. When the employee offers regular updates, the Boss declines.
punchline: The Boss responds to complaints about bureaucracy and poor communication by creating redundant, secretive task forces and refusing any updates, which is exactly the kind of bureaucracy and poor communication that is driving people away.
summary: A manager blames employee turnover on red tape and bad communication, then fixes it with secret duplicate committees and no status reports.

title: Nailing Goals Nobody Ever Mentioned

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How are you doing on your unspoken objectives?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm referring to the goals I have in my mind that I've never mentioned.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How are those going?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm totally nailing them.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how he is progressing on objectives the Boss has only thought about and never communicated. Dilbert is confused, so the Boss explains they are goals in his own mind. Dilbert then claims he is totally succeeding at them.
punchline: Since the goals were never stated, Dilbert can claim to be meeting them with no possibility of being proven wrong, which mocks vague performance expectations and unverifiable self-assessments.
summary: A manager quizzes an employee on secret goals he never shared, and the employee cheerfully claims perfect success.

title: Faking Optimism About New Products

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And that's my suggestion for our next product.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How do we know that ten other companies aren't working on the same idea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, that's always a possibility.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There are seven billion people on Earth. I'll bet a million of them had this idea.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's irrational to think that any new product is likely to be a hit.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: On the other hand, we only get paid if we pretend to be optimistic about new products.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All in favor of faking our optimism, raise your hands.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I could get was fake buy-in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the only kind there is.

setting: Conference room meeting, then the boss's office
situation: Dilbert pitches an idea for the next product in a meeting, and Wally points out that many other people have likely had the same idea and that success is statistically unlikely. Wally then notes they only get paid for pretending to be optimistic, and the group raises their hands to fake enthusiasm. Dilbert reports to the boss that he only got fake buy-in.
punchline: Genuine buy-in for new products doesn't exist in corporate life; everyone just pretends to be optimistic because that's what gets them paid.
summary: A product pitch gets rational skepticism until the team realizes that performing enthusiasm is what the job actually requires.

title: Therapist Complains, Dilbert Turns Tables

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People always try to take advantage of me.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I know what you mean.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I lost five pounds and my husband didn't notice!

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I came home last night and he hadn't even cleaned the garage like he promised.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I had to park on the street!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagina-tion, or have you found a clever way to make people pay to listen to you complain?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Tell me more about how you think I'm clever.

setting: A therapist's office with a couch
situation: Dilbert lies on a therapist's couch and says people take advantage of him. Instead of helping, the therapist responds by airing her own petty marital complaints about her husband not noticing her weight loss or cleaning the garage. Dilbert points out she has found a way to get paid to complain, and she answers by fishing for more flattery.
punchline: The therapist deflects Dilbert's accusation by turning his insight into a compliment, asking him to elaborate on how clever she is, which confirms she is exploiting the session for her own benefit.
summary: A counselor hijacks her patient's appointment to vent about her own household grievances, then fishes for praise when he calls her out.

file: 2012/2012-05-15_confusing_multiple pages_public speaking_real words_small text_unpersuasive_computer_desk_no one can read_technology.gif
title: Unreadable Chart Or Confusing Pages

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want me to put the chart on one page, which would make the text too small for your audience to see?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or do you prefer a multiple-page approach that is confusing and unpersuasive?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's probably better if no one can read it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I won't bother using real words.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss how he wants a chart for a presentation formatted, offering two bad options: everything on one page with text too small to read, or spread over several confusing pages. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, decides it is better if nobody can read it. Dilbert responds that he won't even bother putting in real words.
punchline: The Boss prefers a presentation nobody can read, so Dilbert sarcastically concludes he may as well fill it with meaningless text.
summary: Offered two terrible ways to lay out a presentation chart, the boss opts for illegibility, and his engineer cheerfully agrees to skip actual content.

file: 2012/2012-04-08_lunch date_not attracted_technoloigy_only like tech_people are creepy_delivery system_viruses_germs_picture_photoshop_people hater.gif
title: Wally Becomes a Digisexual

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, do you want to go to lunch?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, thanks. I'm a digisexual now.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm no longer attracted to people.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I only like technology.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People creep me out. You're basically a delivery system for viruses, germs, and unreasonable favor requests.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm willing to take a picture of you, but that's as far as I'll go.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is the most disturbing conversation I've ever had.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thank goodness for Photoshop.

situation: Alice invites Wally to lunch, and he declines, announcing he is now a 'digisexual' who is only attracted to technology. He explains that people creep him out as carriers of germs and favor requests, then offers only to take her picture. Alice is disturbed, and Wally's closing remark implies he will edit the photo.
punchline: Wally reveals he will use Photoshop to alter Alice's photo to suit his tastes, implying she isn't acceptable as-is, while insulting people as mere delivery systems for germs and annoying requests.
summary: A coworker's lunch invitation is rebuffed by Wally, who claims to only be attracted to gadgets and plans to digitally doctor a snapshot of her.

file: 2012/2012-01-17_actions & defenses_billion dollars_business ethics_golden key_rich people_top 1%_flying unicorn.gif
title: Billion-Dollar Settlement Buys Secret Club

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a billion dollars to settle your claim of discrimination against short, bald, nearsighted guys.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm in the top 1% now. I wonder where we hold our secret meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ask the tiny flying unicorn with the golden key.

situation: The Boss hands a check for a billion dollars to a short, bald, nearsighted coworker (Wally) to settle a discrimination claim. Wally, now suddenly part of the top 1%, wonders where the wealthy elite hold their secret meetings. The Boss sarcastically tells him to ask a tiny flying unicorn carrying a golden key, who appears in the last panel.
punchline: The secret gatherings of the ultra-rich are treated as an absurd myth, so the only way in is a fantasy creature with a golden key.
summary: A man handed a fortune to drop his grievance asks how to join the wealthy elite's hidden gatherings and is told to consult a whimsical winged creature.

title: Don't Explain Filtration To Turtles

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This design would be inefficient.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How do you know that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes it's better if the aquarium owner doesn't explain to the turtle how the filtration system works.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (silent panel: Dilbert's tablet lies on the desk as the coworker sits with arms crossed)

situation: Dilbert, holding a tablet, declares that a design would be inefficient. When a coworker asks how he knows, Dilbert answers with an odd analogy about an aquarium owner and a turtle, implying the coworker is the turtle who shouldn't be told how things work. In the last panel the tablet sits on the desk and the coworker stays unimpressed.
punchline: Dilbert compares the coworker to a turtle in an aquarium who is better off not understanding the system, which is a condescending way of saying he won't explain his reasoning because the coworker wouldn't understand it.
summary: Pressed to justify a design critique, Dilbert replies with a pet-tank metaphor that casts his questioner as an uninformed reptile.

title: Daydreaming Startup Is Worse Than Job

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'm escaping the mental prison of this job by creating apps in my mind and fantasizing about running a start-up.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! The start-up is too much work! The stress is killing me! Take me back to my prison!

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'm back. Did I say anything embarrassing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's all relative.

situation: At a meeting table, a coworker confesses that he escapes his dull job by imagining running a start-up. Mid-daydream he panics that the imaginary start-up is too stressful and begs to return to his 'prison' job. Once back, he asks Dilbert if he said anything embarrassing.
punchline: Dilbert's dry 'It's all relative' implies the coworker has just embarrassed himself by shouting out loud, while also noting that even an imaginary start-up makes a miserable job look good by comparison.
summary: A worker who dreams of startup freedom gets overwhelmed by his own fantasy and gratefully retreats to his dreary job, publicly blurting it all out.

file: 2012/2012-11-08_inventions_waterworks_invented filter_raw sewage_pure drinking water_clean water_upper container_drank contaminated water.gif
title: Sewage Filter Demo Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a filter that can turn raw sewage into pure drinking water in seconds.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Glug glug glug

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The clean water ends up here in the upper container.

setting: Laboratory or office with a water filter machine on a table
situation: Dilbert, in a lab coat, proudly announces his invention that turns raw sewage into drinking water. A bald coworker immediately grabs a glass and gulps down the liquid from the machine. Dilbert then explains that the clean water collects in the upper container, implying the man drank the untreated sewage.
punchline: The coworker drank the liquid before Dilbert explained which container held the clean water, so he almost certainly chugged raw sewage.
summary: A scientist's eager audience member samples the output of a sewage purifier before learning which part actually dispenses the safe water.

file: 2012/2012-11-19_business ethics_gotcha fees_airlines_make moneky_terrible battery life_high five.gif
title: Gotcha Fees and Faulty Chargers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You need to have more "gotcha" fees. That's how airlines make their money.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, you could design your product to have a terrible battery life, then sell extra chargers for ten times your cost.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And maybe the chargers could break after two months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: High five!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss to add hidden "gotcha" fees the way airlines do. He suggests designing a product with a terrible battery and then selling overpriced chargers, which should also break after two months. The Boss enthusiastically responds with a high five.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is openly predatory and the Boss eagerly embraces it, showing how companies gleefully profit by deliberately frustrating and trapping their customers.
summary: A scheming consultant coaches his boss on squeezing customers with sneaky fees and deliberately flawed accessories, and the boss celebrates the plan.

file: 2012/2012-01-30_complaining_conversation_ask ed_dumb guy_liar_bad breath_braggaty_large pores_combover_describe me_behind my back_insecure guy_steers conversation.gif
title: Describing Ed Behind His Back

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You should ask Ed about this.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is Ed the dumb guy who talks too much or the liar with the bad breath?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's the braggart with large pores and a combover.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. How do you describe ME behind my back?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're the insecure guy who steers the conversation to himself.

situation: Alice tells a seated coworker to ask Ed about something, and the two trade unflattering descriptions of Ed to work out which Ed is meant. Dilbert walks up, overhears them, and asks how they would describe him behind his back.
punchline: Dilbert's question proves the coworker's insulting description of him right, since he turns a conversation about Ed into one about himself.
summary: Two coworkers casually trash a colleague's looks and habits until a eavesdropping Dilbert asks for his own review and gets an honest one.

title: Boss Can't Understand Any Technology Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't sign off on this technology plan because I don't understand it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To be fair, you wouldn't understand ANY technology plan, including the "do nothing" scenario.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is this one of those cases where context isn't helpful?

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: The Boss refuses to approve a technology plan because he doesn't understand it. Dilbert points out that the Boss wouldn't understand any plan at all, even the one where nothing is done. The Boss then wonders aloud whether Dilbert's remark is a case where context isn't helpful.
punchline: Dilbert's explanation that the Boss is baffled by everything doesn't help, and the Boss is too clueless to realize that the context is actually an insult to him.
summary: A manager balks at a proposal he can't follow, and an engineer's polite clarification only reveals that the manager is lost on every possible option.

title: Schrödinger's Quantum Computer Project Status

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's your quantum computer prototype coming along?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Great!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: The project exists in a simultaneous state of being both totally successful and not even started.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can I observe it?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: That's a tricky question.

situation: The Boss asks an engineer about the progress of a quantum computer prototype. The engineer first says it's going great, then admits the project is simultaneously totally successful and not even started. When the Boss asks to observe it, the engineer says that's a tricky question.
punchline: Like a quantum system collapsing when observed, the engineer's project can claim to be successful only as long as nobody checks it, since observation would reveal that nothing has been done.
summary: An employee dodges accountability by borrowing quantum physics jargon to claim his project is in two contradictory states until someone looks.

title: Nine Months Late Performance Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I finished your performance review.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Terrific. It's nine months late and all you did was sign what I wrote.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I also read it, but I'm not 100% positive.

situation: The Boss hands Carol her completed performance review. Carol points out that it is nine months overdue and that he merely signed the review she wrote herself. He admits he may have read it, but isn't entirely sure.
punchline: The Boss's uncertainty about whether he even read the review shows how little attention he pays to managing his staff.
summary: A manager delivers an overdue review that his own employee wrote for him, and can't even confirm he read it.

title: Cubicles Lower Intelligence, Office Proves Otherwise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would be more productive with my own office. Studies show that cubicle workplaces lower intelligence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't be sure that's true because your cubicle lowered your intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... Why does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because I have an office.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a private office, citing studies that cubicle workplaces lower intelligence. The boss turns the argument around, saying Dilbert's own cubicle-dulled intelligence makes his claim unreliable. Dilbert is briefly persuaded by the circular logic, and the boss points to his own office as proof he is the smart one.
punchline: The boss uses circular, self-serving logic to dismiss the request, implying that having an office is what makes him intelligent enough to be right.
summary: A request for better workspace gets rejected with a tidy bit of reasoning that conveniently flatters the person holding the corner office.

title: Six Coffees, Icy Roads, Guardrail

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're just getting here?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's zero degrees and the roads are all ice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I drank six cups of coffee before leaving the house and sat in traffic for two hours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're three hours late.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I spent the last hour stuck to a guardrail.

situation: The Boss checks his watch and asks Wally why he is arriving so late. Wally blames icy roads and says he sat in traffic for two hours after drinking six cups of coffee. When the Boss points out he is three hours late, Wally adds that he spent the final hour stuck to a guardrail.
punchline: Wally's excuse keeps escalating, and the last detail, his car being stuck on a guardrail, shows his driving or weather woes are far worse than he first admitted, while accounting for the missing hour.
summary: A tardy employee piles on increasingly absurd reasons for showing up hours behind schedule, ending with a car lodged on a guardrail.

file: 2012/2012-02-28_collaboration tools_human contact_internet & world wide web_judegment_long term goal_meetings_suite of tools.gif
title: Collaboration Tools to Avoid People

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm designing a suite of internet collaboration tools.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's part of my long-term goal to eliminate all forms of direct human contact.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: That's messed up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're exactly what I'm trying to avoid.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, presents a diagram of an internet collaboration tool at a projection screen to a few seated coworkers. He explains that his real aim is to eliminate all direct human contact. When an attendee calls this messed up, Wally replies that the attendee is exactly the kind of person he is trying to avoid.
punchline: Wally's collaboration software is really designed to let him avoid collaborating with people in person, and he insults the person who objects by saying they are precisely what he wants to escape.
summary: A lazy, antisocial engineer reveals that his networking software exists so he never has to deal with coworkers face to face, then snubs the one who calls him out.

title: A Monkey Could Do Your Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would feel more motivated if I knew how my assignment fits into the big picture.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't need to be motivated. A monkey could do your assignment while eating a banana.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Like this. Ooh-ooh-ooh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we're moving in the wrong direction.

setting: Office hallway beside a cubicle wall
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he'd be more motivated if he understood how his assignment fits into the big picture. The boss dismisses the request, saying a monkey could do the work while eating a banana. He then acts out a monkey, hopping and going 'ooh-ooh-ooh', while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: Dilbert asks for purpose and context, and the boss responds by insulting the work's difficulty and literally acting like a monkey, which makes the conversation go the opposite way from motivating.
summary: Asked to explain why an assignment matters, a manager instead belittles the task and mimics a primate.

title: Engineers Squirm Under Interrogation

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Why are all the engineers in this meeting squirming when I talk?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Did your boss order you to act like team players during this meeting and later thwart me by inaction?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Answer me!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Squirm

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Squirm

situation: A red-haired man leading a meeting notices the engineers squirming whenever he speaks. He asks Dilbert whether their boss ordered them to pretend to be team players and then quietly sabotage him through inaction. When he demands an answer, the engineers can only squirm nervously, which confirms his suspicion.
punchline: The engineers' wordless squirming is an answer in itself, revealing that they were indeed told to feign cooperation while passively undermining him.
summary: A meeting leader accuses his squirming engineers of faking cooperation on their boss's orders, and their nervous silence gives them away.

title: Trivia Win Triggers Aggressive Insults

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been aggressive recently.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I haven't noticed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think my testosterone is all jacked up because I won the company's online trivia contest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now get out of my way, useless worm.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, I'm starting to see it.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker holding a coffee mug that he has been aggressive lately, and the coworker says he hasn't noticed. Dilbert blames a testosterone surge from winning the company's online trivia contest, then immediately insults the coworker and tells him to get out of his way.
punchline: Dilbert demonstrates his newfound aggression by calling his coworker a useless worm, finally making the coworker aware of it, and the cause is the absurdly trivial victory of an online trivia contest.
summary: After a small office quiz victory supposedly floods him with hormones, Dilbert proves his aggressive streak by hurling an insult at a colleague who hadn't noticed anything.

title: Boss Congratulates Himself on Absence

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been so busy lately that I haven't had time to manage you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It must have been a nightmare for all of you to be without my leadership for so long.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This might be a good time to lead us to the next topic on the agenda.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss admits he has been too busy to manage his team. He then smugly assumes the staff suffered without his leadership. Alice responds by sarcastically suggesting he lead them to the next agenda item.
punchline: The Boss believes his absence was a hardship, but Alice's dry remark implies his leadership is useless and the team did fine without him, so he may as well just move the meeting along.
summary: A manager assumes his team was lost without his guidance, and a coworker pointedly steers him back to the meeting's agenda.

title: Insulting Your Boss In The Interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do you want to leave your current job?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: My boss is a pointy-haired loser, but he's smart enough to know when he's being insulted right to his face.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I'm looking to improve on that situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You came to the right place.

setting: Interview room with a conference table
situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss interviews a job candidate and asks why she wants to leave her current job. She bluntly calls her own boss a pointy-haired loser, and says she wants a better boss. The interviewer, who is himself a pointy-haired boss, fails to notice the insult and cheerfully assures her she has come to the right place.
punchline: The Boss doesn't realize the candidate is insulting him, and is so oblivious that he takes the description of a loser boss as a compliment and agrees he's the improvement she wants.
summary: A job seeker trashes her pointy-haired superior to the face of her pointy-haired interviewer, who is too clueless to recognize himself.

file: 2012/2012-03-09_dating_internet & world wide web_dating site_social media_propsects_addicted_facebook_pain meds_prescription pain meds_eye contact_relationships_technology.gif
title: Dating Site Prospects: Two Addictions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got two good prospects on this dating site.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One is addicted to Facebook and the other is addicted to prescription pain meds.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sort of a tie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But only one of them is likely to make eye contact.

setting: Dilbert's desk at home, at his computer
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer browsing an online dating site and reports that he has found two promising matches. He explains that one is addicted to Facebook and the other to prescription pain medication. Dogbert says it's a tie, and Dilbert points out that only one of them is likely to look him in the eye.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of a good dating prospect is a choice between a social media addict who stares at a screen and a painkiller addict, and he picks based on who might make eye contact, showing how low his standards and dating options are.
summary: Dilbert weighs his two online dating matches, both with addictions, and concludes that the pill-popper at least might look at him.

title: Boss Suggests Changes as Questions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why don't you change this box to say "virtual"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because I don't want it to look like it was written by an ignorant blob in an ugly wool suit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You probably shouldn't put your suggestions in the form of questions.

situation: The Boss, sitting across from Dilbert with a paper in hand, suggests changing a box on a document to say "virtual," phrasing it as a question. Dilbert takes the question literally and answers it by insulting the Boss, saying the change would make the document look like it was written by an ignorant blob in an ugly wool suit. He then advises the Boss to stop phrasing suggestions as questions.
punchline: By answering the Boss's rhetorical suggestion as a literal question, Dilbert gets to deliver an insult under the cover of a straight answer, then blames the Boss's phrasing.
summary: Taking his manager's polite-sounding suggestion at face value, an engineer answers it with a blunt insult and a lesson in how to give direction.

title: Civility Died At A Meeting

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's a good time to get together and discuss my project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every interaction I've had with you has been a waste of time. I have no reason to think it will be different in the future.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sheesh! How did civility die?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you invited it to a meeting.

situation: A coworker stands at Dilbert's cubicle and asks when they can meet to discuss his project. Dilbert bluntly answers 'never' and explains that every past interaction has wasted his time. When the coworker complains that politeness has vanished, Dilbert suggests civility died by being invited to a meeting.
punchline: Dilbert implies that meetings are so tedious and soul-draining that they kill anything good, including civility, and so the coworker has only himself to blame.
summary: A blunt cubicle dweller refuses a colleague's request for a meeting and then blames meetings themselves for the death of politeness.

file: 2012/2012-10-24_death & dying_death certificate_staple on head_no return messages.gif
title: Stapling Death Certificate to Head

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You haven't returned any of my messages, so I took the liberty of making a death certificate for you.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'll just staple it to the back of your head so everyone can see it.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Are we good here?

situation: A coworker with big curly hair tells a colleague at his desk that he has ignored her messages, so she made a death certificate for him. She then announces she will staple it to the back of his head, and in the last panel she has done so while he sits stiffly, wide-eyed, with a paper stuck to his head.
punchline: Ignoring someone's messages is treated as being dead to them, and she escalates to violent, passive-aggressive office retaliation, then casually asks if everything is fine now.
summary: A frustrated coworker responds to being ignored by officially declaring the offender dead and fastening the paperwork to his skull.

title: Speechwriter Has No Economic Value

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Google has offered to buy our company for $100 million just to get our engineers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I agreed to the deal because I'm a modern day slave trader who believes engineers are property and the rest of you have no economic value.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who wrote my speech?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Someone with no economic value.

situation: The Boss addresses the company from a podium and announces that Google wants to buy the firm solely to acquire its engineers. Reading the prepared speech, he blurts out that he is a modern day slave trader who thinks only engineers have value. He then asks who wrote it, and a voice from the audience answers.
punchline: The speechwriter, one of the non-engineers the speech just declared worthless, is the one who wrote the insulting speech, and the boss's own words condemn him to be the target of the sarcastic reply.
summary: A boss reads an acquisition speech that insults everyone except the engineers, then wonders aloud who could have written such a thing.

title: Layoff Comes With Cardboard Box

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, the merger has made your job redundant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As a reward for your years of hard work, feel free to use one of our cardboard boxes to get your junk out of here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh. It looks like we forgot to hide the good boxes.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Ted that a merger has made his job redundant. He then offers Ted a cardboard box as a 'reward' for his years of service. Ted leaves carrying his belongings in the box, and the Boss realizes they forgot to hide the good boxes.
punchline: The Boss presents a cardboard box as a generous parting gift to a laid-off employee, then regrets that Ted got a good one, showing how stingy and callous the company is even while firing him.
summary: A manager fires an employee after a merger and grudgingly lets him pack up in a box, then laments that a decent box was left out in the open.

title: Punishing Success With Budget Cuts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've been asked to cut our budget by 30%.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't make sense. We met all of our objectives last year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A different part of our company had a huge loss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shouldn't you cut their budget, not ours?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Their budget isn't big enough to make a difference to the bottom line.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So our strategy is to punish success, and reward failure?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just do your job and leave the strategy to management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hypothetically, if I do my job poorly, would that be good or bad for me?

situation: In a meeting, the Boss announces that their department must cut its budget by 30%. Dilbert points out that his team met all its objectives while another division had the huge loss, but the Boss explains the failing division's budget is too small to matter. When told to leave strategy to management, Dilbert asks what would happen if he did his job poorly.
punchline: Since the company's strategy visibly punishes success and rewards failure, Dilbert sarcastically wonders whether doing poor work would actually benefit him.
summary: A department that hit every goal gets slashed funding because a different division lost money, prompting an employee to question whether incompetence pays better.

file: 2012/2012-10-30_controlling gaze_lazy_management experts_managers & supervisors_one on one meetings_regular does_theiveing_underlings_work ethic_toxic saboteur_business.gif
title: Boss's Gaze Makes Employee Lazier

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Management experts say bosses should have frequent one-on-one meetings with underlings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently, you need regular doses of my controlling gaze to prevent you from evolving into a lazy, thieving, toxic saboteur.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's working great. So far I feel less lazy about doing the other things you mentioned.

situation: The Boss stands by Alice's desk holding a coffee mug and announces that he is following expert advice to hold frequent one-on-one meetings. He explains, insultingly, that he must keep watch over her so she doesn't become a lazy, thieving, toxic saboteur. Alice deadpans that it's working, because she now feels less lazy about doing the other bad things he listed.
punchline: Alice sarcastically turns the Boss's accusation around, implying that his insulting meetings have made her feel less guilty about being a thief and saboteur, not less so.
summary: A manager's patronising check-in with a worker backfires when she coolly implies his distrust is licensing her to misbehave.

title: Sarcastic Thanks for Book Loan

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It was a great book. I'll loan you the paperback.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks. I love it when other people decide how I'll spend my free time.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't tell when you're kidding.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Paperbacks are awesome. I'm a big fan of clutter.

situation: A coworker enthusiastically offers to lend Dilbert a paperback of a book he enjoyed. Dilbert responds with obvious sarcasm about others dictating his free time. When the coworker says he can't tell if Dilbert is kidding, Dilbert answers with more sarcasm, claiming to love clutter.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcasm is so heavy that the coworker still can't tell it's sarcasm, and Dilbert's reply only doubles down on the insincere enthusiasm, revealing he doesn't want the book.
summary: A well-meaning book loan gets a deadpan sarcastic reception from Dilbert, who then answers a question about his sincerity with yet more sarcasm.

title: Leadership Book Blamed on Underling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I read a book about how to be a great leader, and realized I don't do any of those things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm surprised that a book with so many errors could get published.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It must have been written by a disgruntled underling.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do those exist?

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: The Boss stands with coffee mugs alongside Dilbert and Wally and says he read a book on being a great leader and found he does none of the things it recommends. Rather than reflect, he decides the book must be full of errors and was written by a disgruntled underling. Wally sarcastically asks whether such people even exist.
punchline: The boss dismisses advice he fails to follow by blaming a disgruntled employee, while Wally's sarcastic question implies his management makes plenty of disgruntled underlings.
summary: Confronted by a management book that describes everything he gets wrong, a clueless supervisor decides the book itself is flawed and a resentful subordinate must have written it.

title: Buffer Overflow Bucket of Water

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Interview question

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: How would you diagnose a buffer overflow problem?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: I'd put the circuit board in a bucket of water and look for air bubbles.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: That sounds right.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: I just diagnosed a problem with your interview question.

situation: An interviewer asks a job candidate how he would diagnose a buffer overflow problem. The candidate gives a nonsensical hardware answer about dunking a circuit board in water and looking for air bubbles, and the interviewer says it sounds right. The candidate then reveals the interviewer's question is itself flawed because he doesn't understand the topic.
punchline: The interviewer's approval of an absurd answer exposes that he doesn't know what a buffer overflow is, since it is a software bug and not a physical circuit board fault.
summary: A candidate gives a ridiculous answer to a technical question and, when the interviewer accepts it, realizes the interviewer has no idea what he is asking.

title: Every Employee Needs a Nemesis

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My old nemesis retired, so I asked Randy to take over that function because he's ineffective at everything he does.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The physics of work requires that each employee be matched with an anti-employee called a nemesis.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: I don't know who my nemesis is.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Uh-oh. You got a hider. They're the worst.

setting: Office conference table during a meeting or lunch
situation: Dilbert tells Randy, a coworker, that he has been assigned to be Dilbert's new nemesis because he is ineffective at everything. Dilbert then explains that the 'physics of work' requires every employee to have an opposing anti-employee. Randy says he doesn't know who his own nemesis is, and another coworker warns that he has a 'hider', the worst kind.
punchline: Randy's own nemesis is a secret one who hides from him, which the coworker says is the worst kind, and the pseudo-scientific 'physics of work' makes office rivalry sound like a law of nature.
summary: Dilbert recruits a hapless colleague as his new rival, claiming workplace physics demands everyone have an opposing counterpart, and the colleague learns his own rival is hiding.

title: Bottle Cap Hoax Teamwork Award

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Thanks to your leadership, we collected twenty thousand bottle caps to help fund chemo for poor children.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And thanks to your . . . whatever. . . we checked Snopes.com and learned that the bottle cap thing was an Internet hoax.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I only brought one Teamwork Award mug, so you'll have to take turns drinking from it.

situation: A bald coworker addresses the Boss and Dilbert at a meeting, crediting the Boss's leadership for collecting twenty thousand bottle caps for children's chemo. He then reveals the whole charity drive was an internet hoax debunked by Snopes.com. He ends by giving them a single Teamwork Award mug to share.
punchline: The coworker sarcastically rewards a wasted, hoax-based charity effort with a Teamwork Award mug, and the single shared mug underscores that the effort deserved no real praise.
summary: After a charity bottle cap drive turns out to be a hoax, a coworker sarcastically presents the leaders with one shared award mug.

title: Google Glasses Reveal Reasons Not Friends

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Those must be the Google glasses that give you information about your environment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, and I see seventeen reasons to not be your friend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll sweep your dumb tweets off to the side.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This is unsettling.

situation: A coworker notices Dilbert wearing Google Glasses and comments on their environmental-information feature. Dilbert replies that the glasses show him seventeen reasons not to be her friend, then gestures in the air as if swiping her dumb tweets aside. She finds the experience unsettling.
punchline: Wearable augmented-reality glasses let the wearer see everything unflattering about the people around him, such as their social media posts, and he openly dismisses them in front of their faces.
summary: A man in smart glasses coldly judges a colleague using her online history while waving away her posts in mid-air.

title: Rescheduling Over Ten Minutes Late

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm sorry I'm a few minutes late for our 10:50 meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We'll have to reschedule because I have another meeting at eleven.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Reschedule? I'm only ten minutes late!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tell that to my 11:10.

situation: Asok arrives a few minutes late to a 10:50 meeting with Wally, who refuses to continue and says they must reschedule because he has another meeting at eleven. In the last panel Alice, apparently the person waiting for the 11:10 slot, protests that she is only ten minutes late, and Wally tells her to take it up with his 11:10.
punchline: Wally treats lateness as a scheduling rule that lets him dodge meetings, and the rotating late arrivals are each turned away to make way for the next.
summary: A man arrives slightly late to a meeting and gets turned away by a colleague who claims he has another appointment coming up.

file: 2012/2012-05-18_job description_mindless zombie_team work_wate time_tasks_waste time_never shows intitaive.gif
title: Wally's Job Description Dilemma

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Should I waste my time doing tasks that are not in my job description?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or should I be a mindless zombie that shuns teamwork and never shows initiative?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take your time. I'm good either way.

situation: Wally stands in front of the Boss's desk holding his coffee mug and asks aloud whether he should do work outside his job description or be a mindless, uncooperative zombie. The Boss sits at his desk and calmly tells him to take his time, saying either choice is fine with him.
punchline: Wally frames his laziness as a choice between wasting time and being a zombie, and the indifferent Boss shows he doesn't care which, since he benefits or loses nothing either way.
summary: An employee weighs doing extra work against doing nothing, and his apathetic manager is happy with whichever he picks.

title: Containing the Angry Female Colleague

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Settle down, honey. I didn't ask for your opinion. I'm telling you what we're going to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Lower the containment unit! She's going to blow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will it be safe?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right after you die.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss condescendingly calls Alice 'honey' and tells her he doesn't want her opinion. Alice gets visibly furious, so Dilbert panics and calls for a containment unit to be lowered over her. In the last panel, the Boss asks when it will be safe to let her out.
punchline: Dilbert says it will only be safe after the Boss dies, implying Alice's rage is justified and will last as long as he is alive.
summary: A patronizing boss dismisses a colleague and provokes such rage that she has to be sealed in a vault, from which she can only emerge once he is dead.

title: Stylish Cool Replacement for Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, this is Lars. He's a better version of you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is what you would look like if you were stylish and cool and fun to be with.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can it do math?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That will matter on the same day that all the ugly people die.

setting: Office, a plain wall with a green gradient background
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to Lars, a look-alike who is a stylish, cool, fun version of Dilbert, dressed in a yellow shirt. Dilbert responds by asking whether Lars can do math. The Boss dismisses technical skill as irrelevant.
punchline: The Boss implies that competence will only be valued when all the ugly people are dead, meaning never, since appearance and style always win out over ability.
summary: Management presents a polished, charming clone of an engineer and brushes off the engineer's concern about whether the replacement has any actual skills.

title: Real Golf Versus Xbox Golf

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I played golf at Pebble Beach over the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I played that course on Xbox.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's totally different.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I used a full spectrum lamp to simulate sunlight.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I got fresh air!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should get a house that has windows. They're terrific.

setting: Office break area beside the coffee maker
situation: A coworker brags about playing golf at Pebble Beach over the weekend, and Dilbert says he played the same course on his Xbox. When the coworker insists it's not the same, Dilbert says he used a full spectrum lamp to simulate sunlight. The coworker boasts about the fresh air, and Dilbert suggests he get a house with windows.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the only advantages of real golf, sunlight and fresh air, are things he already gets from ordinary windows at home, so his video game is just as good.
summary: A man bragging about a real golf weekend gets matched point for point by a homebody whose virtual round lacks nothing but a trip outdoors.

title: Speaking Truth To Power Insultingly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you respect those who speak truth to power?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what that means.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In this case it means you're ignorant, bald, and overpaid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you respect me yet, or should I keep going?

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert standing on the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, asks The Boss whether he respects people who speak truth to power. The Boss admits he doesn't understand the phrase, so Dogbert demonstrates by calling him ignorant, bald, and overpaid. The Boss grows visibly angry, and Dogbert asks if he's earned respect yet.
punchline: Dogbert literally speaks 'truth' to the powerful boss by insulting him accurately, then sarcastically asks whether this earns the respect the boss claimed to give truth-tellers.
summary: A talking dog shows his clueless executive what honest feedback to authority looks like by delivering a string of accurate insults.

file: 2012/2012-08-24_average person_offer low prices_prices_products on sale_raising prices_smart enough.gif
title: Fake Sales Versus Everyday Low Prices

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We're going to stop pretending our products are always on sale and instead offer low prices all the time.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The average person is smart enough to know that our so-called sale prices are our normal prices anyway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever talked to an average person?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me again why we're raising all of our prices?

situation: A manager at a meeting announces the company will drop its permanent fake sales in favor of consistently low prices, assuming customers already see through the sale gimmick. Dilbert skeptically asks whether he has ever actually spoken to an average person. The Boss, now confused, asks why the company is raising all its prices.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcasm suggests the average person is not smart enough to see through fake sales, and the Boss's confusion shows that dropping the sale pricing quietly turns into a price increase.
summary: A plan to ditch phony sales rests on a flattering view of customer intelligence that Dilbert doubts, while the boss muddles the whole idea into a price hike.

title: Robot Shark Is Actually Dolphin

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hearing some complaints that you built a robot shark to patrol the so-called territorial waters around your cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's a robot dolphin. I can see how people might be confused.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need you to smile more.

transcript.speaker: Robot Dolphin
transcript.text: Whatever.

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Alice that coworkers have complained about a robot shark she built to patrol the area around her cubicle. Alice insists it is a robot dolphin and says she understands why people might mistake it. Her robot, which still looks like a shark, is told to smile more and answers with a bored 'Whatever.'
punchline: Alice sarcastically passes off her obviously menacing robot shark as a friendly dolphin, and its surly 'Whatever' shows it is just as hostile as she is.
summary: An employee defends her cubicle-guarding robot by claiming it is a harmless dolphin, while the sulking machine plainly behaves like a shark.

title: Pantless Weasel Does Our SEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a pantless weasel to do our search engine optimization.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He'll help us game the system and corrupt the integrity of all Internet search results for our industry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your new job title is "Accomplice."

situation: The Boss stands beside a weasel he has hired to handle the company's search engine optimization and explains that the weasel will manipulate search results across their whole industry. He then turns to Dilbert, who sits quietly at his desk, and assigns him a new job title tied to the scheme.
punchline: By naming Dilbert an "Accomplice," the Boss openly admits the SEO plan is unethical and deliberately drags Dilbert into the wrongdoing.
summary: A manager brings in a shady animal consultant to rig web rankings and cheerfully informs a coworker that he is now officially complicit.

title: Blaming Poor Communication For Missed Task

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you finish the tasks we talked about in the last meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, because your communication skills are so poor that I had no idea I was supposed to do a task.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did I have a task?

situation: The Boss asks the people at the meeting table whether they completed the tasks assigned in the last meeting. Dilbert replies that he didn't do his because the Boss communicated so poorly that he never realized he had been given one. Wally, sitting nearby with his coffee mug, then asks whether he had a task too.
punchline: Wally's question shows that the Boss's communication really is so bad that people leave meetings without knowing they were assigned any work, and Wally is happy to exploit the same excuse.
summary: A manager's vague delegation leaves his team unaware they were ever given assignments, and one employee quietly checks whether he can use the same alibi.

title: Faking Engagement Before Deciding Anyway

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: Before I make my decision, I'd like to ask for your opinions.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: It's supposed to make you feel "engaged."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you actually plan to listen to us?

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: I'm hoping it will look that way on the outside.

situation: A bald manager seated at a meeting table tells Dilbert and The Boss he wants their opinions before making his decision. He then admits that soliciting input is only meant to make employees feel engaged. When Dilbert asks if he will actually listen, the manager says he only hopes it will appear that way to outsiders.
punchline: The manager openly admits that asking for opinions is a hollow gesture meant to create the appearance of employee engagement rather than a real willingness to listen.
summary: A decision-maker confesses that consulting his staff is purely for show and that he has no intention of heeding their advice.

title: Power to the Lazy Rally Cry

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I say we throw future generations under the bus and do as little work as possible until we die.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Power to the lazy!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That sounded more awesome when I practiced it in the bathroom mirror this morning.

situation: At a meeting table, Wally proposes sacrificing future generations and doing as little work as possible until everyone dies. He then raises a fist and shouts a rousing slogan. Nobody responds, and he admits it sounded better when he rehearsed it in his bathroom mirror.
punchline: Wally's lazy, selfish rally speech falls flat in front of a silent audience, exposing that even his stirring slogans are rehearsed in advance for effect.
summary: A slacker delivers a rehearsed rallying cry for laziness at a meeting and gets stony silence in return.
keywords: do as little work as possible

title: Too Paranoid To Talk

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So, Dilbert, what else are you working on lately?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd rather not say because you have a habit of misinterpreting everything you hear and then bad-mouthing it later.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He basically said he's too paranoid to talk to people.

transcript.speaker: Other Coworker
transcript.text: He sounds crazy.

setting: Office meeting table, then a hallway
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert what he is working on, and Dilbert declines to answer, saying the coworker misinterprets everything and then bad-mouths it. In the last panel the coworker recounts the exchange to someone else, framing Dilbert as paranoid.
punchline: By spinning Dilbert's accurate accusation into a story about Dilbert's paranoia, the coworker proves exactly the bad-mouthing habit Dilbert warned about.
summary: A gossiping colleague instantly confirms Dilbert's suspicion by retelling his refusal to chat as proof that he is unhinged.

title: Shared Leadership Means Taking the Blame

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm moving to a shared leadership model.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each of you will take on one piece of the leadership role.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's my piece?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see. I have you down for something called... Blame.

situation: The Boss announces he is switching to a shared leadership model in which each employee takes on one piece of the leadership role. Dilbert asks which piece is his, and the Boss consults a paper and assigns him the role of 'Blame'.
punchline: Under the guise of 'shared leadership', the Boss keeps the credit and authority while handing his subordinate the only part of leadership he doesn't want: taking the fall when things go wrong.
summary: A manager pretends to spread leadership duties among his staff, then hands one employee the thankless job of being the scapegoat.

file: 2012/2012-10-02_engineers_wages_hiring engineers_google_million per year_change the world_average engineer pay_money.gif
title: Change the World by Cutting Pay

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hiring engineers

transcript.speaker: Engineer Candidate
transcript.text: Google offered me a million dollars a year. What's your offer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Work for us and you can change the world!

transcript.speaker: Engineer Candidate
transcript.text: Change it how?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By lowering the average pay of engineers.

setting: Interview room with a conference table
situation: The Boss is interviewing an engineer who says Google offered him a million dollars a year and asks what the company will pay. The Boss responds with a vague pitch about changing the world. When the candidate asks how, the Boss admits the company's contribution would be lowering engineers' average pay.
punchline: The Boss's inspiring 'change the world' pitch turns out to mean the company will make the world worse for engineers by driving down their salaries, which is a stark contrast to Google's offer.
summary: A job candidate with a lucrative competing offer is told the company's mission is to reshape the world by making engineers poorer.

file: 2012/2012-10-18_capitalism_electronic mail_colorful opions_email_advertising plan_discoverable record_describing advertising_pinocchio doing backstroke.gif
title: Deniability Is Capitalism's Essential Ingredient

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please stop using email to express your colorful opinions of our marketing campaign.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't need a discoverable record of you describing our advertising plan as "Pinocchio doing the backstroke in Satan's septic tank."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember that capitalism without deniability is the same as poverty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eh?

situation: The Boss sits at his desk and tells Dilbert to stop putting his harsh opinions of the marketing campaign into email. He warns that such messages create a discoverable record, then adds that business needs deniability to prosper. Dilbert, standing by the desk, responds with a puzzled 'Eh?'.
punchline: The Boss cynically admits that businesses depend on being able to deny embarrassing or damaging truths, so honest written criticism threatens the whole system.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for emailing his blunt, unflattering critique of an ad plan and explains that profit depends on plausible deniability.

title: Walk Off the Worm Infestation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The bad apple you hired is ruining the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just walk it off, you big baby. I want solutions, not problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ouch! Stupid bad apple!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Walk it off.

situation: Dilbert, covered in green worms, complains to the Boss that the bad apple he hired is ruining everyone else. The Boss dismisses him, telling him to walk it off and bring solutions rather than problems. Moments later the worms attack the Boss, who yelps in pain, and Dilbert throws his own dismissive advice back at him.
punchline: The Boss callously brushes off the problem until it affects him personally, and then Dilbert repeats his own 'walk it off' advice back to him.
summary: A worm-ridden employee is told to tough it out by his boss, who promptly gets bitten by the same worms and receives his own advice in return.

title: CEO Drinks Sewage, Best Day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me tell you what kind of day I had at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There was some confusion about my water purification prototype, and our CEO drank eight ounces of untreated sewage.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So... best day ever?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It'll be hard to top.

situation: Dilbert comes home and tells Dogbert about his day at work. A mix-up with his water purification prototype led the CEO to drink eight ounces of untreated sewage. Dogbert deadpans that it must have been the best day ever, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: Dilbert is delighted that his CEO accidentally drank sewage, showing how much he dislikes upper management and treating it as the highlight of his career.
summary: A harmless-sounding engineering mishap turns out to be a triumph for one employee when his executive gets a mouthful of sewage.

title: Chronically Late Coworker Sees Through Trick

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's meet before the project meeting to go over a few things.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nice try.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We chronically late people know when we're being played.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your pre-meeting is a trick to get me to show up on time for the real meeting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But that won't work because poor planning isn't the cause of my chronic lateness.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I make people wait for me because I enjoy the power and I don't care about anyone's feelings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. I'll see you at the project meeting at ten.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nice try. I know the meeting is at 10:30.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you keep a job?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That attitude is exactly why I don't like people.

situation: Dilbert asks a chronically late coworker to attend a pre-meeting before a project meeting. The coworker sees through the ploy, admits he is late deliberately because he enjoys making people wait, and then calls Dilbert's bluff when Dilbert gives him a false meeting time.
punchline: The coworker is not only habitually late out of spite, he is also too wise to every scheduling trick, and he blames Dilbert's reasonable question for why he dislikes people.
summary: A coworker who is late on purpose outwits every attempt to get him to a meeting on time and then takes offense when asked how he stays employed.

title: Ignoring Specs Is Easier, Says Wally

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Based on a true story

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: I completed the wireframe and passed it off to our coders.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's great. Did you incorporate all of my specs?

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: I didn't see any specs from you. Maybe my spam filter ate your email.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I'll resend them and you can start from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: Yes, I certainly could do that.

transcript.speaker: Designer
transcript.text: Or I could ignore your input, enjoy my deep feeling of accomplishment, and hope for the best.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That sounds easier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I accept your wise counsel, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I guess your search for relevance marches on.

situation: At a meeting, a designer says he finished the wireframe and handed it to the coders. Dilbert asks whether his specs were included, and the designer claims his spam filter ate Dilbert's email. Dilbert offers to resend them so the designer can start over, but the designer decides to ignore the input and hope for the best, and Wally agrees that is easier.
punchline: The designer's spam-filter excuse is a cover for skipping Dilbert's input, and Wally's approval of the lazy option leaves Dilbert's contribution irrelevant.
summary: A colleague dodges Dilbert's requirements with a convenient excuse and happily chooses the easy path over redoing his work.

title: Wally Lives in the Restroom

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Have you seen Wally?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's been in the men's room for two days.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He used to leave when he was done reading the paper. But he switched to an iPad and now he doesn't know when he's finished.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He has to come out to eat.

transcript.speaker: Pizza Delivery Man
transcript.text: I have a pizza for the third stall.

setting: Office hallway outside the men's room
situation: Alice asks Dilbert where Wally is, and Dilbert says Wally has been in the men's room for two days. He explains that Wally used to leave once he finished reading the newspaper, but now he reads on an iPad, which has no natural end. Alice assumes Wally will have to come out to eat, but a delivery man arrives with a pizza for the third stall.
punchline: An endless digital feed removes the natural stopping point of a newspaper, so Wally never leaves the stall and even has his food delivered to him there.
summary: A tablet's bottomless content keeps a lazy coworker camped in a bathroom stall so long that his meals are brought to him.

file: 2012/2012-04-20_business ethics_competitors network_elbonians_bribe blogger_limited capacity_self control_bury in woods.gif
title: Wearing Down Dilbert's Ethical Resistance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you hack into our competitor's network and make it look as if the Elbonians did it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you bribe a blogger to write good things about our company?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that I've worn down your limited capacity for self-control, I need you to bury something in the woods, no questions asked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to commit a series of unethical acts, starting with hacking a competitor and framing the Elbonians, then bribing a blogger. Dilbert refuses both. The Boss then reveals he was deliberately exhausting Dilbert's willpower before asking him to bury something in the woods, and Dilbert gives in.
punchline: The Boss uses the psychology of ego depletion on purpose, wearing down Dilbert's resistance with absurd requests so he will agree to the real, sinister one (probably a body) without asking questions.
summary: A manager deliberately drains his employee's willpower with outrageous demands so that a shady final request gets an easy yes.

title: Free Software That Begs for Upgrades

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Want some free software?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's it do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All it does is beg you for upgrades. And if you upgrade, then it begs you to upgrade again and so on.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And it makes all of your other software run slow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And it's free?

setting: The Boss's office, with an establishing shot of the office building
situation: Dogbert offers the Pointy-Haired Boss some free software and then honestly describes what it does: it nags for upgrades endlessly and slows down all his other software. Instead of being put off, the Boss is impressed that it costs nothing.
punchline: The Boss fixates on the price tag and ignores the obvious drawbacks, showing how 'free' can override any sense of quality or usefulness.
summary: A talking dog pitches a useless, nagging, system-slowing program, and his gullible boss is sold the moment he hears it costs nothing.

title: Paid Not to Work or Sue

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you agree to give me no work, I will agree to not sue you with some sort of bogus employee claim.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My existence will make your empire seem larger, and stockholders will get stuck with the bill for my paycheck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why does that seem like a fair plan?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We live in an awful world.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: Wally proposes a deal to the Boss: give him no work, and in return he won't file a bogus employee claim against the company. He explains that his headcount will make the Boss's empire look bigger while shareholders pay his salary. The Boss asks why this seems fair, and Wally simply says the world is awful.
punchline: Wally openly admits he is running a legal-threat racket that exploits corporate empire-building, and the only justification he offers is that the world is terrible.
summary: Wally strikes a deal with his boss to draw a salary for doing nothing in exchange for not threatening a frivolous lawsuit.

title: Sarcastic Link to Decision Definition

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need something called a "decision."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might not know what that word means, so I emailed you a link to its definition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did people do sarcasm before the internet?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe they didn't need to.

situation: Dilbert tells a person seated at a desk that he needs a decision from them. He sarcastically says he has emailed them a link to the definition of the word, in case they don't know it. Later, holding a coffee mug, he muses to a coworker about how people did sarcasm before the internet, and the coworker replies that maybe they didn't need to.
punchline: The coworker's reply implies that people in the past didn't need sarcasm because they weren't dealing with such frustratingly indecisive people, which suggests modern workplaces are uniquely maddening.
summary: A frustrated engineer mocks a slow-moving colleague by emailing a dictionary link, then wonders how sarcasm survived without the web.

file: 2012/2012-08-25_business ethics_fake 50%_dumb customers_smart shoppers_$400 per hour_freaking genius.gif
title: Consultant Discount Makes Boss Feel Brilliant

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your fake 50% sale prices make dumb customers feel like smart shoppers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why am I paying you $400 an hour to tell me what I already know?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Usually I charge $800 per hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes! I'm a freakin' genius.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, explains to the Boss that his fake 50% sales trick customers into feeling like smart shoppers. The Boss complains that he is paying $400 an hour for obvious information. Dogbert replies that his usual rate is $800, and the Boss takes it as proof that he got a half-price deal.
punchline: Dogbert applies the same fake-discount trick to the Boss, who falls for it and feels like a genius for getting a 'half-price' consultant.
summary: A consultant demonstrates the very pricing con he is describing by pretending to halve his fee, and the gullible client happily proves the point.

title: Quote Wasted, Effort Nets Out Same

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I worked every night for a month to come up with a detailed quote for one of our potential customers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then those weasels used our quote to get a better price from their regular vendor!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you really do all of that work?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, but it nets out the same.

situation: At a meeting table, a coworker complains that he spent a month of nights preparing a detailed quote for a prospective customer, only for the customer to use it to negotiate a lower price from their usual vendor. In the last panel, Dilbert asks if he really did all that work, and the coworker admits he didn't.
