punchline: The coworker's outrage over his supposed hard work is hollow because he never did the work, but since the customer's use of the quote was equally pointless, he claims the outcome is the same either way.
summary: A man grumbles about being exploited after supposedly slaving over a sales quote, then confesses he never actually did the labor he's complaining about.

title: Asok's Overcorrected Assertiveness Training

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need to teach you to be more assertive in meetings.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: You're a miserable human being and I hope you die in a long, painful way!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dial it back a little.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I hope you die quickly?

situation: The Boss tells Asok he needs assertiveness training for meetings. Asok immediately demonstrates by screaming a vicious insult and death wish at the Boss. The Boss asks him to tone it down, so Asok revises the wish to a quick death.
punchline: Asok misunderstands assertiveness as extreme hostility, and his 'toned down' version is still a death wish, just a more merciful one.
summary: Told to be more forceful in meetings, a timid employee overshoots into abuse and then offers only a mildly kinder curse when asked to soften it.

title: Boss Uncomfortable With Happy Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It makes me uncomfortable when they appear to enjoy working.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It feels like I'm not doing my job.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Same planet, different reality

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Suffer!

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss stands holding a coffee mug and thinks to himself that he feels uncomfortable when employees seem to enjoy working. He concludes it makes him feel like he isn't doing his job. In the last panel he glares at Dilbert, who is happily working at his computer with headphones on, and silently wishes suffering on him.
punchline: The boss believes his job is to make employees miserable, so a happy worker makes him feel like he is failing as a manager.
summary: A manager secretly resents a contented employee because he thinks good management means making people unhappy.

title: Users' Suggestions Ruined Our Product

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We interviewed hundreds of users and turned all of their suggestions into features.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As it turns out, every user we talked to was an idiot, and their dumb suggestions ruined our product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In hindsight, we probably should have talked to people who work outside this building.

setting: Conference room during a project presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a slide showing many stick-figure users pointing at a computer, explaining that the team turned every user suggestion into a feature. He then admits the users were idiots and their suggestions ruined the product. He concludes that they should have consulted people from outside the company, while the Boss and a coworker sit listening.
punchline: The users the team consulted were actually their own colleagues inside the building, so the product was ruined by bad advice from the very people who should have known better.
summary: A product team learns too late that building every feature a group of insiders requested produced a terrible result.

file: 2012/2012-02-19_charge customers_free features_customers_abusive realtionship_move in direction_put up with.gif
title: Customers Tolerate Abusive Pricing Changes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've decided to charge customers for features they currently get for free.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Have you considered how our customers might react?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Obviously.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'd like to hear how that reasoning process went.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Customers love us and they will put up with anything we dish out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... it's sort of an abusive relationship?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not yet, but we're trying to move in that direction.

situation: The Boss announces that the company will start charging customers for features that were previously free. Dilbert and a coworker question whether he has thought about customer reaction, and the Boss explains that customers love the company and will tolerate anything. When Dilbert calls it an abusive relationship, the Boss says they are working toward that.
punchline: The Boss treats customer loyalty as a license to exploit them, and admits he aims to make the relationship truly abusive.
summary: A manager plans to monetize free features, banking on customers' devotion, and cheerfully aspires to a relationship that exploits them even more.

title: Lawyer Settles Discrimination Claim Generously

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: I've been asked to settle your claim of discrimination against the company.

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Your complaint is that they discriminate against you for being short, bald, and nearsighted.

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: I might have a conflict of interest, but my final offer is one billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Plus a statue and an apology.

situation: The company lawyer visits a short, bald, nearsighted employee who has filed a discrimination claim against the company. The lawyer recites the complaint, then admits he may have a conflict of interest, since he shares those very traits, and offers one billion dollars. The employee takes advantage and demands a statue and an apology too.
punchline: The company's own lawyer is short, bald, and nearsighted too, so his conflict of interest makes him absurdly overgenerous in settling a claim against his employer.
summary: A corporate attorney sent to settle a discrimination complaint realizes he shares the plaintiff's traits and responds by offering a ridiculous fortune.

title: Boss's Golden Rule Fails Test

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can make this a great place to work by following the Golden Rule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Treat others as you would want them to treat you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's dumb.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not dumb!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's test your rule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like it if someone gave you a hundred dollars?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. So give me a hundred dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or else forever live as a hypocrite who doesn't follow his own dumb rule.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Snork!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Snork!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate your engineering guts!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least you're making sense now.

situation: The Boss presents the Golden Rule as a way to improve the workplace, and Dilbert calls it dumb. The Boss proposes to test it, but Dilbert turns the test around: since the Boss would like to receive a hundred dollars, the rule implies he should hand some over. Wally and Alice snork at the Boss's predicament.
punchline: Dilbert traps the Boss with his own rule, forcing him to either pay up or admit he is a hypocrite, and the Boss's angry outburst is the first thing he's said that makes sense.
summary: A manager's attempt to defend a workplace maxim backfires when an engineer applies it literally to the manager's own wallet.

title: Cooler Clone Meeting Awkwardness

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is it awkward being in the same meeting as a cooler version of yourself?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Scoot back so I can get a clear view. This guy really makes my engine purr.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A little more...

situation: Alice, seated beside Dilbert and a bald coworker in an orange shirt, asks the coworker whether it is awkward to share a meeting with a cooler version of himself. She then tells Dilbert to scoot back so she can get a clear view of the cooler guy she finds attractive. In the last panel Dilbert leans back in his chair, apparently attending a different meeting remotely, and asks for a little more.
punchline: Alice is not talking to Dilbert but about the cooler version of him on the other side, and Dilbert, oblivious, happily scoots back believing the attention is somehow for him, making him the butt of the joke.
summary: A woman at a meeting flirts with a more attractive double of a colleague and has the wrong man shift his chair to improve her view.

title: Fraudulent Analysis Pleases The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished the fraudulent analysis you requested to support the decision you already made.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a total betrayal of shareholders and a slap in the face for anyone who values rational behavior.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks. That's exactly what I wanted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

situation: Dilbert tells the seated Boss he has finished the analysis the Boss requested to justify a decision already made, and openly calls it fraudulent. He adds that it betrays shareholders and insults anyone who values rational behavior. The Boss is unbothered and simply thanks him for delivering exactly what he wanted.
punchline: Dilbert frankly admits the analysis is a fraud and the Boss doesn't care, showing that management only wants rubber-stamp justification for decisions, not truth.
summary: An employee hands over a bogus report built to back a decision that was already made, bluntly condemns it, and his boss happily accepts it anyway.

title: Boss Claims Hubris Suits Him

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've read that smart people make bad decisions because of their hubris.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hubris? What is that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Beats me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But obviously I'm a prime candidate to get it.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Catbert he read that smart people make bad decisions because of hubris. When Catbert asks what hubris means, the Boss admits he has no idea. He then confidently declares that he must be a prime candidate to suffer from it.
punchline: The Boss is so ignorant he doesn't know what hubris is, yet his hubris leads him to assume he is smart enough to be at risk of it.
summary: A manager repeats a claim about clever people and arrogance without understanding the word, then flatters himself that he must be vulnerable to it.

title: Ghostwriter Mocks Boss's Autobiography

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I finished ghost-writing your autobiography.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "I was ridiculously lucky. The end."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was hoping you'd include something about all of my hard work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You didn't work any harder than your gardener, and he lives in his truck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What about my vision and my intuition?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My first draft had a chapter on your hallucinations and magical thinking.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But I covered that ground with the title: "I'm a delusional sociopath and you can too."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm starting to regret paying you in advance.

situation: Dogbert, hired as a ghostwriter, delivers the finished autobiography to the Boss. The book is just one sentence crediting luck, and Dogbert shoots down each of the Boss's attempts to claim hard work, vision or intuition. He then reveals the book's title calls the Boss a delusional sociopath.
punchline: The ghostwriter has already been paid, so he writes an honest and insulting autobiography that exposes the Boss as a lucky, delusional sociopath, and the Boss realizes too late he can't demand a refund.
summary: A hired ghostwriter hands over a one-line memoir attributing his client's success to luck and then insults him in the title.

file: 2012/2012-01-08_appearences_big cubicle_loose weight_project leader_status system_toilet paper holder_wider cubicle.gif
title: Promotion Comes With Wider Cubicle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations! I'm naming you Project Leader.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As such, you are entitled to a cubicle that is three inches wider than standard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like the one I have.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't have a choice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It is critical that we maintain the integrity of the status system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Otherwise our CEO will look like a jerk for having a private bathroom with a trained falcon as a toilet paper holder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. Where's my larger cubicle?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the awkward part.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't have one. I need you to lose weight until it looks as if your cubicle is larger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And if I don't?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The falcon needs an assistant.

situation: The Boss promotes Dilbert to Project Leader and says the promotion entitles him to a wider cubicle, insisting it is needed to preserve the company's status hierarchy. When it turns out no larger cubicle exists, he tells Dilbert to lose weight so his cubicle will appear bigger, and threatens him with a job as the CEO's falcon assistant if he refuses.
punchline: A promotion's reward is a status symbol the company can't actually supply, so the employee must shrink himself to fake it, under the threat of a ridiculous punishment tied to the CEO's absurd private bathroom falcon.
summary: A promotion's promised perk turns out not to exist, so the employee is ordered to slim down to make the illusion work.

title: Thinking Out Loud About Google Buyout

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Google offered to buy our company for $100 million just to get our engineers!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Huh. I wonder if I can convince the other engineers to jump ship today and share $100 million amongst us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did he just say?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing. Just thinking out loud.

situation: The Boss announces that Google offered to buy the company for $100 million purely to acquire its engineers. Dilbert, standing nearby, muses aloud that the engineers could simply quit and split that money among themselves. When the Boss asks what he said, Dilbert claims he was only thinking out loud.
punchline: By boasting that the engineers are the real prize, the Boss accidentally gives them the idea to cut out the company and keep the money, and Dilbert lamely covers his slip.
summary: A boss brags about a tech giant's huge offer for his staff, and an engineer realizes the staff could just take the payout themselves.

file: 2012/2012-06-29_copyright & trademark_farmers & farm workers_violates patents_close compnay_lawyer_off grid_legal.gif
title: Patent Violations Send Lawyer Farming

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Our new product violates 73 Google patents, 14 Apple patents, 52 Oracle patents, and 37 Microsoft patents.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: There is no hope. I recommend that we close the company and become farmers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a lawyer with more fight in him.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: I'm off the grid.

situation: A lawyer holding a tablet tells the Boss that the company's new product infringes hundreds of patents held by Google, Apple, Oracle and Microsoft. He sees no hope and recommends shutting the company down and becoming farmers. The Boss asks for a lawyer with more fight, and the lawyer has already changed into overalls and a straw hat, declaring himself off the grid.
punchline: The lawyer is so convinced the patent situation is hopeless that he immediately quits the legal world and becomes a farmer, proving the Boss's request for a fighter is too late.
summary: Faced with a mountain of patent infringements, a defeatist attorney abandons the company for a life of farming before his boss can ask for a tougher one.

title: Higgs Boson Brings Biblical Warning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gasp! I've found the Higgs boson!

transcript.speaker: Voice from above
transcript.text: Build an ark!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing but trouble.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

setting: Dilbert's lab with a particle experiment on a workbench
situation: Dilbert, in a lab coat, excitedly announces that his equipment has detected the Higgs boson. A lightning bolt and a booming voice, apparently God, orders him to build an ark. Dilbert reacts by switching off the apparatus, concluding that the discovery will bring nothing but trouble.
punchline: The 'God particle' literally provokes a divine response, and since the last time God said to build an ark it meant a catastrophic flood, Dilbert wisely shuts the experiment down.
summary: A scientist's big physics breakthrough triggers a heavenly command that makes him promptly pull the plug on his work.

title: Generous Boss Grants Five Minutes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You did good work this week. I give you permission to leave early today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's five minutes before my normal quitting time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your work was good, not great. Get over yourself.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and magnanimously praises his work, granting him permission to leave early. Dilbert points out that it is only five minutes before his normal quitting time anyway, which the Boss takes as an insult to his generosity.
punchline: The Boss's supposed reward is trivially small, and when Dilbert notices, the Boss turns it into a put-down by claiming the work was only good, not great, so Dilbert shouldn't expect more.
summary: A manager offers a cheap perk that amounts to almost nothing, then belittles the employee for noticing.

title: Elbonian Customer Greeting Etiquette Prank

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Sven, our biggest customer from Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! No handshake. That's an insult. The first time you meet an Elbonian you kiss his mitten.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seriously?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, we're just getting started.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to Sven, a big customer from Elbonia. When Dilbert reaches out to shake hands, the Boss stops him and says the proper Elbonian greeting is to kiss the visitor's mitten. Dilbert bends down to do it, and the Boss says this is only the start of the etiquette.
punchline: The Boss is happily (and perhaps absurdly) demanding increasingly humiliating rituals from employees to appease a valuable customer, implying the kowtowing will only get worse.
summary: A manager makes an employee stoop to kiss a foreign client's mitten to avoid cultural offense, warning that the groveling has barely begun.

title: Wait Until It Peaks, Then Invest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The stock market is up today. I wonder if this is a good time to get in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you wait until it goes up even further, then you'll KNOW it's a good investment.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you still bitter about your last raise?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not as much as I was a minute ago.

setting: Office break area, with the men holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss, looking at his phone, wonders aloud whether it's a good time to start investing in the rising stock market. Dilbert advises him to wait until the market climbs even higher so he can be certain it's a good investment. Wally asks if Dilbert is still bitter about his last raise, and Dilbert says he is a little less bitter than a minute ago.
punchline: Dilbert's advice to buy only once prices have risen further is a bad strategy meant to make the Boss lose money, which eases Dilbert's lingering resentment over his small raise.
summary: A boss mulls buying into a rising market and receives deliberately terrible timing advice from a resentful employee who enjoys the prospect of his loss.

title: Google Beat Boss's Software Bet

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we're going to bet the company on our new software product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: While you were talking, Google created that product, gave it away for free, and killed it for lack of interest.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Is it too soon to take back my fake buy-in?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company will bet everything on its new software product. Dilbert, glancing at his phone, reports that Google has already built the same product, given it away free, and shut it down for lack of interest. A coworker then asks whether he can withdraw the enthusiastic support he faked earlier.
punchline: The coworker's agreement was insincere all along, and now that the product is doomed he wants to back out of it before the failure sticks to him.
summary: A boss stakes the company on a product that a tech giant has already launched and discarded within the span of one speech.

file: 2012/2012-10-16_business ethics_wages_saved company millions_no bonus_ceo plans_500 million_acquisitions_go team_money.gif
title: No Bonus Despite Saving Millions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, your great work this year saved the company $10 million.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I can't give you a bonus because our CEO plans to write down $500 million for acquisitions gone bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go team!

situation: The Boss sits across his desk from Alice and praises her for saving the company $10 million this year. He then explains that she won't get a bonus because the CEO is about to write down $500 million in failed acquisitions. He finishes with a cheerful 'Go team!' while Alice glares at him angrily.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully offers empty team spirit in place of a deserved bonus, because executive blunders have wiped out the value of Alice's real contribution.
summary: A manager praises an employee's huge savings, denies her a reward because of the executive's costly mistakes, and tries to cheer her up with a rallying cry.

title: Competitor Buys Our Software, Freemium

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our competitor just bought ten million copies of our software.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They plan to give it away for free to entice people to buy their own product that has more features.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll be part of their freemium strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's just showing off.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss, who is holding a coffee mug, that a competitor has purchased ten million copies of their company's software. The competitor intends to give those copies away free to lure customers toward its own, more feature-rich product. The Boss reacts only by saying the competitor is showing off.
punchline: The Boss misses the threat that his own product is being used as a free promotional tool for a rival, and instead treats it as mere bragging about the competitor's wealth.
summary: A rival turns your company's own product into a giveaway lure for its better offering, and your manager just sees it as flashy spending.

title: Cubicle Territorial Waters Enforced By Roboshark

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop using the aisle behind my cubicle. It's distracting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Everything within twelve feet of my cubicle are my territorial waters.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't enforce that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Tell that to my Roboshark.

situation: Alice, peering over her cubicle wall, complains that a coworker whistling as he walks down the aisle behind her cubicle is distracting. She declares a twelve-foot zone around her cubicle to be her territorial waters, and when he says she can't enforce it, she points out her Roboshark, a menacing shark-shaped robot on wheels that is now facing him.
punchline: Alice backs up her absurd claim of sovereignty over the aisle with a threatening robotic shark, making her territory enforceable after all.
summary: A cubicle dweller turns the hallway near her desk into her own maritime domain and defends it with a toothy robot.

title: Boss Late, Insults Everyone's Importance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's because the least important thing I do is way more important than all of you put together.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One way to look at it is that I'm great at setting priorities.

situation: The Boss walks into a meeting holding a coffee cup and apologizes for being late. He then explains that even his least important task outranks everyone in the room. He reframes his tardiness as proof of his skill at prioritizing, while Dilbert, Wally and Alice sit and listen.
punchline: The Boss's 'apology' is actually an insult, claiming his trivial activities matter more than his employees, and he spins his lateness as good prioritization.
summary: A tardy manager turns his apology into a boast, announcing that his most trivial chores outrank the entire team.

title: Who Really Works For Whom

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You only do the things I put on your schedule.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And if we consider recent declines in your home's value, I make more money than you do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's your point?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's as if you work for me now.

situation: An employee sitting at her computer tells the Boss that he only does the things she puts on his schedule. She adds that, once the drop in his home's value is counted, she has more net wealth than he does. She concludes that it is effectively as if he works for her now.
punchline: The employee uses the Boss's falling home value to claim she out-earns him, and with his calendar already in her hands, she declares that she is now effectively his boss.
summary: A subordinate argues that she now outranks her manager because she controls his calendar and has become wealthier than he is.

title: Motivated By Rectangular Paper Money

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you feel when I give you positive feedback?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Underpaid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do you feel when I give you negative feedback?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Under-appreciated.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then what motivates you?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The government makes rectangular pieces of paper.

setting: Boss's office, with an establishing shot of the office building
situation: The boss quizzes an employee about how she reacts to positive and then negative feedback, and both answers reveal she feels shortchanged. When he asks what actually motivates her, she points to money, describing it as rectangular pieces of paper made by the government.
punchline: The employee sarcastically reveals that only money motivates her, since praise leaves her underpaid and criticism leaves her underappreciated.
summary: A manager probing for ways to inspire a worker learns that cash is the only thing that moves her.

file: 2012/2012-09-16_emergency_lostphone_company id_keys_critical folder_self generated crisi_dead battery_small brown purse.gif
title: Lost Phone, Missing Purse

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Emergency! I can't find my phone and I'm late for a customer meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe it's with your company I.D. badge that you had to drive all the way home for this morning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It might be with your keys that you lost after lunch.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe it's under the critical folder that you couldn't find before your last meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe it's wherever you created your last self-generated crisis.

transcript.speaker: Woman in purple
transcript.text: I just remembered I put my phone in my purse because the battery is dead.

transcript.speaker: Woman in purple
transcript.text: Has anyone seen a small, brown purse?

situation: A coworker bursts into a meeting panicking that she can't find her phone and is late for a customer meeting. Alice sarcastically suggests she look wherever she has previously lost other things. The coworker then realizes she put the phone in her purse, only to discover she has now lost the purse.
punchline: After being mocked for constantly losing things, the coworker solves one problem only to immediately lose the purse that holds the phone, proving Alice's point.
summary: A habitually disorganized coworker's frantic search for her phone ends with her misplacing the very purse that contains it.

title: Write Your Own Monitoring Software

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have a budget for the network monitoring software you need, so you'll have to write it yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good plan. I'll check back with you when I'm done doing that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your calendar look like in the year 2040?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sort of a grid with square boxes.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert there is no budget for the network monitoring software he needs, so Dilbert must write it himself. Dilbert cheerfully agrees and says he will check back when finished. He then asks the Boss what his calendar looks like in 2040, and the Boss obliviously describes a grid of square boxes.
punchline: Dilbert implies that writing the monitoring software himself will take about three decades, and the clueless Boss misses the sarcasm entirely and answers the question literally.
summary: Told to build his own software because funds are lacking, an engineer sarcastically hints at a decades-long timeline that his oblivious manager fails to grasp.

title: Abstraction Makes Meeting Attendees Weightless

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: The project management framework embodies a project life cycle and five major project management process groups.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Oh no! The extreme level of abstraction has made us weightless!

transcript.speaker: Dark-Haired Coworker
transcript.text: That doesn't even make sense.

setting: Conference room during a project management meeting
situation: In a meeting, a bald coworker recites dense project management jargon about frameworks, life cycles and process groups. Dilbert and the coworker suddenly float up off their chairs, papers and a coffee mug drifting around them, and exclaim that the abstraction has made them weightless. A third coworker, left sitting at the table as they float out of frame, deadpans that it makes no sense.
punchline: The jargon-filled talk is so abstract that it literally lifts people off the ground, and the one grounded listener points out that the whole thing is nonsense, just like the buzzword speech that caused it.
summary: Management buzzwords get so lofty that two meeting attendees float away, while the one left behind complains about the logic.

title: Headphones Fail to Deter Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My headphones will cleverly discourage people from trying to chat with me.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He has headphones. What do we do?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Blow on his neck.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Be careful. He might start flailing his noodle-sized arms in your direction.

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk wearing headphones, confident they will keep coworkers from chatting with him. Asok and Alice approach, and when Asok asks what to do about the headphones, Alice suggests blowing on Dilbert's neck. As Asok leans in, Alice warns him that Dilbert may flail his thin arms at him.
punchline: Dilbert's clever plan to avoid conversation is defeated instantly, since coworkers simply bypass the headphones, and Alice mockingly dismisses his only possible defense as harmless flailing of skinny arms.
summary: A man counts on his headphones to ward off chatty colleagues, but two coworkers cheerfully plot around them and mock his feeble self-defense.

file: 2012/2012-01-23_money_flew to veags_difficult game_few beverages_drop dead_adult bevarages_goaway_est_co workers_pai gow_weekend.gif
title: Hungover Coworker Mocked About Vegas

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard you flew to Vegas and played pai gow all weekend.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Go away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a difficult game to learn after having a few adult beverages.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Drop dead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd you do?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Leave me alone!

situation: Dilbert stands over a coworker's desk holding a coffee mug and cheerfully brings up the coworker's weekend trip to Vegas playing pai gow. The coworker, who appears hungover and irritable, repeatedly tells him to go away. Dilbert keeps prodding with remarks about drinking and gambling until the coworker snaps and spills his coffee.
punchline: Dilbert pretends to be making friendly small talk but deliberately needles his clearly hungover, gambling-loser coworker until he cracks, implying the guy lost money and is in no state to discuss it.
summary: A man keeps chatting about a colleague's boozy gambling weekend until the miserable, hungover victim finally explodes.

title: Dogbert's Radio Show Insults Everything

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Customers are threatening to boycott us if we continue to advertise on Dogbert's radio show.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert insulted every man, woman, child, and organic substance in the known universe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He called the moon something that rhymes with totem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Modem?

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that customers are threatening to boycott the company over its advertising on Dogbert's radio show. He explains that Dogbert has insulted absolutely everyone and everything, even the moon. The Boss, trying to guess the rude word Dogbert used, offers a wrong answer.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he guesses 'modem' as the insulting word that rhymes with 'totem', missing the obvious vulgar answer ('bottom').
summary: A manager is told that a radio host's universal insults are costing the company customers, and he responds with a naive guess at the offending rhyme.

file: 2012/2012-09-03_anger_apathy_computer programmers_preventer of information_business case_teamwork seminar_goldfish crackers.gif
title: Mordac Feeds on Dilbert's Anger

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I, Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services, reject your business case because you used the old template.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Ha ha ha! I feed on your anger and frustration! And now I will eat like a king!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good luck with that. I've been dead on the inside since the teamwork seminar.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Sheesh. I'm living on goldfish crackers.

situation: Mordac, head of Information Services, rejects Dilbert's business case on a petty technicality: he used the old template. Mordac gleefully announces that he feeds on Dilbert's anger and frustration, but Dilbert is emotionally numb and gives him nothing to feed on. Mordac is left snacking on goldfish crackers.
punchline: Dilbert has been so emotionally drained by corporate life (specifically a teamwork seminar) that he has no anger left for Mordac to feed on, leaving the petty bureaucrat hungry.
summary: A bureaucrat who thrives on his victims' rage goes hungry when his target is already too numb from workplace training to react.

title: Acquaintance Price Chart for Birthday Collection

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm collecting money for Scott's birthday present.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me check my acquaintance price chart to see what he's worth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have change for used gum?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you want it in lint or bent staples?

situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut approaches Dilbert, collecting money for a colleague's birthday present. Dilbert consults a chart on his phone to decide how much the person is worth, then offers used gum and asks for change. The coworker plays along by offering change in lint or bent staples.
punchline: Dilbert values the colleague's friendship at essentially nothing, offering used gum, and the collector answers with equally worthless 'change' in lint or bent staples.
summary: A cheapskate Dilbert consults a chart to price a mere acquaintance and pays with trash, and the fundraiser snarks back with junk change.

file: 2012/2012-03-17_civil liberties_internet & world wide web_internet law_bad for business_press relase_impinge_freedom of speech_selfish liars.gif
title: Selfish Liars Defend Free Speech

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company opposes passage of the new internet law because it would be bad for our business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that sounds selfish, so we'll issue a press release saying the new law would impinge freedom of speech.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So... we're selfish liars?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't get more free than that!

situation: At a meeting, the Boss explains that the company opposes a new internet law because it would hurt business. Since that sounds selfish, he decides to publicly claim the law threatens freedom of speech. Alice summarizes this as being selfish liars, and the Boss proudly says that is about as free as it gets.
punchline: The Boss twists the idea of freedom of speech into the freedom to lie shamelessly for corporate self-interest, treating his own dishonesty as a virtue.
summary: A company disguises its profit motive as a principled stand on free expression, and the boss cheerfully accepts the label of liar.

file: 2012/2012-05-21_bluetooth_bluetooth headset_cyborg_doctors_ear_full human_happiness_intraocular lenses_inventions_pill form_powered by chemistry_streaming video_surgically enbed_vision correction_dentits_special surgery_psychology.gif
title: Cyborg Dreams, Doctor Prescribes Pills

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know I'd be happier as a cyborg than a full human.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want you to surgically embed a Bluetooth headset in my ear, powered by my own body chemistry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I'd like intra-ocular lenses with vision correction and streaming video over Bluetooth.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Happiness only comes in pill form.

setting: A doctor's office, with Dilbert lying on an exam table
situation: Dilbert lies on an exam table and tells his doctor he would be happier as a cyborg. He requests a surgically implanted Bluetooth headset powered by his body chemistry, then adds eye lenses that stream video. The doctor ignores the request and says happiness only comes as a pill.
punchline: Dilbert wants elaborate cybernetic upgrades to feel happy, but the doctor dismisses it all and reduces happiness to a prescription antidepressant.
summary: A man asks his physician for tech implants to become a cyborg, and the physician answers that contentment is only dispensed as medication.

title: Brilliant Diagram From Unqualified Woman

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm not trained as an engineer, but I think this diagram might solve your problem.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Ooh! This is brilliant! It's hard to believe you have no qualifications whatsoever!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Is that sarcasm?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Ignorance is underrated!

situation: A big-haired woman with no engineering training hands an engineer a diagram she believes could solve his problem. The engineer is delighted by how good it is and gushes that it's hard to believe she has no qualifications. She asks whether he is being sarcastic, and he replies that ignorance is underrated.
punchline: The engineer's praise for her lack of qualifications is barbed, but his claim that ignorance is underrated suggests he genuinely values an outsider's untainted perspective, leaving it ambiguous whether he is being sarcastic or sincere.
summary: An outsider with no technical background offers a diagram that impresses a skeptical engineer, whose compliments land awkwardly close to insult.

title: Executive Team Blames Everything Else

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new executive team got together and figured out the source of all of our problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the problem that the executive team keeps changing, and that means the company strategy keeps changing?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Is the problem that all of our meetings turn awkward?

setting: Conference room during an executive meeting
situation: The Boss announces that his new executive team has identified the root cause of the company's problems. Dilbert suggests the real cause is the constantly changing executive team, which makes company strategy change constantly. A bald executive with glasses responds by offering an entirely different and trivial problem: awkward meetings.
punchline: Dilbert points to the obvious root cause of constant executive turnover and strategy churn, but the executives dodge accountability by blaming something trivial like awkward meetings.
summary: Leadership proudly claims to have found the cause of the company's troubles, but when the real culprit is named, they pivot to a far less threatening explanation.

title: Dogbert Gives Gift of Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Merry Christmas. I got you the gift of absolutely nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nothing to unwrap, nothing to clutter the house, nothing to return, nothing to assemble, and not a single thing to feel guilty about.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You totally get me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It was the least I could do.

setting: Dilbert's home kitchen table on Christmas morning
situation: Dilbert, in a green bathrobe holding a coffee mug, sits at a table with Dogbert on Christmas. Dogbert announces that his gift is absolutely nothing and lists all the hassles it spares Dilbert. Dilbert is genuinely pleased, and Dogbert says it was the least he could do.
punchline: Dogbert's gift of nothing is both a lazy non-gift and, to introverted Dilbert, the perfect present, and his closing line doubles as a pun on doing the bare minimum.
summary: On Christmas morning, Dogbert presents his owner with an empty gift that spares him every holiday hassle, and the grateful recipient calls it perfect.

title: Feng Shui Consultant Replaced by Wizard

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The feng shui consultant you asked for is overbooked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I found a guy who is heavily into astrology, black magic, and voodoo.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you trying to tell me something?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask him. He's also psychic.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the feng shui consultant he requested is booked up. As a substitute, Dilbert brings in a wizard in a starry robe and pointy hat who practices astrology, black magic, and voodoo. When the Boss suspects a hidden message, Dilbert suggests asking the wizard, since he is also psychic.
punchline: Dilbert implies he is hinting that the Boss deserves a hex, and sarcastically tells him to let the psychic wizard figure out the real message.
summary: A manager's request for office decorating advice gets filled by a robed sorcerer, and his suspicion that it's a veiled insult is met with a deadpan suggestion to consult the mind-reading mystic.

file: 2012/2012-12-23_fear_managers & supervisors_snake_cublicle_culture of fear_motivate_short term_first step_urinals_electrified_office plant_pain_tactics_business.gif
title: Culture of Fear Motivation Tactics

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you find the snake in your cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I put it there because I'm trying to motivate you with a culture of fear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That only works in the short term!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A leader takes the first step without knowing where the next step will be.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So get to work. And by the way, one of the urinals is electrified.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's only set to stun, so don't be a baby about it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: His office plant is clear.

situation: Dilbert screams after finding a snake in his cubicle. The Boss admits he planted it to motivate employees through a culture of fear, and when Dilbert objects that fear only works short term, the Boss answers with leadership platitudes and then reveals that a urinal has been electrified. Wally casually mentions that the Boss's own office plant is safe.
punchline: The Boss's absurdly hostile motivation tactics escalate to booby-trapping the restroom, while Wally calmly notes the one place that is safe is the Boss's own office, hinting that the Boss is protecting himself while terrorizing everyone else.
summary: A manager sabotages his staff with a hidden reptile and a rigged restroom fixture in a misguided attempt to inspire productivity through terror.

file: 2012/2012-12-06_happiness_work ethic_career advice_work hard_destroy helath_personal life_happiness advice_psychology.gif
title: Career Advice Costs You Happiness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice, do you have any valuable career advice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Work so hard that it destroys your health and crowds out any chance of having a personal life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't that make me... unhappy?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You didn't ask for happiness advice.

setting: Office break area by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert asks Alice for career advice while they stand near the coffee machine. Alice tells him to work so hard that he ruins his health and has no personal life. When Dilbert points out that this would make him unhappy, Alice replies that he only asked about careers, not happiness.
punchline: Alice treats career success and personal well-being as entirely separate, implying that getting ahead requires sacrificing your happiness and that she sees nothing wrong with that.
summary: Asked how to get ahead at work, Alice recommends total self-sacrifice and then shrugs off the misery it would cause.

title: Ignoring Questions Leaves Boss Thinking Success

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your Pointy-Haired Boss wants to know if you tested the new 3-D printer yet.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why aren't you answering my question?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What-ever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Success.

situation: Alice stands at Dilbert's cubicle and asks whether he has tested the new 3-D printer, relaying a question from the Boss. Dilbert sips his coffee and says nothing, so Alice demands to know why he won't answer, then gives up and storms off. The Boss peeks over the cubicle wall, thinking 'Success,' as if he wanted the two of them to clash.
punchline: The Boss quietly considers it a win that his employees ended up irritated with each other rather than getting any actual answer about the printer.
summary: A silent coworker frustrates the colleague sent to question him, and the manager who engineered the encounter secretly counts the friction as a triumph.
